📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that when we think of the Solar System, we often view it as a self-contained entity, isolated from its cosmic neighborhood. However, scientists have long known that the planets of the Solar System are subject to activity in nearby star systems, including supernovae and other energetic astrophysical events. For example, it is established that intermediate elements and the heaviest elements on the periodic table are created when stars reach the end of their life cycle and explode, sending their outer layers (with these elements) into space.

Industry observers note that these include intermediate elements ranging from carbon and oxygen to iron, nickel, and radioactive isotopes thereof, as well as heavy elements like zinc, silver, tin, gold, mercury, lead, platinum, and uranium. At the Helmholtz-Zentrum Dresden-Rossendorf (HZDR), Prof. Anton Wallner and his team have debuted the SUPREME project to uncover traces of these elements. Their goal is to use them to reconstruct the history of cosmic events in our neighborhood and shed light on how the heaviest elements are created in nature.

The project was recently awarded a â¬3 million grant ($3.29 million USD) through the European Research Council's (ERC) Advanced Grants program. Prof. Wallner and his team were one of 319 leading research groups across Europe selected for funding totaling â¬838 million ($918.86 million USD) to pursue projects that could lead to major scientific breakthroughs. The SUPREME project aims to address two fundamental questions in modern astrophysics, focusing on the past 500 million years.

First, there's the question of how nearby supernovae have affected Earth and biological evolution since the Cambrian Period (ca. 538.8 to 485 million years ago), the geological era that coincided with the rapid explosion of complex marine life (aka. the Cambrian Explosion). When the Cambrian began, the continents were largely located in the southern hemisphere and were mostly barren. But as the period progressed and gave way to subsequent geological eras, life began to emerge from the oceans, giving rise to plants, mammals, dinosaurs, and eventually primates.

Supernovae, when they happen in our cosmic neighborhood, distribute heavy elements like gold, platinum, lead, and zinc to Earth. Credit: NASA.

Second, there's the question of how the heaviest elements in the Universe are created and distributed; in this case, to the Earth and Moon. To answer these questions, researchers at the SUPREME project will search for extremely rare radioactive isotopes in lunar samples provided by NASA, deep-sea sediments, ice cores, and other geological archives. These archives preserve the history of interstellar material that arrived on Earth over eons, allowing scientists to identify and date nearby supernovae and other nearby energetic events.

Industry observers note that their work will build on the first detection of radioactive isotopes created by a rapid neutron-capture (r-process) event in history, the process by which about half of all atoms heavier than iron are created in the Universe. This occured in June 2026, when scientists from the HZDR made the first significant measurement of curium-247 and plutonium-244 in interstellar matter trapped on Earth. As Prof. Sebastian M. Schmidt, the Scientific Director of HZDR who led the discovery team, said in an HZDR statement:.

This award is a remarkable recognition of Anton Wallner's internationally leading research. SUPREME addresses fundamental questions about the origin of the elements and the history of our cosmic environment while building on measurement capabilities that are unique worldwide. We are proud that this pioneering work is being carried out at HZDR.

Industry observers note that to detect and measure rare radioactive isotopes, the researchers will use HAMSTER (Helmholtz Accelerator Mass Spectrometer Tracing Environmental Radionuclides), a latest state-of-the-art accelerator mass spectrometry (AMS) facility developed by Wallner and his team and installed at HZDR in 2025. Combined with an innovative laser-based technology that dramatically reduces measurement background, the team will be able to detect individual atoms with unprecedented sensitivity, opening new possibilities for astrophysics and other scientific applications.

The results of this project are expected to provide unprecedented insights into the history of our cosmic neighborhood and its possible influence on Earth's geology and species evolution. "Securing one of the European Union's most competitive research grants is an outstanding accomplishment," said Saxony's Minister of Science, Sebastian Gemkow. "This distinction is not only a major milestone in the recipients' scientific careers, but also a significant gain for Saxony as a leading research and innovation hub.".

His work is featured in The Ross 248 Project and Interstellar Travel edited by NASA alumni Les Johnson and Ken Roy. He also hosts the podcast series Stories from Space on Patreon. #77250. Tech Report: Just 2 Weeks of Ultraprocessed Foods May Change How Your Brains Respond to Food

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1226 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Scitechdaily ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Just 2 Weeks of Ultraprocessed Foods May Change How Your Brains Respond to Food

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1226 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Just two weeks of eating ultraprocessed foods may be enough to alter how the developing brain responds to rewarding foods.
  • It has been revealed that “Among the younger participants, consuming a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks was associated with decreased brain response to a rewarding food — a milkshake — in the orbitofrontal cortex,” said Emma Leslie, the study’s first author.
  • Sources indicate that the orbitofrontal cortex helps the brain evaluate rewards, make decisions, and regulate eating behavior.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Just two weeks of eating ultraprocessed foods may be enough to alter how the developing brain responds to rewarding foods. In a Virginia Tech study, adults ages 18 to 21 showed reduced activity in a brain region involved in food rewards and decision-making after following a diet rich in ultraprocessed products. Participants aged 22 to 25 showed no significant changes.

It has been revealed that “Among the younger participants, consuming a diet high in ultraprocessed foods for just two weeks was associated with decreased brain response to a rewarding food — a milkshake — in the orbitofrontal cortex,” said Emma Leslie, the study’s first author. The findings, published in the journal Obesity, suggest that sensitivity to ultraprocessed foods may vary even within a relatively narrow age range.

Sources indicate that the orbitofrontal cortex helps the brain evaluate rewards, make decisions, and regulate eating behavior. It is also among the last brain regions to fully mature, with development continuing into the mid to late 20s. “The orbitofrontal cortex is still undergoing development in all of our participants, but the younger you are, the more rapid the development,” said neuroscientist Alex DiFeliceantonio of Virginia Tech’s Fralin Biomedical Research Institute at VTC. “It’s also an area of the brain that has been shown to be active in people who are dieting or who are trying to reduce their craving for high-calorie foods.”.

The brain findings build on earlier results from the same experiment. Researchers previously found that participants ages 18 to 21 consumed more calories after following the ultraprocessed diet, even when they were not hungry. Older participants did not show the same pattern. “This was especially interesting given our previous findings showing that younger participants also consumed more calories at a buffet-style meal after the ultraprocessed diet,” Leslie mentioned. “Together, these findings raise interesting questions about whether certain developmental periods may be particularly sensitive to ultraprocessed food exposure.”.

Recent findings suggest that to investigate the effects of food processing, researchers recruited 22 adults ages 18 to 25, including seven who were 21 or younger. Each participant completed two dietary interventions lasting two weeks each, separated by a four-week break. The order of the diets was randomly assigned.

One diet contained no ultraprocessed foods, while the other supplied 81 percent of calories from ultraprocessed products. Both provided identical proportions of carbohydrates (50 percent), fat (35 percent), and protein (15 percent). Researchers also matched fiber, added sugar, saturated fat, sodium, energy density, and overall nutritional quality. Calorie intake was adjusted to maintain each participant’s weight, allowing the team to examine the effects of food processing without major differences in nutritional composition or weight change.

In a recent development, before and after each dietary period, participants underwent functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), which measures changes in blood oxygenation associated with brain activity. During the scans, a pump delivered either a highly processed milkshake or a tasteless solution through a straw-like device. Among younger participants, the orbitofrontal cortex responded less strongly to the milkshake after the ultraprocessed diet, but its response increased after the diet without ultraprocessed foods. Neither diet produced significant changes in the older group.

Sources indicate that because the diets were closely matched nutritionally, conventional measures of dietary quality did not readily explain the observed differences. “The diets were matched on macronutrients, energy density, and micronutrients, so it’s something other than nutrition that is leading to changes in the brain and behavior,” DiFeliceantonio said. “Could it be additives? Chemicals produced during the processing itself? It’s an open question.”.

Industry observers note that ultraprocessed foods often contain industrially manufactured ingredients or additives that are uncommon in home kitchens. Researchers have not determined whether particular ingredients, processing methods, or combinations of factors explain the brain changes observed in this trial. In the United States, ultraprocessed products account for more than half of young adults’ diets. Their consumption has also been associated with metabolic syndrome, cardiovascular problems, and other health conditions, although such associations do not establish that processing itself causes those outcomes.

The orbitofrontal cortex is involved not only in evaluating food rewards but also in decisions that can influence when someone stops eating. “This study is important because you have this change in an area of the brain known to govern self-control and potentially put a stop to eating,” DiFeliceantonio mentioned. “This is giving us insight into how ultraprocessed foods are affecting the bodies and brains of younger people, who might be especially vulnerable to their effects. And that’s important to know for things like dietary guidelines, doctor recommendations, and policy decisions.”.

However, the researchers found no association between participants’ diet-related changes in brain responses and changes in how much they ate. Although younger adults highlighted differences in both measures, the study did not establish that altered orbitofrontal activity caused increased calorie consumption. The neurological and behavioral effects could involve separate or overlapping mechanisms that require further investigation.

The study included only 22 participants, and just seven belonged to the younger age group. The age-related findings were exploratory, meaning they were identified through analyses that require confirmation in larger studies. Researchers also cannot yet determine whether the observed brain changes persist, reverse after dietary changes, or influence eating habits over longer periods.

According to recent reports, “The intervention lasted only two weeks, so we don’t know whether these changes persist over time or translate into long-term differences in eating behavior,” Leslie said. Future experiments will need to examine whether the effects remain after participants resume their usual diets and whether similar changes occur consistently across larger and more diverse populations.

Recent findings suggest that diFeliceantonio and Virginia Tech nutrition researcher Brenda Davy hope to extend their work to people younger than 18, whose brains are undergoing more rapid development. “In the U.S., adolescents have the poorest overall dietary quality and consume more ultraprocessed foods than any other age group,” Davy stated. “Dietary habits are established early in life and typically persist into adulthood. We hope to continue to study how highly processed foods affect young people’s eating habits and health, which ultimately could impact dietary guidelines for this age group.”.

Leslie, who completed her doctorate at Virginia Tech and continued her research as a postdoctoral associate at the University of Michigan, is also examining how ultraprocessed foods influence reward-related behavior. “I’ll be investigating the addictive potential of ultraprocessed foods and exploring food policy strategies to address challenges in the modern food environment,” Leslie stated. “Ultimately, I hope this work will help identify who may be most vulnerable, why, and how we can better support healthier eating behaviors.”.

Reference: “Effects of Controlled Diets High in and Free of Ultraprocessed Food on the Brain of Emerging Adults” by Emma H. Leslie, Maria L. M. Rego, Monica Ahrens, Wenjing Yu, Mary Elizabeth Baugh, Anastasia Groccia, Rhianna M. Sullivan, Han Lee, Ryann Kolb, Delbert L. Herald, Collin Gregg, Valisa E. Hedrick, Kevin P. Davy, Benjamin Katz, Brenda M. Davy and Alexandra G. DiFeliceantonio, 18 November 2026, Obesity. DOI: 10.1002/oby.70341.

The research was supported by a grant to DiFeliceantonio and Davy from the Eunice Kennedy Shriver National Institute of Child Health and Human Development, part of the National Institutes of Health. Leslie was also supported with an exercise health sciences graduate fellowship from Dr. Ray A. Gaskins.

Scientists Discover That a Simple Change in Walking Habits Could Improve Blood Sugar Control

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (504 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have discovered that a simple change in how daily exercise is distributed could improve blood sugar control, particularly in people at risk of type 2 diabetes.
  • How you distribute exercise throughout the day may influence how well your body regulates blood sugar.
  • The differences emerged after six weeks, despite both groups performing similar amounts of physical activity and burning comparable amounts of energy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have discovered that a simple change in how daily exercise is distributed could improve blood sugar control, particularly in people at risk of type 2 diabetes.

How you distribute exercise throughout the day may influence how well your body regulates blood sugar. A randomized trial published in Obesity found that frequent, short walks improved several measures of glucose regulation more than completing the same amount of walking in one continuous session.

The differences emerged after six weeks, despite both groups performing similar amounts of physical activity and burning comparable amounts of energy.

Industry observers note that researchers recruited 30 inactive adults with overweight or obesity who reported sitting for more than six hours daily. Participants were assigned to complete 45 minutes of brisk walking five days per week for six weeks, either in one continuous session or in approximately five-minute breaks spread throughout the day.

According to recent reports, continuous glucose monitoring indicated that the short-walk group increased its time within the target blood sugar range from 82% to 94%. In contrast, the continuous-walking group experienced a decline from 89% to 80%.

Participants taking frequent walking breaks also had more stable glucose levels, largely because they experienced fewer unusually low readings rather than lower average or peak blood sugar levels.

Industry observers note that laboratory tests showed that participants who took frequent walking breaks experienced more favorable changes in glucose tolerance, indicating differences in how their bodies cleared glucose from the bloodstream. However, neither approach produced a detectable improvement in insulin sensitivity.

Researchers suggest that repeated muscle activity may influence glucose uptake and utilization, although the exact mechanisms remain uncertain.

According to recent reports, “Our findings suggest that how we distribute physical activity throughout the day may be just as important as how much we do,” said corresponding author Audrey Bergouignan, PhD, Director of Research at the French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS) and Associate Professor at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus. “Rather than relying solely on a single exercise session, regularly interrupting prolonged sitting with short walks may offer additional benefits for blood glucose regulation, especially in people at risk of developing type 2 diabetes.”.

The findings suggest that interrupting prolonged sitting may offer glucose regulation benefits beyond those associated with total exercise duration.

Recent findings suggest that however, the trial was small and lasted only six weeks. It also lacked a non-exercise control group, and participants’ diets were not controlled during glucose monitoring. Further research is needed to determine whether these improvements translate into long-term health benefits, particularly for people with prediabetes or type 2 diabetes.

It has been revealed that reference: “Interrupting Prolonged Sitting Improves Glucose Regulation More Than Continuous Walking in Adults With Overweight/Obesity” by Ana J. Pinto, Nathan P. De Jong, Josiane L. Broussard, Chantal Simon, Carlos Mendez, Andrew H. Lange, Laura Schreck, Zhaoxing Pan, Daniel H. Bessesen and Audrey Bergouignan, 18 November 2026, Obesity. DOI: 10.1002/oby.70349.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Why late November 2026 is prime Uranus observing season.

Recent findings suggest that the outer planets are ever so slowly starting to sneak back into the evening sky this month. First, Saturn crossed this mark last month on October 4th, then Neptune followed suit on September 26th. Now, the planet Uranus makes the transition, crossing opposition next week.

Opposition occurs on November 25th. On âU.S. Thanksgiving-eve.â We say âoppositionâ for an outer planet, as a point at which it seems to rise âoppositeâ to the setting Sun as seen from our Earthly vantage point. Orbiting the Sun at a leisurely pace once every 84 years, Uranus has a synodic period of 370 days, meaning oppositions for the planet only slide forward about five days each year. This year sees Uranus reach opposition in the astronomical constellation of Taurus, between the Hyades and the Pleiades open star clusters.

Uranus at opposition for 2026. Credit: Stellarium.

Shout out to the Full November Beaver Moon nearby on the same date as opposition 2026, fresh off of occulting the Pleiades for the Arctic on November 24th.

It has been revealed that uranus reached aphelion 20 Astronomical Units (AU) from the Sun in 2009, and is now inbound toward perihelion 18.3 AU distant in 2050. In 2033, Uranus will pass the point in Taurus where it was discovered by Sir William Herschel on March 13th, 1781, between the horns of the Bull very near the constellation's border with Gemini. Uranus made spurious appearances on star charts of the era at least 20 times prior to discovery.

The discovery position of Uranus. Credit: Dave Dickinson/Starry Night.

Uranus reached its southernmost point in the sky in 2007, and crossed the celestial equator multiple times from 2011-2012. Uranus crosses the ecliptic plane northward in 2029. Uranus reaches its northernmost in 2032, and then begins the long trek southward. The Moon wonât resume occulting the planet Uranus again until a cycle starting on September 29th, 2029.

The Moon occults the Pleiades on November 24th. Credit: Occult 4.2.

Observing +5.5 magnitude Uranus is as easy as sweeping the suspect field at low power, and looking for a blue-green âstarâ that obstinately refuses to snap into focus. To my eye, Uranus looks like a tiny planetary nebula or perhaps a distant fuzzy comet. In fact, thatâs exactly what Herschel thought heâd first discovered, back on that fortuitous night in 1781. He later correctly realized after following the new object for several nights that it was a distant, and therefore intrinsically large object far out in the solar system beyond Saturn, then thought to mark its outer boundary. All of this happened in his backyard garden in Bath, England. We can, however, be thankful that the name âGeorgeâ that Herschel proposed to honor his benefactor King George the III didnât stick (!).

It has been revealed that one of Herschel's speculum metal mirrors and telescopes at the London Science Museum. Credit: Dave Dickinson.

Sources indicate that can you see Uranus with the naked eye? Topping +6th magnitude near opposition, itâs knocking on naked eye visibility from a good dark sky site. At the eyepiece, Uranus only shows a 4â disk at around opposition, barely resolvable with a telescope and tough to tease out detail.

Industry observers note that A fine capture of Uranus from 2017. Credit: Szabolcs Nagy.

Uranus is tipped over 98 degrees (prograde) on its side, the result of some ancient encounter with another large body early in the solar systemâs history. Currently, weâre staring nearly directly at the rotational (north?) pole/hemisphere of the planet, which will be pointed nearly directly towards us in late 2029.

Challenge: Catching the Uranian Moons.

Though Uranus has 29 known moons, only five are within potential reach of amateur telescopes, with +13.9 magnitude Titania being the brightest. Orbiting Uranus once every 8.7 days, Titania reaches a greatest elongation of 28â from Uranus. We once saw a sharp view of the moons observing through the Steward Observatoryâs Kuiper Telescope in the Santa Catalina Mountains outside of Tucson, Arizona. They were a surprisingly easy catch through the enormous 61â telescope.

A fine capture of Uranus and its moons. Credit: Ralph Smyth.

A planetarium program such as Stellarium and Starry Night will show you the current orientation of the moons of Uranus, to help parse them out from any nearby background stars.

Sources indicate that the orbits an orientations of the major Uranian moons. Credit: Starry Night.

According to recent reports, the orbits of the moons are at the moment nearly perpendicular to our view in 2026, though theyâre edge-on and can transit Uranus as seen from our view once every 42 years. This last occurred on 2006-2009, and will happen again starting around 2048.

Industry observers note that hubble captures a shadow transit of Ariel in 2006. Credit: NASA/ESA/L. Sromovsky/University of Wisconsin.

Will we return to Uranus in the coming years? To date, only one mission has seen the planet close up: NASAâs Voyager 2, which flew past Uranus and its moons in 1986. Cassini-style orbiters have been proposed, though such a mission would be a lengthy affair, needing to first make the trip to the distant ice giant then slow down to enter orbit. As it stands, such a mission would be feasible for around the 2040s time frame.

According to recent reports, JWST's view of Uranus and its rings. Credit: NASA/JWST.

Recent findings suggest that certainly, Uranus calls out for a dedicated mission. But you can explore the planet yourself tonight as it nears opposition for 2026.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prepare for fellow guests to go back for seconds when you bring these editor-approved dishes to the function.

There’s an inherent camaraderie in potluck dinners that makes it one of the best ways to feast. And, whether it’s Friendsgiving or an anytime dinner party, potlucks make hosting more of a group effort and a participatory activity. The final dish lineup is often greater than the sum of its parts, thanks to the personal efforts of each of the guests.

According to recent reports, granted, hosts should keep track of what categories (sweet, savory) they have designated or delegated to their guests in order to avoid a smorgasbord of, say, 12 onion dips (although that sounds like heaven to me). Otherwise, enjoy the far more unbuttoned, go-with-the-flow glow of a holiday potluck dinner, which thrives when it rounds up travel-friendly feuilletés, pillowy focaccia loaves, and vegetarian-friendly options.

Below, the Eater staff chimed on a handful of our annual favorites.

Sources indicate that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Making this appetizer is kind of like making a giant sandwich (positive). The feuilleté is filled with layered, thin slices of ham, Swiss cheese, and Dijon mustard, and given a nice heavy cream-and-egg wash sheen. If I have time, I’ll head to my local cheese shop and see what Swiss varieties the mongers are excited about, but I also love the ease of using a pre-sliced cheese [assumes Sandra Lee voice] from the grocery store. My favorite is Sargento’s baby Swiss for its mild, nutty flavor and creamy texture. I should also mention that this appetizer is easy to transport; you can cut it into a million tiny squares if you’re attending a massive party, or several larger squares if it’s a more intimate event. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Recent findings suggest that this is a bit of a project dish, perfect for a competitive friendsgiving or a cold weather potluck with a collection of amazing home cooks. Don’t skip the fried garlic breadcrumb topping, I think it completes this luscious macaroni and cheese. But I’ve also had plenty of friends adjust this recipe for picky family members, just using the incredible bechamel cheese sauce without all the herbs and garlic topping. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

Sources indicate that dirty martinis have never been dirtier or more ubiquitous (at least not in my elder millennial lifetime) and, like the Caesar, the briny, olive-y flavor has become a format that can be replicated in other edible forms. (Dirty martini deviled eggs, hello.) This dirty martini dip is a perennial fave for the savory snackers; it’s a classic cream-cheese-based party dip but with substantial flavor. I like it with ridged chips, like Ruffles. I always serve it at my annual holiday party to rave reviews. Would be incredible alongside a caviar service! — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

Deb Perelman, Smitten Kitchen; Shilpa Uskokovic, Bon Appétit.

It has been revealed that I love to cook, but I’m generally not much of a baker — I don’t generally have the patience for fiddly presentation or precise measurements, and given I lack a sweet tooth, there isn’t a ton of motivation for that to change. The one exception is bread, where I’ve steadily improved my game over the years, and I’ve found focaccia to be a welcome addition to any potluck. I have a standard recipe from a bread-making class that I tend to default to, but sometimes the occasion requires something more festive. In those instances, I turn to variations like this bagel-esque concoction from Smitten Kitchen (a great addition to any brunch spread), or this cacio e pepe twist from Bon Appétit, which adds a bit more zip and character to a standard focaccia recipe. And if you have less of an aversion to fiddly-ness than I do, just Google “decorative focaccia” to see how people much more artistic than I am fashion flowers from tomatoes, rosemary, and onion slices to top their breads — if you really want to show off. — Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Sources indicate that back when I was deep in my potluck moment, a friend at a gathering once remarked, “You love a phyllo pie.” It was then that I sheepishly realized that I did, having brought one to several gatherings this friend had attended. There are many reasons for that. They travel well: You can pack the pie up still in the springform to provide support during the journey. They’re easy to prep: You can make the fillings ahead of time and assemble the day of. And they’re not very fussy when you arrive at your destination: Simply ask your host if you can pop it in the oven briefly, and at this time of year, you can almost always glom the warmth off something else that’s in there.

The recipe that set me off on this course came from Ottolenghi’s Shelf Love. It features cauliflower in a thick cheese sauce, making it perfect for the colder months when people want hearty food. I’ve found that the concept is welcoming to many different vegetables and all kinds of cheese; I’ve swapped in mushrooms and beans, or added caramelized onions or leeks, or taken liberties with Gruyère and greens. At gatherings with attendees who are vegan or lactose-intolerant, I’ve made them dairy-free (store-bought phyllo is generally vegan). In warmer months, or when I’d rather bring a skillet instead of a loaded springform, I opt for an approach to phyllo pie more like this spanakopita-esque recipe from Hetty McKinnon. But the format pairs well with many vegetables, and I always want to make sure to keep the vegetarians at the potluck well-fed. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Industry News: A Common Meat Triggers a Unique Muscle-Building Peptide, Study Finds

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (803 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A latest study found that lean ground pork triggered a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle growth.
  • In a recent development, A newly introduced study suggests that the way the body processes protein after exercise may depend on more than how much protein a meal contains.
  • Published in Molecular Nutrition & Food Research, the research examined how different protein sources affect amino acids and peptides circulating in the bloodstream after resistance exercise.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A latest study found that lean ground pork triggered a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle growth.

In a recent development, A newly introduced study suggests that the way the body processes protein after exercise may depend on more than how much protein a meal contains. Researchers found that lean ground pork produced a distinctive increase in a naturally occurring peptide linked to muscle protein synthesis, the biological process responsible for building and repairing muscle proteins.

Published in Molecular Nutrition & Food Research, the research examined how different protein sources affect amino acids and peptides circulating in the bloodstream after resistance exercise. The findings suggest that the structure and composition of whole foods may influence how protein is digested and made available to the body.

Researchers at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign analyzed blood samples and muscle protein synthesis measurements from two randomized controlled trials involving healthy young adults.

Industry observers note that following resistance exercise, participants consumed one of five nutritional treatments: low-fat ground pork, high-fat ground pork, black beans and rice, an isolated nutrient beverage containing amino acids and other nutrients, or a carbohydrate-only control drink. Each protein-containing treatment supplied approximately 20 grams (0.7 ounces) of protein, allowing researchers to compare the body’s responses to different nutritional sources.

Among the five treatments, lean ground pork was the only one to produce a statistically significant increase above baseline in circulating dileucine, a peptide composed of two linked leucine molecules. Blood concentrations rose approximately 90 to 120 minutes after consumption. Dileucine has been associated with muscle protein synthesis, although scientists are still investigating its specific role in muscle metabolism.

In a recent development, peak dileucine concentrations after lean ground pork consumption were significantly higher than those measured after the isolated nutrient beverage and carbohydrate control. However, the differences compared with high-fat ground pork and the beans-and-rice meal were not statistically significant.

Recent findings suggest that lean ground pork also produced the highest peak concentrations of leucine, an essential amino acid involved in regulating muscle protein synthesis. These levels were significantly higher than those following high-fat ground pork, beans and rice, or the carbohydrate control, but were not significantly different from the isolated nutrient beverage.

“These findings suggest that the body’s response to protein is influenced by more than the amount consumed,” remarked Nicholas A. Burd, PhD, corresponding author and researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign. “Seeing how the whole-food matrix affects the release of amino acids and peptides into the bloodstream gives us a clearer picture of how dietary protein may actually drive muscle protein synthesis and remodeling.”.

Across the protein-containing treatments, researchers identified a modest but statistically significant positive relationship between peak dileucine concentrations and changes in muscle protein synthesis. The same association was not observed with conventional leucine measurements.

Importantly, this does not establish that dileucine directly stimulates muscle growth or that lean ground pork produces greater muscle gains than other foods.

In a recent development, one possible explanation involves the food matrix, which encompasses a food’s physical structure and the interactions among its components. Researchers proposed that grinding meat could disrupt connective tissue, potentially making proteins more accessible to digestive enzymes and changing how amino acids and peptides enter the bloodstream.

It has been revealed that the results add to research investigating how whole-food protein sources influence the body’s response to exercise. Although the protein content of a meal remains relevant, differences in food structure, fat content, and digestion may affect the timing and composition of nutrients reaching the bloodstream.

According to recent reports, “Consumers often think about protein in terms of how many grams are on their plate, but science is showing us there is much more to the story,” stated Kristen Hicks-Roof, PhD, RDN, LDN, Senior Director of Human Nutrition at the National Pork Board. “What’s exciting about this research is that it helps us better understand how a familiar food like ground pork delivers protein and how the body responds to it after exercise. Ground pork represents an crucial opportunity to connect emerging protein science with practical, nutritious meals people already enjoy.”.

Further studies will be needed to determine whether these short-term biological responses translate into meaningful differences in muscle growth and recovery. Researchers also need to examine how dileucine behaves when protein sources are consumed as part of typical mixed meals and whether similar responses occur in older adults and other populations.

Reference: “Whole-Food Protein Sources Differentially Modulate Postprandial Plasma Dileucine Profiles in the Post-Exercise State” by Žan Zupančič, Geoffrey M. Provenzano, Calvin Chen, Gena L. Irwin, Alexander V. Ulanov and Nicholas A. Burd, 19 October 2026, Molecular Nutrition & Food Research. DOI: 10.1002/mnfr.70628.

This study was supported by the National Pork Board.

Industry News: Euclid's Hunt for Strong Gravitational Lenses is Off to a Strong Start

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness.
  • It has been revealed that luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns.
  • One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that if dark matter and dark energy were a part of our everyday lives, we would live in a perpetual state of dumbfoundedness. Imagine living in a world where 95% of the matter and energy were invisible and undetectable. It would be impossible to make sense of our surroundings.

It has been revealed that luckily, dark energy and dark matter aren't everyday concerns. They're interesting problems for people who are intellectally curious about Nature. But for physicisits, the questions surrounding dark matter and dark energy are much more acute. Some of them dedicate their entire lives to understanding dark matter and dark energy. They design and build special telescopes, instruments, and spacecraft to make progress toward an answer.

One of the spacecraft astrophysicists built to study dark matter and energy is the European Space Agencyâs Euclid space telescope.

This artist's illustration indicates the Euclid Space Telescope doing its thing in its halo orbit at L2. The telescope is on a six-year mission to create a 3D map of the sky, revealing how dark energy and dark matter shape the Universe. Image Credit: By ESA, CC BY-SA IGO 3.0, CC BY-SA 3.0 igo, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Special:Redirect/page/128347141.

It has been revealed that dark matter and dark energy are foundational in our Universe. Dark matter doesn't interact with any light, but it's clearly there. It's some form of mass, but we don't know what. Dark matter is a placeholder term.

In a recent development, dark energy is another placeholder term. It describes the force driving the expansion of the Universe. Like dark matter, we can measure its effect, but we don't know what it really is. And the puzzling thing is that dark matter and dark energy make up most of the Universe.

âIt turns out, the stuff humans are made of is relatively rare in the universe,â stated Dr. Douglas Scott, professor at the University of BC's department of physics and astronomy (PHAS) and member of the Euclid collaboration. âAnd what dominates â dark matter and dark energy â is invisible so we're not used to dealing with it. But it makes the universe what it is, it drives how the universe expands and what the past and future of the universe will be. Where did these things come from? What properties do they have? Euclidâs data gives us the potential to answer those questions.â.

This image reminds us that Euclid does more than study dark matter and dark energy. It's a powerful camera, after all, and can also capture stunning images of regular, baryonic matter, the kind that stars, people, and planets are made of. This image is from Euclid's Early Release Observations, and shows the Messier 78 star formation region about 1300 light years away in Orion. This is the first time Messier 78 has been imaged with such width and depth, hallmarks of Euclid's observations. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by J.-C. Cuillandre (CEA Paris-Saclay), G. Anselmi.

In a recent development, euclid debuted in July 2023 and orbits the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), roughly 1.5 million kilometers away from Earth, a popular spot for space telescopes. From that perch, it uses its wide-angle, 600-megapixel camera to capture visible light, and a photometer and a near-infrared spectrometer to measure the redshift of about 10 billion sources out to redshift 2. That's roughly equivalent to about 10 billion years ago, or about 3.7 billion years after the Significant Bang.

Sources indicate that among these sources, Euclid is especially interested in strong gravitational lenses. These are massive objects like galaxies, galaxy clusters, and dark matter halos. These objects can magnify background objects that are otherwise beyond observing. But they're critical for mapping dark matter itself, because their lensing effect is based on the total mass of these objects, not just their visible mass. So strong gravitational lenses are a way to measure the presence of dark matter. But they're not easy to find.

According to recent reports, euclid delivered its first data release on November 12th, called DR-1 Foundation, and it holds a whopping 1.7 million gigabytes of data. The data revealed almost 5% of the night sky in 13 months of observations. That data holds 900 million galaxies, and 60 million quasars, which are the extremely luminous cores of far-away galaxies. Euclid also found 15,000 latest strong gravitational lens candidates, a massive increase in the potential number.

According to recent reports, "Strong lenses have been difficult to find â the odds were about one in 10,000,â mentioned Hrishabh Srivastava, doctoral student in the UBC department of physics and astronomy (PHAS). âBefore Euclid, we had less than a thousand confirmed strong lenses. Now we have 15,000 new candidates.â.

In a recent development, there's more than one type of gravitational lens. This is a collage of some of the different types of strong gravitational lenses Euclid has found so far. The top row highlights, from left to right: a classic galaxyâgalaxy lens, an Einstein ring in a face-on spiral lens, and an inclined dusty disc lens galaxy. The middle row shows an edge-on dusty lens galaxy, a lensed galaxy with visible star-forming regions, and a compound lens.The bottom row shows a galaxy group lens, a lensed quasar, and a galaxy group lens. Image Credit: ESA/Euclid/Euclid Consortium/NASA, image processing by N. Lines and T. Li. Licence: CC BY-SA 3.0 IGO or ESA Standard Licence.

In a recent development, overall, Euclid is expected to find more than 100,000 strong lenses over the course of its nominal six year mission. That would increase the number of known strong lenses by two orders of magnitude, a transformational advance for dark matter science.

âI like to call these gravitational lenses ânature's own magnifying glassesâ to probe the dark matter distribution of our universe,â mentioned Srivastava.

Recent findings suggest that strong gravitational lensing is an vital tool, but so is weak gravitational lensing. They can be used together to build a fuller picture of dark matter and dark energy. The weak gravitational lensing signature is most apparent around massive galaxy clusters. Since weak gravitational lensing extends beyond a cluster's virial radius, it can help constrain a cluster's overall mass.

Finding huge numbers of gravitational lenses is clearly important in the quest to understand the Universe, but Euclid has other tasks, too. It will slowly build a 3D map of the Universe that covers greater than one-third of the sky. This map will comprise the actual tool used to measure dark matter and dark energy. The map will show how matter is distributed, and then that map can be tested against models of the Universe, especially Lambda-Cold Dark Matter, which is the standard Substantial Bang model of cosmology.

Lambda-CDM predicts how matter, including dark matter, is spread throughout the Universe, and how its structure is shaped by dark energy, which drives the Universe's expansion. So Euclid's 3D map can test both facets of Lambda-CDM: dark matter and dark energy. Dark energy is directly tested, and dark matter is tested more indirectly.

Euclid's test of Lambda-CDM won't be in one massive grand finale, where physicists around the world wait with bated breath to find out the answer. The test is ongoing. Each new data release will generate rounds of new research, as physicists and cosmologists dig into it. It'll be fuel for the different lines of detailed research that different teams of scientists pursue. It's like a process of elimination. Eventually, hopefully, the possible answers and explanations for dark matter and dark energy will be constrained and refined until only one is left standing.

Then, in all likelihood, Nobel prizes will be awarded.

Sources indicate that but that won't be the end of cosmology. Newly introduced questions will arise, intellectual curiosity will be piqued in new ways, and the quest to understand the Universe will continue.

But Euclid and its 3D map will be in history of science textbooks for a long time.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the latest Congress.

Industry observers note that the conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a plan to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

According to recent reports, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., stated the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

“I will vote for the delay,” he stated. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

In a recent development, “If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he mentioned, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

Sources indicate that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

Recent findings suggest that “People are voicing opinions on all sides of the challenges. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators noted. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer said, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., said voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

“The cost of living defeated us,” Paul said. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Don’t let cocktails fall by the wayside in the flurry of holiday dinner prep — these drinks make the party.

Recent findings suggest that in the endless iterating that goes into devising a menu for a holiday dinner, there’s one finishing touch that really makes or breaks the vibe: the drinks. The wine and beer will, of course, flow — at these festive events, a bottle of Champagne or sparkling rose is likely to make an appearance — and it’s easy enough to throw together a gin and tonic or screwdriver. But nothing makes a holiday gathering feel chic, totally put together, gloriously intentional, like a batch cocktail, made-to-order martini, or gussied-up punch.

Recent findings suggest that now, we all have our preferences when it comes to strength, spirit, and format. The host’s bandwidth is also a consideration; do you want to make a lot of one thing, or tailor your options to your guests’ preferences? Those questions are for you to answer, but our staff is here to help by providing this rundown of six tried, vetted, and loved drinks to make at your own celebration.

Below, find Eater editor-approved recipes for cocktails that will add the most festive of feelings to every holiday gathering.

Sources indicate that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Sources indicate that I host a holiday potluck with a core group of friends in December, and one of my favorite potential additions is whatever punch that drinks columnist M. Carrie Allan is cooking up over at the Washington Post. A favorite from 2022 was a meringue-topped citrus punch, featuring blood orange, Aperol, and a dramatic meringue topping. Stated topping adds undeniable flair and drama to the presentation, but if you’re daunted by the idea, the punch itself is still a festive, not-too-sweet drink to serve, celebrating winter citrus. —Missy Frederick, editorial director, dining.

Meaghan Dorman’s modern classic is a favorite year-round, but there’s something about the holidays that calls for Scotch. No shade to the nog freaks, but the subtly spiced sour is a pleasant counterpoint to the onslaught of holiday food and beverage maximalism. No need to break out the single malt either, your dusty bottle of Dewars or Monkey Shoulder will do just fine. —Allison Hamlin, director of network development.

The French 75 — the effervescent classic cocktail made with gin, Champagne, and lemon — is already one of my easy-drinking favorites, and I like it even better in punch form, accented with an aesthetically pleasing ice block of cheery lemon slices. What makes it 77 instead of 75? The substitution of St-Germain (or any elderflower liqueur) for simple syrup, adding just a tiny touch of herbal complexity. It’s perfect for New Year’s Eve, but just as refreshing at Thanksgiving or any other holiday table where you want something light and zesty. —Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

As the de facto cook for Thanksgiving, I like to keep the drinks options simple so I can focus on food prep. This cocktail recipe requires only two ingredients, doesn’t require pre-batching, and is easy enough for people to pour on their own. I also like how it uses Basque cider, which is drier than the typical ciders, so it’s not too sweet while still tapping into that cozy fall feeling —Rayna Rossitto, editor, branded content.

I grew up guzzling Broguiere’s eggnog, but I love the more tropical combination of rich, creamy coconut milk, rum, and cinnamon in coquito; the Puerto Rican holiday cocktail was first described to me as “eggnog, if it went on vacation,” and I haven’t looked back since. This version is by bartender Shannon Ponche, and gets extra dressed up in spice for the holidays with the addition of a homemade cinnamon simple syrup, a woody, nutty oloroso sherry, and a splash of spiced Braulio. —Francky Knapp, staff writer.

It has been revealed that there are two schools of thought on a post-dinner drink: You could go for a bracing digestif to “aid digestion,” or you could indulge in a liquid dessert that swaddles you in sugar, fat, and everything nice. I’m notoriously bad at decision making, so I tend to split the difference with an eggy flip tinged with something bitter. Together, a whole egg and syrup (in this case honey syrup) build a comforting base, while an entire 1.5 ounces of cocktail bitters (as opposed to the usual dash or two) ensure you don’t entirely fall asleep in your glass. Angostura is a great option, delivering some classic holiday spice, but any style of cocktail bitters would probably work, as would an amaro. Dry shaking (shaking the liquid ingredients without ice) is key to achieving a frothy texture, and don’t forget the half-ounce of whiskey, which punches up the rest of the flavors. —Nick Mancall-Bitel, editor.

Several members of my husband’s family are Manhattan drinkers, so I expect that my decision to serve the Grandfather cocktail during Thanksgiving appetizers will be a hit. It’s a riff on the classic drink with a hint of fall, courtesy of the addition of Applejack, an apple brandy. It’s smooth and well-balanced. It’s also quite boozy, so I’ll probably look for a slightly lower-proof option to tide us over after that initial round. I’ve had success with a bourbon and ginger ale bar (with various sodas and mixers) in the past, as well as Smitten Kitchen’s fall sangria; maybe this year we’ll go with her (okay, still pretty boozy) apple cider Old Fashioneds. —Missy Frederick, cities director.

SpaceX Dragon Returns to Earth With a Treasure Trove of Scientific Secrets

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (568 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft has returned to Earth carrying an unusual collection of scientific cargo, including cancer research samples, 3D-printed blood vessels, and bacteria studied in space.
  • The uncrewed capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles at 2:03 p.m.
  • Dragon departed the orbiting laboratory at 11:05 a.m.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A SpaceX Dragon spacecraft has returned to Earth carrying an unusual collection of scientific cargo, including cancer research samples, 3D-printed blood vessels, and bacteria studied in space. The experiments could provide valuable insights into human health, lead to better medical treatments, and help astronauts stay healthy on future missions.

The uncrewed capsule splashed down in the Pacific Ocean near Los Angeles at 2:03 p.m. PST, successfully completing NASA’s 35th SpaceX commercial resupply mission to the International Space Station.

Dragon departed the orbiting laboratory at 11:05 a.m. CST on November 20, bringing back research materials that scientists can now examine in detail on Earth. Unlike many spacecraft that deliver supplies to the station, Dragon is also designed to return cargo safely, making it especially valuable for experiments that require further laboratory analysis.

Among the returning experiments is a 3D-bioprinted blood vessel construct created to investigate how blood vessels age and how cardiovascular diseases develop.

Bioprinting is a technology that uses living cells and specialized materials to build structures resembling human tissue. By studying these blood vessel models in microgravity, where objects experience near weightlessness, researchers hope to gain a better understanding of biological changes that may affect people both in space and on Earth.

Dragon also carried frozen tumor organoids that had undergone experimental treatments aboard the space station. Organoids are small, laboratory-grown models that reproduce certain characteristics of human tissues or tumors, allowing scientists to investigate diseases and test potential therapies.

Researchers hope these samples will reveal information that could improve cancer treatments and support personalized medicine, an approach that aims to tailor medical care to the characteristics of individual patients.

Industry observers note that another set of experiments focuses on antibiotic resistance, a growing medical concern worldwide. Frozen microbial samples returned aboard Dragon will help scientists examine how bacteria that resist antibiotic treatments survive, adapt, and evolve in the unusual environment of space.

Sources indicate that understanding these changes could be key for protecting astronauts on extended missions, when access to medical care is limited. The findings may also offer useful insights into how antibiotic-resistant microbes behave.

According to recent reports, the returning cargo included a specialized lighting system that spent more than three years aboard the space station. Researchers used the equipment to investigate how lighting could improve astronauts’ sleep and overall well-being during long missions.

Light plays an vital role in regulating the body’s internal clock, which influences when people feel alert or sleepy. Maintaining a healthy sleep schedule can be especially challenging aboard the space station, which circles Earth roughly every 90 minutes and experiences numerous sunrises and sunsets each day.

Recent findings suggest that the spacecraft’s journey began on October 13, when it released aboard a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Space Launch Complex 40 at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station in Florida. Dragon reached the International Space Station two days later, on October 15.

After spending more than a month at the orbiting laboratory, the spacecraft returned with scientific samples and equipment ready for further examination.

Sources indicate that although the experiments have not yet established upcoming medical breakthroughs, the research could contribute to advances in cancer treatment, cardiovascular health, infectious disease research, and astronaut safety. The results may ultimately benefit patients on Earth while helping NASA prepare for longer journeys deeper into space.

If you buy something from a link, Vox Media may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

We love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

It has been revealed that stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

It has been revealed that since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor.

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development.

Sources indicate that the only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She remarked, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a big hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

It has been revealed that “We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the Fresh York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Anna Theoktisto, Southern Living.

According to recent reports, this zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the Newly introduced York Times.

According to recent reports, I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who states that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Josh Walker & Duolan Li, Bon Appétit.

ESA's Hera Probe Uses "Superhuman" Vision to Inspect NASA's Asteroid Crash Site

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid.
  • In a recent development, the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying.
  • According to recent reports, to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that around four years ago, humanity intentionally hit an asteroid. The Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) was by pretty much all measures a resounding success when it struck the asteroid moonlet Dimorphos going more than 22,000 kilometers per hour. However, we still donât know just how much of a success it actually was - DART was a one-way mission with no real way to track the results of the impact close up. Enter Hera, the European Space Agency (ESA) mission that recently arrived in the binary asteroid system. Now, in a press release, ESA has provided some of the best pictures of the binary system since that fateful day four years ago.

In a recent development, the lack of accurate measurement isnât for lack of trying. Ground-based observatories have been watching 151m wide Dimorphos and its parent asteroid, 780m wide Didymos very closely over the last four years. They could tell that Dimorphos slowed its orbit around its larger companion by about 33 minutes. But some scientists were surprised by the magnitude of the change in orbit, based on the theoretical math done before the mission.

According to recent reports, to help clear up any ambiguity about the math underlying this planetary defense mission, Hera is equipped with three main imaging tools. Its standard âeyesâ are the Asteroid Framing cameras, which handle both black-and-white photography and navigation. The press release showcases an image from this system showing Didymos from roughly 28.5km away, with features down to roughly 2.7m per pixel.

Fraser talks about Hera's final insertion into the binary asteroid system.

In the image, you can clearly see the âspinning topâ shape of the larger asteroid in the pair. Didymos spins at a relatively rapid speed for its size, completing a rotation every 2.2 hours. That energy is strong enough to pull boulders and gravel towards the middle of the asteroid, causing a build-up of material that makes it look fatter in the middle than at its poles.

Sources indicate that however, seeing an asteroid in black in white isnât as scientifically useful as seeing it in âcolorâ. That is what Heraâs second imaging system, the HyperScout H instrument, is designed to do. It monitors the asteroid over 25 different color bands. With that information, HyperScout H can absorb and reflect light with different unique patterns - essentially it can spectroscopy. Comparing the results to lab experiments on meteorite samples on Earth will help determine what Didymos and its smaller companion are actually made up of.

Sources indicate that but why stop at simple hyperspectral imaging when you can also have heat vision? The Thermal Infrared Imager (TIRI), supplied to ESA by Japanâs Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) gives Hera âSuperman-likeâ heat vision according to the press release. TIRI maps the temperature of the surface of the asteroids, and since solid rock dissipates heat much more slowly than porous or fragmented rock, it will also give a good indication of how solid Didymos really is.

Fraser talks about some of the results of the DART test.

In a recent development, crucially, Dimorphos itself, the actual subject of the original DART test, is surprisingly absent from many of the pictures in this first round of releases. In the visible light images, Dimorphos is tucked almost entirely into the shadow of Didymos, appearing as a tiny sunlit spec beneath Didymos in one of the images. But with TIRIâs âSupermanâ view, the entire 151m wide asteroid is clearly in focus, glowing a shade of cool purple in the infrared. Cameras arenât the only thing Hera is carrying either. It will eventually launch two CubeSats, Juventus and Milan, to study the asteroid binary very closely. They will use ground-penetrating radar and even touch down on the surface of Dimorphos in an effort to understand what itstruly made of.

Sources indicate that but ultimately the overarching purpose of the mission is to get a better idea of how effectively we can move an asteroid out of the way if we need to. DART appeared to be a success on the surface. Understanding what really happened to Dimorphos is what Hera, with all its cameras and companion spacecraft, was literally designed for. And weâre just at the earliest phases of that process. The next step is a major release of even sharper images planned for a live event at the Berlin Museum of Natural History on November 25th. Asteroid watchers, and space enthusiasts more generally, should mark their calendars for our first high-resolution view of one of the biggest impacts weâve had on another body in the solar system to date.

Hera surveying asteroids with superhuman vision.

#77238. Ancient Meteorites May Have Delivered One of Life’s Most Essential Ingredients to Earth

Ancient Meteorites May Have Delivered One of Life’s Most Essential Ingredients to Earth

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (814 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient meteorites may hold the key to understanding when and how Earth acquired one of life’s most essential elements.
  • According to recent reports, carbon erupting from Hawaiian volcanoes may have originated deep within Earth’s metallic core, carrying a chemical fingerprint that dates back to the planet’s formation.
  • Industry observers note that researchers analyzing volcanic rocks from Hawaii identified an unusual carbon isotope signature that may trace back to Earth’s core.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient meteorites may hold the key to understanding when and how Earth acquired one of life’s most essential elements.

According to recent reports, carbon erupting from Hawaiian volcanoes may have originated deep within Earth’s metallic core, carrying a chemical fingerprint that dates back to the planet’s formation. A new study suggests that carbon-rich meteorites delivered a substantial amount of Earth’s carbon during its early history, potentially helping supply the element that would eventually become essential to life.

Industry observers note that researchers analyzing volcanic rocks from Hawaii identified an unusual carbon isotope signature that may trace back to Earth’s core. “We think that we found evidence of carbon from Earth’s core leaking into the core-mantle boundaries and traveling all the way to the surface,” indicates lead author Yves Moussallam, an associate professor at Columbia University’s Department of Earth and Environmental Sciences and Lamont-Doherty Earth Observatory. The findings were published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

In a recent development, the researchers examined volcanic rocks from Kīlauea and the Tantalus Rift, two Hawaiian volcanic systems that draw magma from different regions of the mantle. Samples from the Tantalus Rift contained carbon isotope signatures of approximately -5 to -7 per mil, consistent with typical mantle carbon. Kīlauea’s samples, however, had a much heavier signature of approximately -1 per mil, a value rarely observed in previous measurements.

“This signature is very, very distinct from the normal mantle,” says Moussallam. “This means it must have been contaminated by another carbon source and that source is probably carbon from the core.” Although the team considers the core the most likely source, the isotope measurements do not establish that origin conclusively.

Earth’s mantle extends roughly 1,800 miles beneath the crust, separating the surface from the planet’s metallic core. Scientists believe much of Earth’s carbon resides in the core, which cannot be directly sampled. However, research suggests that some materials from the liquid outer core may cross into the mantle and eventually reach the surface through mantle plumes. These rising columns of hot rock can partially melt as they approach the crust, supplying magma to volcanoes. Kīlauea is thought to receive magma from near the center of a plume that originates close to the core-mantle boundary, while the Tantalus Rift samples appear to represent the plume’s outer regions.

Industry observers note that to investigate the carbon carried by these magmas, Moussallam’s team used a recently developed technique to measure carbon isotopes inside tiny pockets of trapped melt. As magma cools, growing crystals can enclose droplets of molten rock before dissolved gases escape. These sealed pockets, called undegassed melt inclusions, preserve carbon dioxide from the original magma. “These melts are fossils of the magma,” Moussallam says.

It has been revealed that the researchers then compared Kīlauea’s unusual carbon signature with measurements from ancient meteorites. Moussallam argues that carbon preserved in Earth’s core should reflect “the signature of the building blocks of Earth when it was created.” The closest similarities appeared in carbonaceous chondrites, a carbon-rich class of meteorites associated with the outer regions of the early solar system.

Industry observers note that chondrites contain some of the solar system’s oldest surviving material, dating back more than 4.5 billion years. “All of Earth is made of chondrites,” Moussallam explains. “They’re the building blocks of all the terrestrial planets.” Scientists distinguish between noncarbonaceous chondrites, associated with the inner solar system, and carbonaceous chondrites, which formed farther from the Sun. How much each group contributed to Earth’s formation remains debated.

In a recent development, the researchers propose that carbonaceous chondrites struck Earth relatively late in its formation, when the growing planet was better able to retain carbon delivered by incoming material. Some of that carbon may have entered the core before eventually moving into the mantle and reaching the surface through volcanic activity. The isotope similarities support this possibility, but confirming that the carbon actually originated in the core will require additional evidence. “We don’t really know. We need more measurements,” cautions Moussallam.

Sources indicate that the proposed journey would connect carbon delivered by ancient meteorites, stored deep inside Earth, and eventually released into the environment where living organisms could incorporate it. “It’s fun to think about. We’re made of carbon, right? To think that some of this carbon might at some point have been linked to iron in the planet’s core, made it all the way to the surface from out of a volcano, and is now part of the biosphere, is very interesting.”.

Reference: “Isotopically heavy carbon in the core” by Yves Moussallam, Damanveer S. Grewal, Guillaume Georgeais, HyunJoo Lee, Estelle F. Rose-Koga, Allan Lerner, Bridgett Holman, Paul J. Wallace, Natália Gauer Pasqualon, Olivia E. Anderson and Matthew G. Jackson, 9 November 2026, Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. DOI: 10.1073/pnas.2610912123.

#77236. Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up
