General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

Earth's Atmosphere Took Three Deep Breaths of Oxygen Before the Oceans Caught Up

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1453 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets.
  • According to recent reports, earth is one significant system.
  • Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago, along with the rest of the planets. Life appeared somewhere between about 4.28 and 3.8 billion years ago; it's difficult to determine clearly. An oxygen atmosphere is a more recent development for Earth, in geological timescales, and understanding how that happened is a big part of understanding the present-day Earth.

According to recent reports, earth is one significant system. The atmosphere, the oceans, and life itself are all parts of the system. In some respects, they can be studied in isolation. But when trying to understand Earth and its long history, they need to be understood together. The system changed significantly when life changed. Somewhere around 2.4 billion years ago, cyanobacteria appeared, and they brought a fresh trick with them: photosynthesis.

Cyanobacteria used sunlight to split water molecules apart. That did two things: it generated their chemical energy, and it released free oxygen into water, which eventually found its way into the atmosphere. That was a monumental stage of Earth's development that eventually led to an ozone layer, letting life flourish on the surface. The oxygenation of the atmosphere also led to complex life like us.

Sources indicate that but this all happened a long time ago. At first, the oxygen didn't accumulate in the atmosphere, and figuring out how it all played out isn't simple. Scientists know that the oxygenation history of the ocean and the atmosphere are coupled, but there are many questions. Some researchers argue that the atmosphere's oxygenation took place in different stages, one of which was the Great Oxygenation Event (GOE), while others have argued that the process was smoother. The debate continues.

New research in The Innovation highlights how Earth's atmosphere was oxygenated in three distinct steps, and that the deep ocean lagged behind in each case. In the last of the steps, deep ocean oxygenation lagged behind by 600 million years.

The research is titled "Stagewise oxygenation of the Earthâs atmosphere and oceans," and the authors are Haiyang Wang and Chao Li, geochemists at the Chengdu University of Technology.

"Earthâs surface oxygenation was a protracted, multi-step process," the authors write. "It is widely accepted that atmospheric O2 rose through three major steps, each closely linked to key evolutionary innovations.".

It has been revealed that the oceans and the atmosphere are linked, and during the quest to understand Earth's oxygenated atmosphere, researchers used the geological rock record to understand ocean chemistry. The well-known banded iron formations are a part of this. They record the ocean's oxygen levels. The atmosphere doesn't hold an ancient record, so the ocean's geological record was used as a proxy for the atmosphere's evolution and oxygenation, too.

So scientists largely think that three stages of rising oxygen created the modern atmosphere: the GOE about 2.4 billion years ago, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event about 800 to 540 million years ago, and the Paleozoic Oxygenation Event about 400 million years ago.

Industry observers note that the researchers reiterate the understanding that ocean and atmospheric oxygenation are coupled. Research shows that on billion year timescales, episodes of rising atmospheric oxygen precede the same episodic rise in ocean oxygenation, "whereas on shorter, million-year timescales, their redox states could diverge, exhibiting negative coupling," they write.

"Here, we synthesize geochemical, sedimentological, and palaeobiological evidence to reconstruct this coupled and dynamic atmosphere-ocean oxygenation history and to reassess its timing, mechanisms, and ecological consequences," the authors explain.

This work hinges on new geochemical proxies that give researchers a clearer picture of what happened so long ago.

"Recent advances in geochemical proxies, most notably sulfate triple-oxygen isotopes (Îâ²17O), provide new constraints on atmospheric oxygenation, complementing and in some cases revising interpretations from traditional ocean redox proxies," the authors explain.

The researchers say that this sulfate (SO4)offers a cleaner way to understand the oxygenation of the atmosphere. That's because of the isotopic composition of atmospheric oxygen, which is recorded when sulfate forms. It has a deficit of the isotope oxygen-17. So the sulfate can be used to track the rise of atmospheric O2, putting dates on each rise in atmospheric oxygen.

Industry observers note that they found that the GOE is unchanged, sitting between 2.4â2.1 billion years ago. But this work changes the dates of the second and third oxygen rises.

The second, the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event was 1.3â1.0 billion years ago instead of 800 to 540 million years ago. The Paleozoic Oxygenation Event was 0.42â0.36 billion years instead of 0.44â0.41 billion.

It has been revealed that the researchers found something else, too. The previous dates for the Neoproterozoic and Paleozoic events still record something. But instead of dating atmospheric oxygen, they date the delayed oxygenation of the deep ocean. They lagged behind the oxygenation of the atmosphere by about 200 and 30 million years, respectively.

According to recent reports, this graphic illustrates the results from new research into the oxygenation of Earth's atmosphere that highlights how Earth's O2 rose unevenly: shallow seas first, then the atmosphere, and much later the deep ocean. During a 2-billion-year transition, atmosphere and ocean O2 sometimes diverged despite long-term rise. Ocean oxygenation was highly variable, with extreme spatial heterogeneity over time. Image Credit: Stagewise oxygenation of the Earth's atmosphere and oceans. Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

In a recent development, on shorter timescales, the link between ocean and atmospheric oxygen is still the defining feature in this work. But it reveals that a change in one could've pushed the other in the opposite direction. The researchers think that what seems like a signal of rising oxygen levels is actually a drop. When a pulse of oxygen enters the ocean, it oxidized organic carbon and sulfide in the oceans. The organic carbon becomes CO2, and the sulfide becomes sulfate. The more organic carbon and sulfide there was in the ocean, the more it depleted atmospheric oxygen.

Industry observers note that over longer, billion year timescales, the atmophere is oxygenated as photosynthesis continues. But on shorter timescales, it can't keep up.

Sources indicate that "Earthâs surface oxygenation history reflects a dynamic and nonlinear interplay among atmospheric O2 evolution, land and ocean redox buffering, and ecological innovation," the authors write. "Overall, the trajectory from localized Archean oxygen oases to the globally well-oxygenated surface environments of today underscores how atmosphere-ocean oxygenation both governsâand is reciprocally shaped byâthe evolution of life.".

Industry observers note that this figure indicates the evolution of Earth's atmosphere-ocean redox states through time and space. (A) Before 2.4 Ga: atmosphere and oceans were largely anoxic, with oxygen restricted to localized, shallow-water oxygen oases. (B) From 2.4 to 1.0 Ga: atmospheric O2 remained low; oxygenated waters were confined to the ocean surface, and oxygen oases developed primarily along continental shelves. (C) Between 1.0 and 0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 increased but fluctuated, while oxygenated waters progressively penetrated to greater depths, with shelf environments continuing to host oxygen oases. (D) Since â¼0.41 Ga: atmospheric O2 approached near-modern levels; deep oceans became pervasively oxygenated, whereas mid-depth waters developed oxygen minimum zones (OMZs) that waxed and waned (solid curves) in response to high organic matter export and oxygen consumption. DOC, dissolved organic carbon. Image Credit: Wang and Li 2026, The Innovation.

Industry observers note that it all happened in stages, as the different elements fed back on one another. This work demonstrates that during Earth's long path to an oxygenated atmosphere, the ocean and atmosphere didn't change in lockstep on shorter timescales. "Throughout the 2-billion-year oxygenation transition, atmospheric and oceanic oxygen levels were episodically decoupled on shorter timescales, superimposed on a long-term trajectory toward global oxidation," they write.

Recent findings suggest that the pair of researchers acknowledge some of the weakness in the evidence that paints this picture. The record of oxygen isotopes in sulfate is coarse, not exquisitely detailed. Beyond one billion years ago, the levels aren't well-constrained. So it's still more open to interpretation. There may be other steps in the path to oxygenation that aren't clear yet.

Industry observers note that understanding how life and the planet co-evolved together is a monumental task. Scientists know it happened, but all of the details are difficult to detect. But if it happened here, it almost certainly happened on any other habitable worlds.

"These deep-time perspectives illuminate the co-evolution of life and Earthâs surface environments and provide a conceptual framework for evaluating planetary habitability," the authors write.

#77235. Earth’s Ozone Hole Swells to More Than Twice the Size of the United States

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1174 w)

Earth’s Ozone Hole Swells to More Than Twice the Size of the United States

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1174 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An unusually powerful polar vortex caused the Antarctic ozone hole to swell to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, covering more than twice the area of the United States.
  • Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, making it one of the largest observed in nearly five decades.
  • The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An unusually powerful polar vortex caused the Antarctic ozone hole to swell to its seventh-largest size on record in 2026, covering more than twice the area of the United States.

Unusual weather patterns over Antarctica caused the ozone hole to expand dramatically in 2026, making it one of the largest observed in nearly five decades. Despite its extraordinary size, scientists from NASA and NOAA emphasize that Earth’s protective ozone layer continues to recover and remains on course to heal later this century.

The 2026 Antarctic ozone hole ranked as the seventh-largest in 48 years of observations, based on its average seasonal area. Scientists attributed the expansion primarily to an exceptionally strong polar vortex, a powerful circulation of winds surrounding Antarctica. However, they also noted that decades of international efforts to reduce ozone-destroying chemicals prevented the hole from becoming even larger.

According to recent reports, between September 7 and October 13, 2026, when ozone depletion was most intense, the hole covered an average of approximately 9.6 million square miles (25 million square kilometers). That is more than twice the size of the United States. Scientists closely monitor ozone high in the atmosphere because it serves as Earth’s natural “sunscreen,” protecting living organisms from harmful ultraviolet radiation. This beneficial ozone in the stratosphere differs from ground level ozone, an air pollutant often produced by human activities.

According to recent reports, “The annual ozone hole has been forming later in the season in recent years, which tells us the ozone layer is healing,” remarked Paul Newman, a senior scientist at the University of Maryland and longtime leader of NASA’s ozone research team at the agency’s Goddard Space Flight Center. “But an unusually powerful polar vortex has extended ozone depletion in the Antarctic this season, allowing the hole to grow to proportions we haven’t seen in a decade.”.

In a recent development, the ozone hole reached its maximum size on September 18, expanding to 10.5 million square miles (27.1 million square kilometers). That was approximately 90% of the size of the largest ozone hole ever measured, which occurred on September 9, 2000.

“The 2026 ozone hole is large but could have been 1 to 2 million square miles (3.5 million square kilometers) larger if ozone-depleting substances were as prevalent in the atmosphere today as they were at their year 2000 peak,” Newman said.

Recent findings suggest that ozone destruction begins with human-made chemicals containing chlorine and bromine. After entering the environment, these compounds gradually rise into the stratosphere, where ultraviolet sunlight breaks them apart and releases chlorine and bromine atoms. These atoms can then participate in chemical reactions involving particles in clouds that form in the extremely cold Antarctic stratosphere, leading to the breakdown of ozone.

In a recent development, A major factor in this process is the polar vortex, a seasonal ring of strong winds that circulates around Antarctica high in the atmosphere. By trapping exceptionally cold air over the continent, the vortex creates conditions that allow polar stratospheric clouds to develop. These clouds provide an crucial environment for the chemical reactions responsible for ozone depletion.

In 2026, the polar vortex was unusually extensive because atmospheric disturbances that normally weaken and disrupt it were less active than usual.

Industry observers note that “The polar vortex was unusually large this year in part because planetary-scale weather systems that typically well up from the lower atmosphere and break up the vortex were especially weak in August and September,” said Amy Butler, a research scientist at the NOAA Chemical Sciences Laboratory. “That weak wave action kept the strongest polar vortex winds further from the South Pole by several degrees of latitude, creating a larger area for conditions ideal for ozone depletion to occur.”.

Although the 2026 ozone hole covered an exceptionally large area, the amount of ozone lost within it was less severe than during some of the most extreme depletion events recorded over the previous 10 to 20 years.

To measure ozone concentrations, NOAA researchers used instruments carried into the atmosphere by balloons rolled out from the South Pole Baseline Atmospheric Observatory. They also collected measurements with the Dobson Ozone Spectrophotometer, an optical instrument designed to measure atmospheric ozone. Their observations demonstrated that ozone directly above the South Pole fell to its lowest concentration of the year on October 17, reaching 105 Dobson units.

It has been revealed that A Dobson unit is a standard measurement used to describe the total amount of ozone in a vertical column of the atmosphere. For comparison, 100 Dobson units would form a layer just 1 millimeter thick, roughly the thickness of a dime, if all the ozone were compressed to standard temperature and pressure at sea level. The lowest concentration ever measured above the South Pole was 92 Dobson units in October 2006.

Sources indicate that satellites have provided another essential source of ozone measurements since 1979. For the 2026 assessment, scientists drew on observations from instruments aboard NASA’s Aura satellite, NOAA-20, NOAA-21, and the Suomi National Polar-orbiting Partnership satellite, a mission operated jointly by NASA and NOAA. Together, these observations help researchers track changes in ozone levels and assess the atmosphere’s recovery over time.

In a recent development, despite the unusually large ozone hole in 2026, long-term measurements continue to demonstrate the benefits of international action to protect the atmosphere. NASA and NOAA scientists point to the Montreal Protocol, adopted in 1987, as a major reason the ozone layer is gradually recovering.

In a recent development, under the agreement, countries committed to phasing out substances that damage ozone, including chlorofluorocarbons, and replacing them with alternatives that pose less risk to the ozone layer. These restrictions have substantially reduced the amount of ozone-destroying chemicals entering the atmosphere.

According to Stephen Montzka, a senior scientist at NOAA’s Global Monitoring Laboratory, chlorine concentrations in the Antarctic stratosphere associated with ozone-depleting substances have fallen by approximately one-third from their peak levels in the 1980s. This decline has helped reduce the severity of ozone destruction, even during years when atmospheric conditions favor the formation of a particularly large hole.

Chlorofluorocarbons and other ozone-depleting compounds were once common ingredients in products and materials used around the world, including refrigerators, air conditioners, and building insulation.

Although many of these chemicals have been phased out, their effects persist. Some remain in the atmosphere for decades, while others continue to escape from aging equipment, discarded products, and landfills. As a result, ozone recovery is a gradual process that depends on the continued decline of these long-lasting pollutants.

Scientists right now estimate that the Antarctic ozone hole will recover by the 2070s as the remaining ozone-destroying substances slowly disappear from the atmosphere. The enormous hole observed in 2026 demonstrates how strongly unusual weather can influence ozone depletion from one year to the next. At the same time, its reduced severity compared with the worst years on record provides further evidence that international efforts to protect Earth’s ozone layer are making a lasting difference.

  • The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Chair Teresa Leger Fernández, D-N.M., conducts a news conference with members of the Democratic Women’s Caucus during a 2025 retreat in Leesburg, Va. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, noted legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

Rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, said she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses announced a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had said they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

The two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack noted she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

Sources indicate that “That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she said when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this concern.”.

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

In a recent development, “We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández stated. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

Tiny Grains of Sand Act as Cosmic Speedometers for Alien Winds

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1005 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes.
  • Sources indicate that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones.
  • Understanding why this is crucial requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Weâve managed to take high-resolution orbital images of many worlds across our solar system, and many of them with an atmosphere have one feature in common - sand dunes. Scientists have been using the size and orientation of these dunes for decades to act like a weather vane, figuring out which way the wind blows on these other worlds. Unfortunately, weather vanes arenât good at telling the full windy story - they canât tell you how fast the wind is going. However, according to a new paper published in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences by researchers at Stanford, sand dunes can.

Sources indicate that earth and Mars, the two most commonly thought of planets with sand dunes, arenât the only ones. Weâve also seen them on Venus, Titan, and, surprisingly, Comet 67P/Churyumov-Gerasimenko. Each is made up of different materials, but all share a crucial characteristic - their âsandâ consists of small grains of similar particles, which could be blown around by wind.

Understanding why this is crucial requires looking at how wind actually moves sand in the first place. When air is moving across a dune, individual grains stay stationary until the wind itself reaches a critical speed known as the transport threshold. Once it rises above that, the grains begin bouncing across the ground in a movement known as saltation. Each time a grain crashes back to the surface, it kicks up other surrounding grains into the air, creating a self-sustaining cascade of moving sand.

Fraser talks about whether Martian dust storms are dangerous.

What was unclear to scientists was whether these motions were primarily driven by violent dust storms that were relatively rare, or moderate winds which are much more common on the other worlds where dunes have been seen. It might seem counter-intuitive that a comet would have âwindâ, but a 2017 study revealed that the âripplesâ ESAâs Rosetta probe found on the comet's surface were created by localized vapor flows caused by extreme day-night temperature cycling.

Recent findings suggest that solving the mystery of what type of wind causes these shifting sands was the focus of the paper. Lead author M. Colin Marvin, a PhD student in the Department of Earth and Planetary Sciences at Stanford, collected wind speed data and detailed grain-size measurements from twenty-four different dune fields spread all over the world. From the Coral Pink Sand Dunes State Park in Utah to the ancient, hundred-meter-tall dunes in the Namib Sand Sea in Namibia, the researchers found a remarkable similarity.

Across every terrestrial site, the most sand was moved when the wind was slightly above the speed required to start moving it. And, crucially, the same relationship also held on a Maritan sand dune. The process didnât require the odd violent gale to get sand moving, just every day wind speeds common throughout the globe. For example, a dune made of sand 0.2 mm across (about the width of two pieces of paper) is mostly moved by winds blowing at only 26 kilometers per hour 10 meters above the ground.

Fraser talks about the Dragonfly mission, which will land next to dunes on Titan.

Recent findings suggest that with that data set in hand, the researchers then turned to simulations. Using a tool called ReSCAL, they grew virtual dunes from flat sand beds using different wind speeds. As part of that process, the team confirmed that, as long as a world has plenty of loosely bound grains of sand and winds that grow rarer as they grow stronger, dunes will largely be formed by the wind speeds that correspond directly to the grain sizes that compose them.

According to recent reports, despite the challenges of finding individual sand grain size from orbit, this technique is useful on more than just Earth. Curiosity has already drilled into the Stimson formation, a layer of sandstone that used to be a windblown dune billions of years ago. Another upcoming interplanetary mission â Dragonfly â is expected to touch down on the surface of Titan, where there are dunes of hydrocarbons, sometime in the 2030s.

It has been revealed that combining the grain size measurements from these missions with the math laid out in the new paper will provide scientists with a rough indication of the history of wind speed in the area. There will also undoubtedly be other missions to other dune-ridden planets - Venus comes to mind as a potential target. And from now on, scientists will be able to read a major part of a worldâs geological history directly written into its sand.

Stanford - Scientists discover sand dunes can reveal wind speeds on Earth and beyond.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With sausage fennel stuffing, crispy green beans, and some very fall-appropriate salads, these are our essential additions to the Thanksgiving table.

Industry observers note that the sides are objectively the best part of Thanksgiving, and it’s not even an argument. Mashed potatoes and stuffing are the reason we’re all convening at the table, right? Aaaaand the whole “gathering with loved ones” thing too, of course.

Recent findings suggest that while we’ve all got our staples, the sides are also the opportunity to really have fun with the meal and showcase whatever upcoming ideas have been simmering since last year’s massive meal. They’re our chance to create a menu with balance, adding a bright, crunchy salad that perfectly offsets the richness of all those buttery potatoes or offering an essential hit of cozy baked pasta with melty cheese.

These are the Thanksgiving sides recipes that Eater editors have vetted as being worth the space on our holiday tables.

Stack more, spend less. Amazon Grocery lets you spend less on all the people who eat your food. Shop Amazon for everyday low prices on groceries and get free same-day delivery with Prime.

Sources indicate that every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Industry observers note that why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

According to recent reports, nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Industry observers note that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

This is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Industry observers note that I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated rapidly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

  • The idea comes from a troubling discovery made several years ago.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a West Coast survey, one in four consumers said they would pay $225 extra for salmon-safe tires, bringing wildlife conservation into an everyday buying decision.

According to recent reports, buying new tires could someday give drivers a way to help protect salmon. A new study suggests that many consumers would pay extra for tires labeled “salmon safe,” potentially creating a market for products designed to reduce harm to fish.

The idea comes from a troubling discovery made several years ago. Research co-led by Washington State University (WSU) scientists found that 6PPD, a chemical added to tires to prevent them from breaking down too promptly, is toxic to coho salmon. When tire debris from roads reaches freshwater streams, the chemical can kill the fish.

According to recent reports, tire manufacturers are now exploring newly introduced formulations that would eliminate 6PPD. As that work continues, economists at WSU wanted to understand whether consumers would voluntarily spend more on tires that could help protect salmon.

“The tire doesn’t exist yet, but we wanted to know how the general population might value the tire after it’s been developed,” noted Joe Cook, a professor in WSU’s School of Economic Sciences and lead author of the study. “As the tire industry explores reformulation, we hope this demonstrates there is a potential market for ‘eco-labeled’ tires.”.

In a recent development, cook, who works at WSU’s Puyallup Research and Extension Center, conducted the research with Wisnu Sugiarto, a professor at Whitman College and former WSU graduate student. Their findings were published in the journal Marine Resource Economics.

Sources indicate that the researchers surveyed nearly 700 residents of California, Oregon, and Washington, asking how much they would be willing to pay for hypothetical salmon-safe tires. They then compared those amounts with what participants reported spending on their most recent tire purchases.

In a recent development, the median willingness to pay was 10% above the previous purchase price, equivalent to roughly $76 more for a set of four tires. That means half of respondents were willing to pay a larger premium, while the other half would pay less.

Some participants placed an even higher value on protecting salmon.

“Approximately 25% of people noted they would pay a premium of $225 for a set of four salmon-safe tires,” Cook said. “This shows that protecting salmon is very important for a sizeable group of consumers in the three states.”.

Recent findings suggest that the results suggest that environmental concerns could influence an ordinary purchasing decision, even when consumers would have to spend more. For tire manufacturers considering alternatives to 6PPD, that willingness to pay could point to a potential market for products advertised as safer for salmon.

However, the researchers emphasized that what consumers say they would voluntarily pay for an environmentally friendly product is different from what manufacturers might charge if regulations required them to remove 6PPD.

It has been revealed that “This study is about voluntary eco-labeling for a hypothetical product,” Cook mentioned. “We aren’t saying that prices would go up this amount if 6PPD is regulated out of tires — that ultimately would depend on what it costs for tire manufacturers to reformulate and how competitive the tire industry is.

“Our results couldn’t be used in a benefit-cost analysis of a state or federal regulation,” he continued. “That would require a different survey approach, but we would be excited to look at that and well-placed to do that work.”.

The researchers hope to continue examining the economic consequences of removing 6PPD from tires, including questions that would help policymakers assess potential regulations.

Sources indicate that reference: “Measuring Consumer Demand for Salmon Safe Tires” by Joseph Cook and Wisnu Sugiarto, 5 November 2026, Marine Resource Economics. DOI: 10.1086/743478.

The study was funded by the nonprofit Salmon Safe, which provides “salmon safe” certifications to products like wine and beer and organizations like farms and construction contractors.

The 38 Best London Restaurants, According to Eater’s Local Dining Expert

📅 28 Jun 2017 | ⏱️ 26 min read (5289 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Eater

⏱️ ~26 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.
  • In a recent development, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine.
  • This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most vital restaurants in the capital.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

In a recent development, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most vital restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

Sources indicate that we upgrade this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

According to recent reports, new to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Recent findings suggest that adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he introduced Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

The best meals in London, from Michelin fine dining to beloved street food, according to a longtime restaurant editor.

In a recent development, the story of the London food scene is one that includes dim sum, Sunday roasts, curries, pizza, sinasir, rarebits, banh mi, udon, pepper pot, sweetbread suya, and natural wine. Across cuisines, neighborhoods, and price points, all these dishes and drinks place London among the very best and most diverse places to eat in the world.

This guide, which I’ve been compiling and iterating on for the better part of the last decade, aims to reflect the best food and most important restaurants in the capital. I want this map to help you navigate a city in which it is all too easy to eat poorly, but in which it is increasingly inexcusable to do so. It will showcase a mix of over three dozen restaurants, which have all done outstanding things in extraordinary times: emerging, surviving, thriving, and continuing to enrich the city and its food culture through more than half a decade of unprecedented change and tumult.

We revision this list regularly to make sure it reflects the ever-changing London dining scene. Our write-ups include insider tips, as well as a rough range of pricing for each destination — ranging from $ for quick, inexpensive meals with dishes largely under $10 (or the equivalent in pounds), to $$$$ for places where entrees exceed $30.

Newly introduced to the map in November 2026: A return to the 38 for Kiln, one of London’s most consistent and innovative modern Thai restaurants, which this year turns 10; Bouchon Racine, a French bistro above a Farringdon pub whose faithful homage to the traditions of simple French cooking have it booked up months in advance; and perhaps the most interesting restaurant to open in London this year: Tramps, a semi-secret, not-often-open restaurant and bar within a gallery space off City Road. Three restaurants added to the map, which collectively exhibit just a portion of the curious plurality of the London dining experience.

Sources indicate that adam Coghlan is a writer and editor based in London. In 2017, he introduced Eater London and ran the site until it ceased daily publication in 2023.

Open for: Lunch through late night.

As Jonathan Nunn wrote in his guide to north London’s best-value restaurants, “Durak, a tantuni salonu run by Dogan Yesil on West Green Road, is the superior late night snack template.” Only the tantuni, a speciality which originates in the city of Mersin on the southern coast of Turkey, is served here. Beef is boiled, seasoned with the likes of tomato, pul biber, sumac, and cumin and subsequently fried in cotton oil before being loaded, meat juices aplenty, inside a thin lavash with chopped parsley, tomato, and onion. It is then given a pleasing bend before being eaten; a selection of high-acid accompaniments — pickled chiles, lemon — provide the necessary cut-through.

Best for: A snack on the way home after a long day.

Mukaddes Yadikar’s restaurant near Walthamstow Central station opened in London in summer 2017. It was London’s first strictly Uyghur restaurant, and has become perhaps E17’s finest neighborhood restaurant. To start, go for the Chaomian, a stir-fry of short noodle snippets wokked with chunks of beef, spring onion, and tomato. Third, and most importantly, get the signature da pan ji (“big plate chicken”): a remarkably deep, savoury, and spicy chicken and potato stew, teeming with Sichuan peppercorns, served with flat hand-pulled noodles. This is a warm, homely, and treasured space to eat in east London.

Best for: Casual dinner with a group.

Open for: Lunch and dinner on weekends, dinner only during the week.

Eater London’s Restaurant of the Year 2022 comprises three discrete yet intertwined endeavors. Downstairs in the basement kitchen, George Jephson butchers whole animals, repurposing them as immaculate charcuterie, while upstairs, chef Mike Murphy uses excellent ingredients to prepare simple plates that lean French and southern European — think trout poached in butter with roe and sorrel; or a roast game bird with quince and bitter leaves. Sommeliers Tom Beattie and Fran Roberts, the duo behind the wine importer bearing both names, run the bar and the floor with a small team. Cadet is a wine bar, a restaurant, a charcutier, and a shopfront; it feels French and it feels London; and, from the moment it opened, it has always felt just right.

According to recent reports, this diminutive Vietnamese shop on Hackney’s Graham Road serves one of the city’s best sandwiches — inside one of the city’s best baguettes. Although the spot has just one table and three or four seats, it’s difficult to think of warmer hospitality than at Bánh Mì Hội-An. The duo behind the counter prepare fresh sandwiches to go, and while the pork classic is excellent, don’t sleep on the turmeric-heavy fried catfish on Mondays, Tuesdays, and Wednesdays; fragrant with coriander, mayo, fermented chile paste, sriracha, and pickled vegetables, it is an object lesson in flavor, texture, and balance.

In a recent development, ex-Noma sommelier Yukiyasu Kaneko’s wine bar, set in a cozy space beneath a railway arch close to London Fields, may yet become the upcoming template for natural wine bars, a category that has grown a little tired and derivative. Few other businesses can rival Yuki’s assured sense of self and pleasing ambience. An extensive (and fairly priced) list includes highlights from the Jura, Savoie, and Loire regions, as well as bottles from elsewhere in the Old World. Food is secondary but not an afterthought, with snacky dishes such as eggs with tahini, house-made potato crisps dressed with sansho pepper, cured beet tops, silken tofu with mushrooms, and made-to-order beef tartare.

Must-try dish: Ask Yuki for his best wines from the Jura or the Savoie.

In a recent development, these days, London has no shortage of excellent latest-age wine bars. It’s been a signature category in the city since the days of P. Franco and the likes of Terroirs before. But in more recent times, spots like Cadet, Hector’s, and Yuki Bar have raised the standard of wine bars sharply. At Goodbye Horses, which opened in the second part of 2024 (and where I enjoyed one of my favorite nights out last year), sommelier Nathalie Nelles oversees one of the most interesting wine lists in the city. Nelles has a penchant for excellent French wines from the Jura, Loire, and Burgundy. Go in the evening to enjoy a selection of small plates, which might include an avant-garde beef tartare, some carefully arranged crostini-like toasts, and a cheese plate. But you’re here to drink, really, and to take in the quite extraordinary interior, hand-painted curtains and long, organically shaped wooden bar — which lend the room a World of Interiors vibe in the best way.

Must-try: Complex savagnins from the Jura, elegant chenin blancs from the Loire Valley, grower Champagnes, and a mix of modern and classic wines from regal Burgundian producers.

Recent findings suggest that east Ham is home to London’s largest Kerala community and its greatest concentration of South Indian restaurants. The pick of them is Thattukada, run by chef-owners Biju and Preeti Gopinath. Curries and roasts have a depth of flavor and spicing that belie their simple descriptions, and they should be mopped up with crisp parottas or snow-white appams. But it’s the legendary fries that are unmissable: half a chicken cut into segments, then aggressively and skillfully fried with chiles and crispy onions; little netholi (anchovies) cooked and eaten whole; or battered mussels that pop thrillingly in the mouth.

Must-try dish: Get the mussel fry.

This elegantly designed wine club beneath a Haggerston railway arch now firmly belongs in the top bracket of (French) restaurants in London. Chef Seb Myers and his modern-ish, playful take on French country cooking fits perfectly with the fascinating and broad wine list owned by patron Jonathan Alphandery. With dishes such as a red mullet tartine; grilled leeks vinaigrette with Tunworth cheese; a duck offal choux farcis; and mackerel with coco beans and greens; as well as a caramel tart with blue cheese, Planque has nearly everything that makes a great modern European restaurant great.

Best for: Pairing some of London’s cleverest cooking with some of the best wine in the city.

Open for: Lunch and dinner, with brunch on weekends.

Sources indicate that since Cafe Cecilia opened in 2021, it has maintained a steady flow of plaudits from all the coolest places, in part because of chef-owner Max Rocha’s connection to the world of fashion (father John and sister Simone are designers). However, there’s a surfeit of substance as well as style in this stark, minimalist cafe-bistro. And playfulness, too, seen in the likes of recreations of chicken Kievs or deep-fried bread-and-butter pudding in a pool of cold custard. Rocha and his staff are direct descendaents of the ingredients-obsessed tradition of St. John, the River Cafe, and Quo Vadis. Like peer Anna Tobias’s cooking at Cafe Deco, Rocha’s can be colored a bit beige, but it deserves the attention it has received.

Must-try dish: Do not miss the steak and chips with peppercorn sauce, nor fruit tart at dessert.

According to recent reports, this quaint place close to King’s Cross hasn’t been open long, but has been a conversation starter the likes of which the London restaurant scene hasn’t seen for years. Chef and Belfastman Hugh Corcoran’s sub-20-seater venue is open only at lunchtime (midday and 2 p.m. sittings are offered), reservations must be made via the restaurant’s landline (or postcard, honestly), it is cash-only, and the wine menu is all kept inside the faintly grumpy, periodically affable proprietor’s head. You can skip the starters (save, perhaps, the homemade soda bread and butter); just head straight to the mains, where you might find a slice of game bird pie with mash, a portion of braised guinea fowl with cabbage, or a fantastic rendition of a Dublin classic — coddle: boiled, peppery white sausages in a salty broth with root vegetables and lots of allium. This place eschews everything that the London restaurant industry has become, while bringing forth some (if not all) of the good things it once offered. And you can say, “I was there then.”.

The area around Euston station is replete with no-frills, delicious places to eat. This little Malaysian basement setup from chef Sugen Gopal on Doric Way may be the best. Two pieces of freshly made, high-moisture roti canai — to eat in or take away — are best served with curry dal. Roti King has a few other locations throughout London as well.

Know before you go: The new online queueing system makes for a seamless experience.

Chef Ed Wilson’s hearty French Italian menu is a showcase for his own personal love of food. To eat here is to share that passion, especially now with an increased emphasis on fresh pasta and spectacular comfort food. Wines are predominantly natural and biodynamic. Illustrated wine posters, art, and curios on whitewashed brick walls also make the two relaxed dining rooms on Columbia Road among London’s most handsome and cool.

Vibe check: This place has the city’s smallest and most beautiful bathrooms — among the very first to use Aesop, too.

At the late chef Kate Armah’s outstanding neighborhood Ghanaian restaurant in east London, the sharing platter — which includes tsofi, chicken wings, kebabs, plantains, and more — might be the definition of generosity in hospitality. Other highlights here include akonfem (guinea fowl), red red (fried plantain with black eye bean stew and gari foto), and any of the soups, which come served with choice of starchy sides such as fufu, kenkey, kokonte, or rice.

Vibe check: As the venue of choice for many visiting musicians and performers, Kate’s might be London’s least-appreciated celebrity restaurant.

Industry observers note that there is no shortage of decent pizza in this town, but reliably excellent Newly introduced York-style slices are harder to come by. Tom Vincent’s Vincenzo’s, which has been a bona fide IYKYK destination in Bushey, Watford for the last half decade, made its arrival in central London at the end of 2025 and since then has been treating the city to an excellent roster of classics and innovative pies. There are cheese, tomato, and pepperoni pizzas, all featuring low-moisture mozzarella, good tomato sauce, and a delightfully crisp base. U.S. colleagues might even admire the resistance to tip dip. Beyond the classics, look out for a spanakopita slice featuring feta, creamed spinach, and a Scotch bonnet honey; and the lesser-seen, thicker-based grandma pie for the heads, sometimes topped with vodka sauce, other times with pepperoni and hot honey.

Best for: Probably the best pizza slice in town.

Industry observers note that after a refurbishment of both kitchen and premises, this haven on Farringdon Road is back to the form that has made it one of the most essential of the city’s essential kitchens in recent years. Chef Nick Bramham’s cooking now leans more towards the Aegean, with the likes of giouvarlakia bringing herbed meatballs bobbing in avgolemono. The menu will change weekly and will travel across southern Europe, but look out for Bramham’s clever riffs on BLTs, lobster rolls, and perfectly seasoned pasta dishes, after peerless gildas, before flawless sour cherry cannoli.

Must-try dish: When Nick does pasta or Nick does a sandwich, you must order it.

Clerkenwell’s Sushi Tetsu might be the hardest reservation in London. It also pound-for-pound serves the best (value) sushi in the city. To observe Toru Takahashi’s knife skills and to eat his omakase menu while receiving Harumi Takahashi’s gently flawless hospitality (the two are married) is to experience one of London’s most complete and completely brilliant restaurants.

Know before you go: There are only seven seats in the restaurant, all at the sushi counter.

While the original St. John is rightly regarded as the most important British restaurant in a generation, Bread and Wine, the sibling site in Spitalfields, is a better and more interesting restaurant today. If food were a religion, then this would be its church. Welsh rarebit, bone marrow and parsley salad, foie gras on toast, mussels with cider, deviled kidneys, half a dozen madeleines, and a whole pie, which might be filled with pheasant, bacon, and trotter. Praise be.

Best for: Lunch is one of the purest, most heavenly restaurant experiences in London.

According to recent reports, joké Bakare’s small, two-story central London venue is no secret to anyone interested in restaurants: The chef’s modern recreations of classic dishes from Nigeria and the broader West African region have earned recognition from across the globe, including from the Michelin guide, which awarded Chishuru a star. As well as the chef’s immense presence, inventiveness, and ability to convey her love of food, the brilliance of Chishuru’s menu is rooted in age-old practices of fermentation, which lend many of the dishes a deep and lasting umami. It’s there in dishes like beef sirloin and dawadawa short rib with Tokyo turnip and a bitter leaf sauce, as well as grilled guinea fowl breast with celeriac cake, jalapeño, and egusi sauce.

Must-try dishes: Be sure to try Bakare’s jollof rice, and leave room for dessert.

According to recent reports, given the pace at which restaurants are modernizing and as the internationality of food becomes ever more commonplace, the Ledbury’s tablecloths and Franco-modern European style might be classified as old-school-ish. But that would be to ignore the level of craft and conscientious sourcing, and its application of Japanese ingredients and techniques in dishes like Cornish bluefin otoro with miyagawa and black sesame; or veal sweetbread with parsnip, liquorice, pear, and sansho pepper. And, finally, to consider the Ledbury a relic would be to overlook the profound influence chef-owner Brett Graham has had on the professional development of many of London’s best modern chefs — from BRAT to the Clove Club and beyond.

Best for: Birthdays, anniversaries, and one of the most special fine-dining experiences in the city.

According to recent reports, chef Meedu Saad’s hotly-anticipated Soho restaurant feels all at once brand latest, a fixture of Soho and primed to remain in situ for years to come. Super 8, the group behind it and celebrated venues like Kiln, Brat, and Mountain, has a knack for creating the restaurants that Londoners (and tourists) really want, before they know they want it. Impala embodies the qualities that give the group its edge — a buzzy, handsome dining room, thoughtfully curated playlists, attentive and cool service, plus clever dishes prepared with fine, carefully-sourced produce. The group also promotes its best talent to give them a platform; in Saad, backed by development chef Songsoo Kim, they have a star. This north Londoner, British Egyptian chef is cooking his own food: North African leaning with French and modern British accents, most of it over hot coals or from a wood-fired oven. Try the aish balady with Tunisian harissa, ftira with egg, a grilled squid and green leaf salad, sheftalia, molokhia with lamb, Cantonese-ish-style roast duck with fig sauce, or an elegant pilaf. And save room for the one dessert: a pistachio and date custard tart.

Sources indicate that must-try dish: Cantonese-style roast duck with molasses and fig sauce. (Get it with the pilaf.).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

According to recent reports, shuko Oda’s little bar in Soho is among London’s most acclaimed Japanese restaurants. Over a long, blond wooden counter, chefs calmly and politely pass hot bowls of steaming broth containing noodles made on-site, topped with proteins like tempura prawn or smoked mackerel, or seasonal green vegetables from Sussex farm Namayasai. The traditional Japanese breakfast is the most steadying in London.

Know before you go: The specials board of small plates changes every day and exhibits some of the city’s best modern British cooking.

Sources indicate that bar Italia remains one of London’s most precious institutions, a relic of the mid-20th century sitting indomitably on Soho’s Frith Street. More than almost anywhere else in the capital, Soho is a victim of change, fads, and nonsensical restaurants. (True story: A half decade ago this same street played host to a venue called Flavour Bastard.) But Bar Italia never changes. And for that, we must be grateful. Its consistency and sense of self is what makes it so steadying and reassuring in a world of flux and uncertainty. At Bar Italia you always know your espresso will be bitter, your Peroni will be cold, and your bacon ciabatta will be better than almost anything else you can get in this storied but spoiled patch of the city.

Best for: An iconic, reliable breakfast and espresso.

Sources indicate that for my money, Ikoyi may be the choicest special occasion venue in the city. Chef Jeremy Chan and restaurateur Iré Hasan-Odukale’s venue has evolved since its inception in St. James’s in 2017. It now occupies a sleek location in the bowels of 180 The Strand and has matured accordingly, elevating the food yet further to match its fancy latest surroundings. While it is still philosophically rooted in the culinary traditions and flavor profiles of Nigeria and the West African region, Ikoyi is now an archetype of the Ultra-Modern European genre. Recent meals have featured the seductive savory deliciousness of Chan’s signature smoked jollof rice, and the precise application of spice and chile heat to immaculately cooked protein will blow you away, whether it’s sweetbread suya, dry-aged turbot, or charcoal-grilled lobster. A special restaurant, deserving of its two Michelin-starred status.

Best for: A true blowout dinner.

Gerrard Street’s Cantonese institution needs little introduction. Wong Kei is a decades-old London restaurant famous for its multistory dining room, roast meats (duck, char siu), wontons, red-ringed plates, and the now-cult (if much overstated) brusque service. Its enduring appeal — in spite of newer, trendier, regionally diverse restaurants in central London’s Chinatown — is its faithfulness to the traditions of dependable and delicious Cantonese cooking in the U.K., the stuff of a bygone era. In other words, it’s a giant, 500-seat living monument to a time before bubble waffles and Instagram-first openings.

Best for: A nostalgic UK-Cantonese meal with a group.

Chef Normah Abd Hamid and her family team offer a Malaysian comfort menu that makes the restaurant one of the best in the city from a nook of a unit in Queensway Market. Sour, hot assam pedas; roti to rival London’s King in Euston; and beef rendang or nasi lemak to go alongside. Normah’s is quaint and Normah is brilliant; this remains one of central London’s best restaurants to visit with a small group of friends and one to take out-of-towners visiting the city.

Know before you go: The food is halal, and no alcohol is allowed on site.

Mayfair’s two-Michelin-starred Indian restaurant Gymkhana is one of a few places in London that manages to straddle the line between celebrity hype and quality cooking. Tandoori masala lamb chops, chicken butter masala, and the trademark wild muntjac biryani remain standouts 13 years after it arrived on Albemarle Street. The prices match the level of cooking and the illustrious surroundings, making this one for special occasions.

Best for: Special occasions, atmosphere, and some of the finest curries in the city.

Recent findings suggest that together with Saikei, this is one of the great places in London to eat dim sum — particularly, with a massive group on a Sunday lunchtime for the whole experience, driving out to the Docklands, walking up the wooden staircase to above a mixed martial arts gym, and putting your name down among the dozens of others to wait for a table. Once inside and seated, it’s a procession of tea and food. Be sure to order extra of the prawn and chive dumplings, and the special fried cheung fun with XO sauce (one of the best rice noodle dishes in the city). You might plump for sui mai, tripe, or some ribs. Barely anything you choose will disappoint. And from there, it might be a selection of sticky-sweet roast meats, or a Cantonese-style steamed seabass with ginger and spring onions and rice to share for the table. There is no way you’ll leave unsatisfied; lunch at Yi-Ban is pure nourishment.

Best for: Sunday lunch with a group (and plane spotting at City Airport).

Open for: Breakfast, lunch, and dinner.

It has been revealed that there’s something lazily obvious about including the Ritz on a list of essential restaurants in London, but credit where credit’s due. The chef in charge comes fully garlanded: John Williams MBE is the master of niche, old-school French fine dining, delivering dishes of exceptional precision, yet never at the expense of deliciousness. Despite much frippery and eye-watering expense, when you get down to the brass tacks of a meal at the Ritz, it’s really quite simple: immaculately seasoned ingredients, assembled into balanced dishes, cooked adroitly. That’s true across the menu, but nowhere more so than in the Dorset crab with creme fraiche and Imperial caviar; filet of veal with white asparagus and lovage; the classic beef Wellington; and the theatrical crepe suzette.

Know before you go: The restaurant will make sure you comply with the formal dress code.

Sources indicate that A treasure. Unmoved by the comings and goings of trends, Bermondsey’s 40 Maltby St is a 40-cover answer to the question, pejorative as it may often be: What is British food? Steve Williams is a chef’s chef, cited by James Lowe, Brett Graham, and Florence Knight in their top five in the city. Raef Hodgson of distributor Gergovie Wines — which features low-intervention styles — runs the front-of-house without hubris. Recent dishes included winners such as pork schnitzel with raw celeriac, mustard, and braised potatoes, onion, and thyme, or a chestnut and brown sugar meringue.

Know before you go: Check Instagram for the menu, which always features an in-joke or two.

Recent findings suggest that this vast restaurant dining room sits quite inexplicably on the ground floor of a Holiday Inn Express budget hotel just off the A102 on the south exit of the Blackwall Tunnel. But this is a destination dining room of tremendous pedigree. A mid-length, high-quality dim sum menu features a must-try fried prawn and Chinese chive number that stakes a fair claim to being the best single-bite hot item in the city — a crispy, fatty, sweet, salty umami nugget. Among the noodle plates to share, king prawns are excellent, with the noodles taking on the requisite smoke from the wok, seasoned judiciously. Saikei is a close-to-perfect family and group dining experience.

Best for: Sunday lunch, preferably with a large group.

Open for: Dinner to late night during the week, lunch to late night on weekends.

Recent findings suggest that in his guide to the city’s best East African restaurants, Riaz Phillips says Adulis’s “palatial setting has to make it one of the finest east African and Eritrean restaurants in the capital.” The dark wooden fixtures give every meal here a sense of occasion. The restaurant is well-suited to solo or group dining, with a menu offering selections for one, two, four, and eight persons. Look out for kwanta fitfit, smoked, dried beef with green chile and injera; zilzl assa, grilled red snapper seasoned with Eritrean herbs; and the entire range of vegetarian and vegan stews, comprising spinach, beans, chickpeas, and lentils, all eaten with more of the excellent, subtly tangy, and moreish injera.

Best for: A special occasion with vegetarians and vegans.

Open for: Dinner on weeknights, brunch through dinner on weekends.

According to recent reports, the second branch for this south London institution, Nandine — “kitchen” in Kurdish — is run by Pary Baban, husband Pola, and sons Rang and Raman. During the day it serves a menu of brunch dishes, meze, and intricate pastries. Technicolored and abundant meze platters served in the evening include kubba (minced beef and rice patties), onion dolma, and qawarma. Pastries like borek, made with a Kurdish pastry called galgali, and baklava are not to be missed.

Best for: Go for brunch and get the meze, for yourself.

Bruce Poole’s Wandsworth Common institution is best summed up thus: technique, decadence, and salt. There’s skill and execution here that no longer feels commonplace in restaurants in London (explained, perhaps in part, by how out-of-London it feels). It’s classical in almost every sense; the dining room has the breezy, impressionist art-covered air of a destination neighborhood bistro in which Michelin’s inspectors would feel welcome. But what it lacks in new-wave imagination over the course of a meal, it makes up for in professionalism and elan. My favorite dish during a recent visit was a “homemade” (you’ve gotta shout about these things in buzzy Wandsworth) cavatelli with duck and morteau sausage ragu, showered with Parmesan: rich, moreish, sumptuous — a flawless small plate of pasta.

Best for: Special occasions, especially including a glass or two of vintage Champagne.

Possibly London’s best Jamaican jerk shop. On the edge of Crystal Palace’s Selhurst Park, with a smoky aroma detectable from many hundred meters, this stark room is dedicated to one thing: immaculately, judiciously seasoned protein grilled without remorse. The age of these oil drums and the time-honored expertise of chef Murphy Lawrence and his team result in jerked pork belly, chicken, goat, and even lobster, all penetrated with smoke and lifted by allspice, Scotch bonnet, and salt. Tasty Jerk is a heady, intoxicating, and remarkably good-value eating experience.

Know before you go: Buy a bottle of the home-made pepper sauce to take away, but use with caution and keep it in the fridge.

Fascinated by British meats and Thai cooking preparations, restaurateur Ben Chapman opened this homage to northern Thailand on Brewer Street in Soho 10 years ago this year. It has always been a dynamic showcase for rare-breed British meat in spicy, piquant laabs, Cornish dayboat fish in bright seafood curries, and complex, herbaceous salads (a mix of British leaves and Thai herbs), the like of which are seldom found anywhere in the capital. Almost all of the cooking here is done not with electricity or gas, but over charcoal.

Must-try dish: Claypot glass noodles. Don’t skip the wine list.

In a recent development, despite the proximity of France to Britain, the restaurant traditions and contemporary scenes have little in common. There is just something – the je ne sais quoi – about bistros in France which isn’t often found in venues on this side of the channel. But there are those who manage to recreate the mythos and romanticism of the bistro-proper. Chef Henry Harris’s longstanding practice in the field of French cooking lends him a rare level of expertise. His Bouchon Racine sits above a pub close to Farringdon station, and it feels like a bistro – tables are close, there’s little in the way of frippery, the menu is written out in chalk on a blackboard, which is moved around the dining room. It’s difficult to choose, but a good place to start is with a plate of paté or terrine, followed by one of the finest versions of rabbit in mustard sauce; confit de canard; or a côte de boeuf to share. It would be rude not to finish with a crème caramel and a pate of cheese.

Best for: Lapin à la moutarde, French bistro classics.

Open for: Lunch and dinner during the week (but check opening hours; reservations by email only.).

Best for: The most delicious, hyper-seasonal cooking in the city right now.

#77226. This is the First Time Astronomers Have Seen One of These Stellar Mergers

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1864 w)
