About three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 to 2023 had CTE

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1031 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A upcoming study estimates that about three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 had CTE, even after accounting for brain donation bias.
  • Almost every former NFL player’s brain that researchers have examined has shown signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the degenerative disease tied to repeated hits to the head.
  • The study estimated that families were more likely to donate a player’s brain if he had clear cognitive symptoms.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A upcoming study estimates that about three in four former NFL players who died from 2008 through 2023 had CTE, even after accounting for brain donation bias.

Almost every former NFL player’s brain that researchers have examined has shown signs of chronic traumatic encephalopathy (CTE), the degenerative disease tied to repeated hits to the head.

The study estimated that families were more likely to donate a player’s brain if he had clear cognitive symptoms.

Researchers at Boston University have now worked out how much that choice skews the picture.

It has been revealed that the team’s estimate: about three in four NFL players who died between 2008 and 2023 had CTE. That includes the roughly five in six whose brains were not examined.

Three in four is lower than the figure from donated brains alone, where more than nine in ten had the disease. But the researchers stated the skew in who donates can’t explain the high rate away.

Julia Gallini, a doctoral candidate in biostatistics at the Boston University School of Public Health, led the analysis with Yorghos Tripodis, a professor of biostatistics there.

Colleagues at the university’s CTE Center, Mass General Brigham and the Concussion & CTE Foundation joined them.

The figure applies to players after death only and states nothing about living former players or current ones.

Gallini mentioned a precise number helps size the problem.

“An estimated 75% prevalence among NFL players who died over a 16-year period is concerning, and suggests we need to increase efforts to support families, diagnose CTE during life, and treat CTE-related symptoms,” she said.

It has been revealed that CTE can only be confirmed after death, by examining the brain. So nearly everything known about it in football players comes from brains donated to a bank in Boston, and a 2017 study of 111 of them found CTE in 110.

It has been revealed that families don’t donate at random. A player who grew confused or forgetful in his last years is the one whose family thinks to call a brain bank.

So the donated brains carry more disease than the full population of former players would.

It has been revealed that epidemiologists call this selection bias. Earlier attempts to allow for it could only bracket the true figure somewhere between roughly 10% and 100%.

The team started with every former NFL player who died between January 2008 and December 2023, 2,362 men in all.

Industry observers note that they were found through the National Death Index, the national register of death certificates. Of those, 396 had donated their brains and 1,966 had not.

The death certificates gave the researchers one fact they could compare across both groups: whether dementia was recorded as a cause of death. It was for 19.3% of donors and 11.2% of the others.

Because many people with failing memory die of something else, the team widened that category using survey estimates of milder cognitive trouble in former players.

Then they ran the comparison 1,000 times to capture the uncertainty.

Recent findings suggest that the result was a ratio. A former player with clear cognitive symptoms was about five times as likely to have his brain donated as one without them.

In a recent development, donors also died younger, at 67 on average against nearly 75. They had played longer too, seven years against under five.

Among the 387 donated brains with a clear verdict, 362 had CTE, or 93.5%.

After adjusting for differences in donation likelihood, the researchers estimated that 74.5% of all 2,362 players had CTE at death.

Industry observers note that the team then tested how much that number depended on their assumptions. They restricted the sample to players who died at 55 or older, then 60 or older, and tried other definitions of who counted as symptomatic.

Across those versions, the estimate ranged from 70% to 86%.

It has been revealed that the main figure sat toward the lower end of that range. The most conservative analysis put the figure at 63.7%.

Suppose symptomatic players had been ten times as likely to donate, rather than five. Even then, the authors calculated, more than 60% of the dead players would have had the disease.

CTE in the brain is not the same as symptoms in life.

Using the same correction, the team estimated that 27.2% of the players had a history of dementia before they died. In the donated group alone, the figure was 64.9%.

The authors said the true lifetime figure is probably higher than 27.2%. The donors it rests on died about eight years younger than the other players, with less time to develop dementia.

Many of the brains with CTE, they added, may have been at an early stage and symptom-free at death.

Matt Hasselbeck, an 18-year NFL veteran who serves as an ambassador for a research study called DIAGNOSE CTE, noted the numbers read to him like a scouting report.

In a recent development, the correction rests on a stand-in. Death certificates and survey estimates of memory trouble stood in for a direct look at the players whose brains were not examined. Dementia is also often left off a death certificate.

Sources indicate that the authors also could not say whether CTE itself shortens life. That is one more reason the estimate stops at the dead and does not reach anyone still living.

Nothing here covers college or high school players, whose death records and symptom surveys don’t exist in the same form.

The authors mentioned those estimates would be far harder to build, and that building them matters for sizing the problem.

Tripodis said the group recognizes the findings may worry living players and their families.

“Discoveries from the brain bank have already brought us significantly closer to a diagnosis during life, at which point our most notable goal will be to develop effective treatments for CTE,” he noted.

Until a living player can be tested for CTE, the dead are the only ones who can be counted.

The full study was published in the journal JAMA Network Open.

Sources indicate that for enthusiasts, tire shopping is an upgrade, not a chore. While the casual driver might treat fresh tires like regular maintenance, anyone who cares about vehicle dynamics knows that what meets the road defines how a truck or SUV rides, tracks, and stops. It is the single most transformative upgrade you can make to your vehicle. For more than 110 years, Cooper tires have catered to drivers who look past the showroom floor and seek out products that overdeliver on performance, capability, and long-term durability.

According to recent reports, and that level of purpose-built engineering is more vital than ever. As vehicles grow heavier and more capable, tires need to do more than simply roll down an interstate. They have to withstand heavy payload demands, sudden weather changes, and unpredictable pavement. Cooper tires are built to that benchmark. Rooted in American engineering and real-world development, Cooper tires are built to an uncompromising standard that live up to their promises. From the rock-crawling STT Pro to the severe-snow-designated Stronghold AT, the Discoverer® family has earned its reputation through real-world testing from Alaskan ice to jagged mountain trails.

The newly introduced Cooper Discoverer® HT adapts that rugged all-terrain lineage for long-distance highway cruising, matching heavy-duty capability with quiet, refined composure. While it retains the structural durability to wander down a gravel trail with a trailer in tow, its core mission is maximizing comfort and control across hundreds of miles of open road.

Where many highway tires trade load capability for a soft ride, the Discoverer® HT is engineered to handle both. Straight, reinforced sidewalls provide the structural foundation needed to maintain an optimal contact patch under load. Whether the vehicle is running light or carrying family, gear, and tongue weight, the tire resists deformation, ensuring consistent steering response and predictable roadholding grip in any condition. It’s engineered for drivers whose tires have to hold their own—providing a dependable, hard-working partner that won’t fold when the truck or SUV is pushed to its limit.

It has been revealed that cooper tires also tackle truck and SUV tire performance, with advanced features. Its proprietary 3-D Micro-Gauge Siping incorporates interlocking zig-zag sipes inside the tread blocks. Under heavy braking, sharp turns, or loaded acceleration, these interlocking sipes lock together to stiffen the tread block, to help support responsiveness. Crucially, these sipes run deep into the tread rubber, ensuring that gripping edges are still present to help with traction. That structural integrity backs up an exceptional UTQG treadwear rating of 720 and a 70,000-mile limited treadwear warranty on passenger fitments.

This is the tire for drivers who expect their trucks or suvs to show up for the long haul. Whether that means towing a camper into the backcountry, handling moving-day payloads, or eating up cross-country interstate miles in quiet comfort, the mission remains the same: a single set of tires that balances real-world traction, refined manners, and hard-working capability.

In a recent development, to fit that wide spectrum of work, Cooper offers the Discoverer® HT across 19 passenger sizes covering 16- to 22-inch wheels (with section widths from 245 to 285 mm), alongside 16 light-truck (LT) options engineered with deeper tread grooves and higher load ratings. Backed by a 45-day satisfaction guarantee and over a century of research and development, the Discoverer® HT delivers what Cooper has always stood for: the quiet confidence that the job was done right.

#77160. How one barley variety defends itself against crop pests and the virus they spread

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1731 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

How one barley variety defends itself against crop pests and the virus they spread

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1731 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In lab tests, fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel barley, and those that did struggled to feed.
  • It has been revealed that aphids are known to feed on the sap of barley plants.
  • It has been revealed that in response, breeders have introduced DNA from a wild relative of barley into commercial crops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In lab tests, fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel barley, and those that did struggled to feed. The variety also slowed the buildup of barley yellow dwarf virus.

It has been revealed that aphids are known to feed on the sap of barley plants. During feeding they can also transmit barley yellow dwarf virus. Plants infected with this virus become yellow and stunted and produce less grain.

It has been revealed that in response, breeders have introduced DNA from a wild relative of barley into commercial crops. Its protective effect was believed to operate mainly after the virus had entered the plant.

This wild DNA is carried by a commercial hybrid known as SY Kestrel. A new study found that the hybrid also makes it harder for aphids to settle and feed.

The aphids avoided its smell and fed poorly on its leaves and they also produced fewer offspring.

The research was carried out by Rumiana Ray’s group at the University of Nottingham. Scientists from Keele University and Syngenta were also involved in the project. SY Kestrel itself was developed by Syngenta.

Funding for the study came from Syngenta, and two of the authors are employed by the manufacturer.

All of the experiments were conducted on young plants in growth rooms and insect cages rather than in farm fields.

Professor Rumiana Ray led the research.

In a recent development, “What makes this discovery particularly exciting is that resistance is not simply about stopping a virus once it enters the plant. We have found that barley can defend itself at different stages of the aphid-plant interaction,” stated Professor Ray.

In severe cases a winter barley crop can lose as much as 50% of its yield to the virus. According to the UK’s Agriculture and Horticulture Development Board, losses of this size are uncommon.

Sources indicate that chemical control is expected to become less effective over time. The authors linked this to growing insecticide resistance in aphids and to their lengthening migration periods.

The bird cherry-oat aphid is regarded as the main carrier of the virus. It picks up the virus from an infected plant and passes it on when it moves to a latest one.

Industry observers note that SY Kestrel contains a block of DNA from Hordeum bulbosum, which is a wild grass related to barley. Within this block lies a resistance region known as Ryd4Hb.

Earlier research had linked this region to the blocking of the virus once an aphid had delivered it.

For comparison the researchers used a second hybrid named Tektoo.

Sources indicate that this hybrid was bred from the same mother line and from a very similar father line. Unlike SY Kestrel, it carries none of the wild DNA.

It has been revealed that aphids from a single laboratory colony were used throughout the experiments on both hybrids. Part of this colony had been allowed to acquire the virus beforehand while the remainder was kept virus free.

In the first experiment, 20 winged aphids were released into a cage that held one plant of each hybrid.

The positions in which the insects settled were then recorded at intervals over the following 24 hours.

Six cages were used in this test and the entire experiment was later repeated in full.

More than 75% fewer aphids settled on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

Sources indicate that A large part of this difference could be attributed to the smell of the plants. In a separate test the air surrounding each plant was collected and offered to aphids with no plant present.

Under these conditions the insects were attracted to the odor of Tektoo but moved away from that of SY Kestrel.

The chemicals that made up each odor were then examined individually by the research team.

Heneicosane was one compound that was present in the air around Tektoo but absent from SY Kestrel. Aphids were attracted to heneicosane and those exposed to it subsequently produced a greater number of young.

According to recent reports, in the air around SY Kestrel two compounds were detected that were not released by Tektoo. When they were tested separately both of these compounds were shown to repel the insects.

According to recent reports, infection with the virus was also found to alter the scent of Tektoo plants. Virus-free aphids preferred the odor of infected Tektoo plants while virus-carrying aphids preferred that of healthy plants.

In a recent development, this reversal has been interpreted in earlier studies as manipulation of the insect by the virus it carries. In SY Kestrel no comparable reversal could be detected by the researchers.

The odor of this hybrid repelled both groups of aphids regardless of whether the plant had been infested.

Despite the repellent odor a number of aphids did eventually settle on SY Kestrel.

Their feeding behavior was studied by attaching each insect to a fine gold wire. With this method the electrical signals from the mouthparts of each aphid could be recorded inside the leaf.

The recordings indicated that aphids on both hybrids were able to reach the tubes that carry sugary sap. No meaningful difference was found between the two plants in how readily these tubes were reached.

Sources indicate that after reaching the sap the aphids on SY Kestrel spent a longer time releasing saliva into the tubes. Sustained drinking of sap in bouts longer than 10 minutes was also markedly reduced on this hybrid.

This impaired feeding was associated with a reduction in the number of offspring produced.

On SY Kestrel the winged aphids carrying the virus produced about 40% fewer young than on Tektoo.

The survival of wingless aphids was also lower on SY Kestrel and their reproduction was reduced as well.

It is well established that plants rely on chemical defenses for protection against insects. In the leaves of SY Kestrel higher levels were found of three compounds that later proved harmful to aphids.

Each compound was tested by adding it to an artificial diet on which aphids fed for three days.

The compounds reduced the survival of aphids that were free of the virus. Aphids carrying the virus were less sensitive, and one of the compounds had no clear effect on them.

In a recent development, the team next examined plants that had been fed on by aphids carrying the virus. Fewer symptoms were seen on SY Kestrel than on Tektoo.

In a recent development, the amount of viral genetic material in the leaves of SY Kestrel was also much lower. By the tenth day the virus could no longer be detected. This measurement was based on three samples from each group.

The virus therefore faced three separate barriers in SY Kestrel.

In a recent development, fewer aphids settled on the plant in the first place. The aphids that did settle fed poorly, and the virus they delivered failed to build up.

“Rather than relying on a single barrier, the crop can discourage aphids from settling, interfere with their feeding and restrict the virus they transmit,” Ray stated.

The efficiency with which each leaf converted light into energy was measured as well.

This conversion represents the first step of photosynthesis and readings were taken daily from the second to the ninth day.

Sources indicate that by the ninth day a decline in this efficiency had been recorded in Tektoo. The decline occurred in Tektoo whether or not the aphids feeding on it were carrying the virus.

A different pattern was observed in SY Kestrel when it was attacked by aphids carrying the virus.

In those plants the efficiency of light conversion remained close to the level recorded in plants without aphids. Feeding by aphids that were free of the virus did lower efficiency in SY Kestrel.

Changes in gene activity and leaf chemistry were recorded at the same time. Immune genes were involved in these changes along with the chloroplasts in which photosynthesis is carried out.

A group of fat-derived molecules that serve as stress signals in plants was affected as well.

According to the authors the continued function of the chloroplasts may help SY Kestrel to sustain its defense signals.

Several other plant viruses are already known to target the same chloroplast proteins. This has not yet been demonstrated for barley yellow dwarf virus.

According to recent reports, SY Kestrel and Tektoo are not genetically identical outside the wild DNA. For this reason the authors acknowledged that some differences between the hybrids may originate elsewhere in their genomes.

The block of wild DNA carried by SY Kestrel is also considerably larger than the Ryd4Hb region itself. In a 2024 study, barley lines carrying a much smaller piece of this wild DNA were examined.

Complete resistance to the virus was observed in those plants. However, there was little evidence that this resistance depended on any change in aphid behavior.

Considered together, the two studies suggest that the smell and feeding defenses may depend on other genes.

Such genes may be located within the larger wild block or in other regions of the plant genome. They have not yet been identified.

Recent findings suggest that the question is important for plant breeding. According to the authors, a smaller wild block may still provide strong resistance to the virus. Some of the defenses against aphids could be lost in the process.

“Understanding these complementary mechanisms offers latest opportunities to develop crop varieties with broader and potentially more durable resistance,” Ray noted.

It has been revealed that dr. James Melichar is the Hybrid Cereals Portfolio Lead Europe at Syngenta.

“This research demonstrates the value of bringing together commercial breeding expertise and fundamental plant science to understand how resistance operates in crops,” noted Dr. Melichar.

“Identifying complementary mechanisms that affect aphid behaviour, feeding and virus infection provides valuable insights for developing barley varieties with broader and more effective protection.”.

The diet tests also have a limitation. In these tests the levels of each compound were estimated from extracts of whole leaves.

Such estimates may not reflect the levels present in the sap that aphids actually consume.

Further research will be needed to identify the genes behind the defenses against aphids. The levels of the compounds in the sap itself will also need to be measured.

The full study was published in the journal New Phytologist.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case.
  • Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.
  • A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Massie will force another vote on releasing files in the Jeffrey Epstein case. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call file photo).

Sources indicate that as Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., enters his final weeks in Congress, he is one step closer to another vote on legislation related to the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

A discharge petition led by Massie aimed at extracting more files from the Justice Department has now received enough support to force a vote on the House floor.

Recent findings suggest that rep. John Garamendi, D-Calif., was the decisive 218th signature on the discharge petition, a procedural tool allowing rank-and-file House members to register their support for a piece of legislation and circumvent leadership to force a vote. Massie and other supporters of the effort say the bill is a bid for transparency.

Earlier this week, Massie stated his pitch to his colleagues was simple.

“They could be a hero if they sign it,” he mentioned, as he chased down the final two signatures as the House returned from recess on Monday. Rep. Adam Smith, D-Wash., signed just before Garamendi.

Massie’s time left in office is ticking down after a challenger backed by President Donald Trump ousted him in his GOP primary earlier this year.

The petition marks the second push led by Massie to require the release of the Epstein files. Last fall, Massie and Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., led a discharge petition on a bill dubbed the Epstein Files Transparency Act, which directed the Justice Department to publicly release documents in its possession related to Epstein and his associate Ghislaine Maxwell.

Sources indicate that the bill passed the House by a vote of 427-1 last November, and in the Senate a few days later. Trump signed the measure shortly afterward.

In a statement this summer, Massie said he believes the Justice Department is still withholding more than 3 million files that it is required to release under the November 2025 law and is “maintaining heavy redactions” on others.

According to recent reports, the new bill would allow state attorneys general, local prosecutors and victims to sue the federal government for withholding such documents. It would also allow victims to privately view unredacted versions of any records that mention them.

Sources indicate that now that the new petition has reached 218 signatures, it must sit for seven legislative days before being called up by anyone who signed it. Last time around, Speaker Mike Johnson, R-La., scheduled a House vote on the initial Epstein bill before that ripening period was over, saying it was a foregone conclusion that the legislation would reach the floor.

It has been revealed that other Republicans who have signed on to the petition this year include Reps. Nancy Mace, R-S.C.; Ralph Norman, R-S.C., and Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., none of whom will be returning next Congress. Rep. Lauren Boebert, R-Colo., backed the initial effort last fall, but her name did not appear on the petition this time.

Allies of the problem in Congress have faced pushback from Trump. While the president suggested during his 2024 reelection campaign that he was open to declassifying some Epstein documents, Trump then shifted gears, calling them a “hoax.”.

“Once you get to 218, you can never sign it," Massie noted. "There's nobody left, no spots left. It goes straight to the floor, and then you can vote for it. But you were never part of the group that actually got it to the floor.".

#77158. Young emperor penguins spend their first year at sea alone, so where do they go?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1533 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Young emperor penguins spend their first year at sea alone, so where do they go?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1533 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Satellite tags tracked young emperor penguins from three Antarctic colonies, revealing where they roam and when proposed marine protections could help.
  • Juvenile emperor penguins are left to fend for themselves at sea for roughly a year after they fledge.
  • The young birds receive no guidance from their parents during this time and many do not survive it.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Satellite tags tracked young emperor penguins from three Antarctic colonies, revealing where they roam and when proposed marine protections could help.

Juvenile emperor penguins are left to fend for themselves at sea for roughly a year after they fledge.

The young birds receive no guidance from their parents during this time and many do not survive it.

Their routes were still found to be strikingly similar in a study of three colonies around Antarctica’s Weddell Sea.

The recurring pattern can help planners estimate when juvenile penguins would spend time inside proposed marine protected areas.

The study was led by Émile Brisson-Curadeau, a postdoctoral researcher at the Centre for Functional and Evolutionary Ecology (CEFE).

Daniel Zitterbart of the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution was a co-lead author. Céline Le Bohec of CEFE and the Centre Scientifique de Monaco shared that role.

“We were struck by the remarkable consistency of the penguins’ movements,” Brisson-Curadeau remarked.

Fishing vessel tracks were mapped as well, although the effect of fishing on the birds’ food was not measured.

Emperor penguins raise their chicks on sea ice that is attached to the coast of Antarctica.

The chicks develop waterproof feathers by late December and then leave for the open sea on their own.

Satellite tags were attached to 48 juveniles at the point when their new feathers had fully grown in.

A total of 28 birds came from Atka Bay at the eastern end of the Weddell Sea.

Around 8,000 pairs breed at that colony and its chicks were tagged over three summers between 2018 and 2023.

The remaining 20 juveniles were taken from Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula on the western side of the sea.

Each of these two colonies supports about 4,000 breeding pairs and their chicks were tagged during a single summer.

The movements of young emperor penguins from the western Weddell Sea had never been documented before this work.

Each tag was secured to the back feathers with tape and glue and weighed under 3% of body mass.

Industry observers note that most tags logged a position every four hours. Twelve of them also carried a pressure sensor for dive depth.

On average the juveniles travelled about 1,050 miles (1,688 km) from their colony at the farthest point of the trip.

The broad outline of this journey had already been described in earlier work carried out at Atka Bay.

No one had checked if it stayed the same across years, or across colonies on both sides of the sea.

In late summer, juveniles from Atka Bay, Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula all swam north.

By March, most had reached the waters just south of the Polar Front.

Here, cold Antarctic water meets warmer water from the north, and nutrient-rich upwelling feeds plankton and fish.

Upcoming sea ice starts forming in April. The penguins turned south to meet it and kept close to it all winter.

The ice reaches its greatest extent in August and September, and the birds moved north with its edge.

Once the ice began to melt, they headed back toward the continent.

By late December, most of the juveniles still being tracked had returned to waters near the coast, where they are thought to molt.

Multiple years of tracking were only available at Atka Bay, which made a direct comparison between years possible there.

Birds tagged in the same year were spread about as far apart as birds that were tagged in different years.

The authors suggest the juveniles may be following two stable features, namely the Polar Front and the sea ice edge.

It has been revealed that from April onward the position of the penguins was closely linked to how far north the sea ice extended. Before April the birds were swimming in open water that lay far away from any sea ice.

A total of 52,710 dives were recorded by the pressure sensors over the course of the study.

The average dive reached a depth of about 220 feet (68 m) and lasted a little more than three minutes.

The deepest dive recorded in the study went down to roughly 1,155 feet (352 m).

Sources indicate that dives tended to be shallow at night and deeper during daylight hours. Deeper dives were also observed farther north and where more of the sea surface was ice covered.

The authors wrote that the birds may feed on lanternfish when they are near the Polar Front.

These small deep-water fish contain more energy than the krill and silverfish eaten by breeding adults closer to Antarctica.

Two marine protected areas are already in place in the region and two more have been put forward. The Weddell Sea proposal has been developed by Germany and the European Union since 2012.

If adopted it would become the largest marine protected area in the world and include waters near all three colonies.

Juveniles from the western colonies already spent part of their time in existing protected areas. This share was 20.6% for Snow Hill Island birds and 29.3% for Jason Peninsula birds.

Atka Bay birds spent only 2.3% of their time in such zones by comparison.

Atka Bay juveniles spent 31.6% of their tracked time in waters covered by the proposed protected areas.

Snow Hill Island and Jason Peninsula birds spent 21.0% and 14.7% of their time there.

Use of the proposed areas peaked in January, during the fledglings’ first weeks at sea.

Death rates among inexperienced juveniles are high in those first weeks at sea so the timing matters.

“Most marine protected areas in Antarctica are planned with penguin colonies in mind,” Zitterbart said.

“They protect the areas around the colonies, which is critical for adult penguins, but they fail to cover the sea areas where juveniles spend their vulnerable early years.”.

Any newly introduced protected area in these waters needs the approval of every member of CCAMLR. This commission was set up in 1982 to conserve Antarctic marine life including krill.

Its members gathered in Hobart in October and left without agreeing on any new protected areas.

The main fishery in the region is aimed at Antarctic krill, which are small shrimp-like animals eaten by emperor penguins.

To estimate overlap the researchers relied on Global Fishing Watch, which is a public dataset of vessel activity.

It uses ship tracking signals to identify where fishing vessels are likely to be operating.

Fishing hours were totaled within about 62 miles (100 km) of each penguin location for the preceding year.

The waters used by juveniles from the two western colonies had more recorded fishing activity in the preceding year than the waters used by Atka Bay juveniles.

Much of this activity took place near the Antarctic Peninsula and in the waters around South Georgia.

Most of the overlap for these western birds occurred outside the boundaries of the planned protected areas.

Around Atka Bay the fishing effort stayed low for most months of the year.

January was the exception since the birds then used zones that had been fished heavily in 2022 and 2023.

Those zones are located within the proposed protected areas. Krill fishing there would be restricted to research and capped at one metric ton per vessel per year.

For comparison a typical fishing vessel in the region harvests about 40,000 metric tons over a year.

“Sustainable management of fishing activities, particularly their timing and intensity in key foraging areas, is essential to securing the food emperor penguins need and limiting the risk of bycatch,” Le Bohec noted.

Around one third of the global breeding population of emperor penguins is found in the Weddell Sea region.

The IUCN moved the species to Endangered in April after projecting that its numbers will halve by the 2080s.

That projection rests largely on the expected loss of Antarctic sea ice.

The study measured overlap in space and time and not the direct effect of fishing on penguin foraging.

According to the authors direct studies of foraging success would give stronger evidence for the value of protection.

Tag losses also reduced the sample as the year went on and only 10 tags still reported in month 12.

Dive data were only available until September because none of the dive-recording tags transmitted beyond that month.

Sea ice extent was relatively stable between 2018 and 2024 including during an El Niño year.

Under continued warming the Polar Front is expected to contract toward Antarctica and winter sea ice could decline.

Juveniles might then travel shorter distances north but struggle to find suitable ice in winter.

A southward contraction would also raise overlap with the planned zones that are concentrated near the continent.

According to the authors it remains to be determined whether this would offset the effects of climate change.

Accelerometers could be used in future work to link penguin foraging success with fishing pressure.

Foraging and breeding success could also be compared before and after protected areas come into force.

The Weddell Sea proposal has not been adopted and most of the juveniles’ year is spent outside protected waters.

The full study was published in the journal Biological Conservation.

The brain’s protective barrier also blocks medicine. This engineer wants a way through

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (283 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Sciencenews

💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Laura Sanders.
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • Industry observers note that rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Mandana Tadayon, Anna Mattson and Laura Sanders.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

Industry observers note that rebecca Pinals hadn’t planned to study neuroscience. But as she watched her grandmother decline from dementia, the chemical engineer decided to apply her talents to the human brain.

It has been revealed that at the time, “one of the big questions was, ‘how do we get access to it?’” says Pinals, of Stanford University. “I thought nanotechnology could be an interesting and useful toolkit to answer those types of questions.”.

One key access point is the blood-brain barrier, a dynamic microenvironment of cells that helps keep pathogens and other contaminants out of the brain. It’s so good at its job that drugs for treating dementia have a hard time penetrating it. It’s vital for researchers to understand this barrier, Pinals says, but it is so thin and fragile that they can’t observe it in real time without risking patient health.

According to recent reports, pinals and colleagues re-created the blood-brain barrier on a microchip. The team reprogrammed stem cells engineered from human skin, then coaxed the cells to form the barrier in a small 3-D chamber on the chip.

“As an engineer, this [system] is perfect,” Pinals indicates. “We love to take things apart and put them back together to learn how it’s made.”.

In a recent development, experts could use this scale model of the blood-brain barrier to figure out how to noninvasively access brains affected by neurodegenerative diseases. Pinals wants to use the device to investigate nanoparticles that could deliver drugs directly to patients’ brains.

According to recent reports, the best vacuum for your home is about more than just suction power and fancy features. It’s really about which type works with your floors, your cleaning habits, and the messes you deal with every day.

Sources indicate that A vacuum that excels at pulling pet hair out of plush carpet and off of upholstered furniture might be overkill for a small apartment with mostly hardwood floors. And while a robot vacuum takes some of the work off your hands, it probably shouldn’t be your only line of defense against stubborn dirt and debris.

After testing dozens of vacuums across different styles and floor types, I’ve learned that there isn’t exactly a one-size-fits-all solution. Here’s what to consider before you buy so you can find the best model, whether you have wall-to-wall carpeting, hardwood, tile, or a little bit of everything.

According to recent reports, carpet tends to hold quite a bit of dirt, dust, crumbs, and pet hair, so you’ll want a vacuum with enough agitation and suction to pull debris from in between the fibers. An upright vacuum, such as the Shark AZ2002 Vertex, is often a good choice, particularly if you have large carpeted rooms or thicker pile. Its motorized brush roll helps lift embedded dirt and hair, while a high-capacity dustbin or bag means fewer trips to the trash can. A sealed filtration system and HEPA filter are worth considering if you’re worried about fine dust and allergens.

It has been revealed that A canister vacuum is another strong option, especially if you have stairs, area rugs, or a mix of carpet and hard flooring. These models offer a separate motorized floorhead or interchangeable attachments, giving you more flexibility than a traditional upright vacuum. They’re not always the easiest to store because of extended hoses and extra pieces, but they’re workhorses.

Shark AZ2002 Vertex Powered Lift-Away Upright Vacuum.

Miele Classic C1 Turbo Team Bagged Canister Vacuum.

Bissell Pet Hair Eraser Allergen Lift-Off Upright Vacuum.

Recent findings suggest that for homes with mostly hardwood, laminate, vinyl, or tile, a lightweight cordless stick vacuum can be a practical choice for everyday cleaning. You don’t necessarily need an aggressive brush roll to clean hard floors, but you do want a floorhead that can pick up fine dust or large debris without scattering everything across the floor.

Industry observers note that some models, like the Dyson V15 Detect, have soft roller brushes that make close contact with hard floors, while others use multi-surface brush rolls that handle both hard floors and low-pile rugs. If your home has a combination of surfaces, look for a cordless stick vacuum with an automatic floor-detection feature that adjusts suction as you move between thresholds.

According to recent reports, cordless convenience is a significant selling point. You can grab your vacuum for a quick kitchen cleanup without dragging out a full-size model or having to look for an accessible wall outlet. Just pay attention to battery life, dustbin capacity, and how much suction you get at the highest power mode. Runtime claims can be optimistic when using motorized attachments or boost settings.

Tangle-resistant brush rolls, anti-hair-wrap technology, and specialized attachments make a noticeable difference when cleaning up after furry friends.

According to recent reports, both uprights and cordless stick vacuums are good choices here. A full-size upright, such as the Bissell CleanView Swivel Rewind offers the power and capacity for more demanding whole-home cleaning (without the hefty price tag, too). They work well for homes with mostly hard flooring where dust, crumbs, and everyday debris tend to accumulate quickly. Many newer models also handle low- to medium-pile carpeting, automatically adjusting suction when they detect a different surface.

If you’re shopping for one, pay attention to navigation, obstacle avoidance, and the size of the dustbin. Self-emptying docks are a huge help if you don’t want to empty the vacuum after every run. Some models, like the Roborock Qrevo Series QV 35A, have mopping capabilities, taking care of two different chores with one home appliance.

It has been revealed that I wouldn’t necessarily recommend a robot as your only vacuum if you have thick carpet, pets, or lots of furniture and tight corners. Think of it as a maintenance tool that handles daily stuff while a traditional vacuum takes care of a more thorough cleaning.

If convenience is the priority, a robot keeps everyday debris under control.

And remember, you don’t necessarily need one machine to do it all. Sometimes the best setup is actually a combination. The right choice is ultimately the one that makes cleaning your floors a little less of a chore.

#77155. Permanent daylight saving time could send millions of kids to school in the dark

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1088 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Permanent daylight saving time could send millions of kids to school in the dark

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1088 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new study estimates that permanent daylight saving time could add more than 2 billion trips to school before sunrise each year across the U.S.
  • In a recent development, permanent daylight saving time sounds like more daylight.
  • It moves from the morning to the evening, and from November to March that would have millions of American schoolchildren leaving home before the sun is up.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new study estimates that permanent daylight saving time could add more than 2 billion trips to school before sunrise each year across the U.S.

In a recent development, permanent daylight saving time sounds like more daylight. The hour doesn’t come from anywhere upcoming, though.

It moves from the morning to the evening, and from November to March that would have millions of American schoolchildren leaving home before the sun is up.

Researchers at the University of Washington counted what that would mean, school by school, in 14 of the 19 states that have already approved the change.

It has been revealed that the bill behind it, the Sunshine Protection Act, has passed the U.S. House but not the Senate, so the count is of a future that hasn’t happened yet.

Horacio de la Iglesia is a professor of biology at the university and the study’s senior author.

“It’s called the ‘Sunshine Protection Act’ because you get an extra hour of light at the end of the day. But you will take that hour from the morning. You could call it the Sunshine Destruction Act,” remarked Professor de la Iglesia.

Guadalupe Rodríguez Ferrante, a postdoctoral scholar in biology at the university, led a team that collected the actual start time of 16,093 public schools serving 8.6 million children.

Enrollment and locations came from the National Center for Education Statistics.

In a recent development, the team then worked out sunrise at each school on every school day. They ran it under three clocks: today’s system of switching twice a year, permanent standard time, and permanent daylight saving time.

Industry observers note that A commute counted as dark if a child would have to leave home 20 minutes before the bell and sunrise hadn’t happened yet. The team added those mornings up across every child in every school.

Across the 14 states, permanent daylight saving time would add about 356 million dark school mornings a year compared with the current system.

Extended to every public school in the country, with a fixed 8 a.m. departure, the figure is 2.14 billion extra dark commutes a year.

In an interview with Earth.com, Professor de la Iglesia remarked the effect would reach nearly everyone.

Industry observers note that “Parents should know that the number of mornings that their kids will go to school in the dark will increase dramatically under permanent DST. This will be true for virtually all children,” he mentioned.

The hardest-hit places are not the northern ones. Georgia, which already has 75 million dark commutes a year under the current clock, would have 146 million.

Washington state would go from about 20 million to 55 million. Mississippi and Alabama, where schools start before 8 a.m. on average, would each go from about 2 million to more than 20 million.

Industry observers note that what matters is where a school is inside its time zone. Sunrise comes later on the western edge of a zone, so Georgia, at the far west of Eastern Time, gets darker mornings than Maine at the far east of it.

Asked by Earth.com what surprised him most when the state numbers came in, Professor de la Iglesia named that pattern.

“That some of the hardest-hit States are not necessarily in a high northern latitude, like Georgia,” he said, and he put it down to Georgia’s position in its time zone.

Rodríguez Ferrante, who answered alongside him, noted the average student in Georgia would leave for school before sunrise on about 86 school days a year under permanent daylight saving time.

In Washington state, much farther north, she said the figure would be about 52.

For a single child in Washington, the change is 28 to 39 more dark mornings a year, depending on the grade level.

The team then turned to a decade of fatal crash records, 2015 through 2024, from the National Highway Traffic Safety Administration’s FARS database.

They kept only school-year weekdays between 7 and 8:30 a.m., which left 10,305 fatal crashes, and 1,754 of them involved a pedestrian.

“Among fatal crashes during the morning school commute, the percentage involving a pedestrian aged 5 to 18 roughly doubled before sunrise,” Rodríguez Ferrante told Earth.com.

She stated the analysis does not show that most such crashes happen in the dark, only that the crashes before sunrise more often involved a school-age pedestrian.

The figure for children rests on 141 crashes, so its range is wide.

In a recent development, the crash records show a pattern, not a cause. The authors wrote that the analysis is observational, that it counts only fatal crashes, and that the far larger number of non-fatal collisions is not in the record.

School districts have spent years pushing high school start times later because teenagers’ body clocks run late.

Permanent daylight saving time would move every start time an hour earlier relative to the sun without changing a single bell schedule, which the authors wrote would reverse those gains.

Industry observers note that morning light also does a job of its own. It helps set the body clock that regulates sleep, mood and appetite, and a child who leaves in the dark misses that cue.

De la Iglesia noted he has heard the argument that schools could simply start later under permanent daylight saving time.

His answer was that everything else would then shift later too, work included, until everyone was back on solar time, which is what standard time already is.

Recent findings suggest that “The U.S. tried year-round DST in 1974, and abandoned it within the year, partly because of dark winter mornings and concern for children traveling to school,” Rodríguez Ferrante said.

According to recent reports, the count assumes every child leaves 20 minutes before class, and the national estimate assumes an 8 a.m. departure everywhere.

Both choices are on the late side, so the authors wrote that the true number is likely higher.

Children who arrive early for a school breakfast program, who are more often from lower-income households, would lose more mornings than the count indicates.

The study estimated how often children would leave before sunrise. It did not measure how those darker commutes would affect their sleep or grades.

Rodríguez Ferrante remarked the bill passed the House in July and has stalled in the Senate, which adjourned for the midterm elections without acting on it.

The full study was published in the journal Current Biology.

#77153. Brain scans reveal a surprising pattern in teens who spend more time on screens

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1288 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Brain scans reveal a surprising pattern in teens who spend more time on screens

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1288 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study of 44 Finnish teens linked more screen time to smaller gray matter volume in a memory region and larger volumes in some other areas.
  • Earlier studies on teenagers and screens have generally associated longer device use with reduced gray matter in the brain.
  • Gray matter is the brain tissue in which the bodies of nerve cells are concentrated.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study of 44 Finnish teens linked more screen time to smaller gray matter volume in a memory region and larger volumes in some other areas.

Earlier studies on teenagers and screens have generally associated longer device use with reduced gray matter in the brain.

Gray matter is the brain tissue in which the bodies of nerve cells are concentrated.

That familiar pattern was also observed in a memory region by a team studying Finnish teens aged 16 to 19.

In regions involved in attention and planning, however, more gray matter was found among the heavier screen consumers.

These results are difficult to interpret because gray matter volume typically decreases as the teenage brain matures.

The research was led by Hannamari Skog, a doctoral researcher at the University of Eastern Finland‘s Institute of Biomedicine.

Her team scanned the brains of 44 teens on a single occasion each.

Habits and brain features that occur together can be identified with this design. Proof that screens altered anyone’s brain cannot be obtained from it.

The participants were recruited from the Physical Activity and Nutrition in Children study in Kuopio in Finland. They had taken part in that project for eight years.

A total of 277 teens attended the project’s eight-year checkup and 60 of them were invited to the brain study.

Those invitations were extended so that the full range of performance on a sprint test would be represented.

Forty-six teens agreed to participate. Two of them were later excluded when structural brain abnormalities were detected on their scans.

The final sample consisted of 25 girls and 19 boys who each underwent magnetic resonance imaging of the brain.

Specialized software estimated gray matter volume in 102 regions of the outer brain and in 10 deeper structures.

Screen use was assessed by questionnaire. Daily hours on phones, tablets, computers, TV and videos were reported by the teens themselves.

The reported average was 9.2 hours per day and about 5.2 of those hours involved phones and tablets.

Individual totals ranged between 2.5 and 19 hours and each figure rested on the teen’s own estimate.

It has been revealed that the content viewed on the screens was not assessed by the questionnaire. Only the number of hours was recorded.

Fitness was measured with a standing long jump and a shuttle run that covered 164 feet (50 meters) in total.

According to recent reports, teens who reported more screen time had less gray matter in the medial temporal lobe. This inner part of the temporal lobe is involved in memory and learning.

Sources indicate that the same link was found for time on phones and tablets alone. It appeared on both the left and right sides of the brain.

According to recent reports, age, sex, head size and body fat were taken into account. The links still held.

Industry observers note that in all, the team ran 72 statistical tests. With that many tests, a few links can appear by pure chance.

So a correction was applied to the results. The memory region links survived it.

In a recent development, skog’s team had predicted this result. The temporal cortex matures late, they wrote, and is particularly sensitive to environmental influences.

For the authors, the finding raises concerns, because the region is implicated in memory disorders.

“Excessive screen time and smart device usage may be harmful to the areas of the brain that are involved in memory and learning,” Skog noted.

The researchers had also expected teens with more screen time to have smaller frontal regions.

Teens with more screen time had larger volumes in two frontal regions. One helps the brain plan movements.

Recent findings suggest that the other is part of the prefrontal cortex. It supports working memory, planning and decision-making.

Sources indicate that total screen time was also tied to a larger area in the occipital lobe. That lobe processes vision.

Time on phones and tablets was linked to larger volumes in two more frontal regions.

“The larger volume in these areas may be particularly related to applications and games that require attention, motor planning and visual information processing,” Skog said.

Some researchers split screen time into active and passive kinds. Active use includes problem-solving or interactive play. Passive use means simply watching.

Recent findings suggest that A 2019 study cited by the team made this kind of split. Gaming was linked to a larger prefrontal cortex in that work.

Social media use was linked to a smaller temporal lobe. The Finnish questionnaire did not distinguish between time spent gaming and time spent on social media.

An earlier analysis from the same Finnish project had a related result. Some working memory scores were higher among teens with more screen time.

Industry observers note that A larger region should not be assumed to be a better one. The prefrontal cortex is also one of the last regions to fully mature.

“During normal brain development in adolescence, there is a reduction in grey matter volume and an increase in brain efficiency,” Skog said.

“The positive link between screen time and the volume of grey matter in these areas may thus also reflect a delay in brain development.”.

Sources indicate that that idea was not tested in this study. Only one scan exists for each teen.

How each teen’s brain changed over time was therefore not recorded.

Larger temporal and frontal volumes had been expected in active and fit teens, but this pattern did not appear.

Sources indicate that the teens reported 92 minutes of physical activity a day on average. More activity was tied to a larger region in the right occipital lobe.

But that link was no longer statistically significant after the correction.

Sources indicate that fitter teens had a larger left parietal lobe. This region helps process sensation and attention.

Better fitness was also linked to smaller volumes in the right hippocampus and one other region.

Neither of those two links remained after the correction, and the authors wrote that both may be chance findings.

Part of the weak result may be explained by exercise intensity, which was not captured by the questionnaire.

The authors wrote that teenagers’ everyday activity may be too light to influence brain volume.

Each teen was scanned just once. So the study can’t show whether screen habits came before the brain differences or after.

According to recent reports, the group of 44 was small and not typical of all teens. Most had a parent with a polytechnic or university degree.

No data on sleep or diet were collected. Either factor could explain part of the pattern.

According to recent reports, skog’s team collected the data in 2018 and 2019. Screen habits may have differed then from the habits seen today, the authors wrote.

The survey recorded screen time by device or broad category, but it did not break down how much time teens spent on specific activities.

Those hours could have been spent on games, videos, schoolwork or social media.

Screen-time apps could capture that detail, the authors wrote, and wearable sensors could measure how hard teens exercise.

“The results provide upcoming information on how everyday lifestyle factors, such as screen time, physical activity and physical fitness, are linked to brain structure in adolescence,” Skog stated.

“However, in light of the results, the connections between lifestyle factors and brain structures in adolescence are complex, and more research is needed to understand their long-term significance.”.

The authors called for larger studies that follow teenagers over years, to clarify whether different kinds of screen use cause differences in the brain.

The full study was published in the journal NeuroImage: Reports.

  • The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul right now chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., leaves the Senate Republicans’ lunch in the Capitol on Tuesday. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call).

Industry observers note that sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., announced Wednesday he plans to serve as the top Republican on the Health, Education, Labor and Pensions Committee when Democrats take control of Congress next year.

The move clears the way for Senate Ethics Chairman James Lankford, R-Okla., to use his seniority to ascend to ranking Republican on the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee, which Paul right now chairs, and touches off several other shifts at the top of other committees.

It has been revealed that the move fit in with Sen. Lisa Murkowski’s bid to use her seniority to succeed Senate Appropriations Chair Susan Collins, R-Maine, as top Republican on the Appropriations panel. If Paul did not go to the top spot on HELP, Murkowski, R-Alaska, would be next in line for that committee in the next Congress.

It has been revealed that murkowski is second in seniority on Appropriations to Collins, who was defeated for reelection. But she faces a potential challenge from Sen. Jerry Moran, R-Kan., who is next in line behind her.

Paul said in a press release that he prepares to bring the same approach to the HELP Committee as he did as chairman of Homeland, where he said he “challenged entrenched bureaucracies, forced federal officials to answer for their actions, and pulled back the curtain on what Washington tried to keep hidden.”.

He cited calling Dr. Anthony Fauci before the committee to probe the former federal health official’s role in pandemic-related shutdowns and the origin of the COVID-19 virus, and releasing thousands of pages of pandemic-related documents. The panel voted in August to hold Fauci in criminal contempt of Congress for declining to answer questions about the pandemic during a highly charged hearing.

Related: Fauci could face criminal contempt charge following panel vote.

Paul, an ophthalmologist, remarked at HELP he will “stand against efforts to put Washington between Americans and their doctors, their children’s schools, and their paychecks.” He predicted “a rush toward socialism unlike anything we have seen” when the Democrat-controlled Congress convenes in January.

Lankford, in a separate statement, confirmed his interest in becoming the ranking member of the Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee. In many areas, he remarked, the panel can work in a bipartisan manner, and over the past decade he “worked across the aisle to improve emergency communications in federal buildings, strengthen the United States Postal Service, increase federal cybersecurity preparedness, government transparency, and the use of artificial intelligence.”.

But he added that his job also would be to “push back on a [Democratic] majority that goes too far . . . Oversight is responsible, but obstruction is unacceptable.”.

Lankford said he would work together with the likely committee chair, Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., “when we can agree and be a fierce opposition if there is an attempt to undercut our nation’s security.”.

Latest Update: Migrating birds may be bringing unusual ticks to Hungary

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (943 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Volunteers in Hungary found 29 Hyalomma ticks over five years, raising the question of whether the ticks are starting to breed there.
  • Hyalomma ticks can carry the virus that causes Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a serious and sometimes life-threatening illness.
  • For five years, scientists in Hungary have been asking people to send in any of these ticks they find.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Volunteers in Hungary found 29 Hyalomma ticks over five years, raising the question of whether the ticks are starting to breed there.

Hyalomma ticks can carry the virus that causes Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever, a serious and sometimes life-threatening illness. They usually live in warm, dry places, but lately they keep turning up in Hungary.

For five years, scientists in Hungary have been asking people to send in any of these ticks they find.

What they’ve learned so far raises a simple question: are the ticks just passing through, or are they starting to settle in?

At the HUN-REN Centre for Ecological Research in Budapest, Éva Szabó, Gábor Földvári and their colleagues in the Eco-epidemiology Research Group run the project.

Hyalomma ticks usually live in warm, dry parts of Africa, the Middle East, Asia and southern Europe.

Young Hyalomma ticks often feed on birds, including birds that migrate long distances. Adult Hyalomma ticks feed mostly on large animals such as cattle and horses.

According to recent reports, the way these ticks feed helps explain how far they can travel. A young Hyalomma tick usually stays on the same animal while it grows.

For Hyalomma marginatum, that’s about three weeks. Ixodes ricinus, the most widespread tick in Hungary, lets go after less than a week each time.

The authors linked the ticks’ spread north to climate change.

The European Centre for Disease Prevention and Control keeps a map of where Hyalomma marginatum has turned up in Europe.

Scientists watch these ticks closely because of a virus some of them carry.

Recent findings suggest that the World Health Organization names Hyalomma ticks as the main carrier of Crimean-Congo hemorrhagic fever virus. The study’s authors wrote that it’s the most key tick-borne virus affecting people.

Sources indicate that how many people get sick from it each year isn’t clear, because many infections cause no symptoms. The authors cited an estimate of 10,000 to 15,000 cases worldwide.

The World Health Organization estimates that 10% to 40% of reported cases in outbreaks are fatal.

A vaccine has seen limited use in Eastern Europe, and no vaccine is widely available. Treatment relies on supportive care.

Recent findings suggest that hyalomma ticks hunt their hosts instead of waiting on plants. Dragging a cloth through vegetation, the traditional way to collect ticks, doesn’t work well for them.

So the team relies on citizen scientists instead.

The researchers opened a website called TickWatcher in April 2021.

Industry observers note that four years later, they added a free phone app called PragmaTick. People send in a photo of an odd-looking tick, and an expert checks it.

In a recent development, by late November 2025, the website had about 107,000 visits. The app had been downloaded 2,500 times. Volunteers had made 1,014 submissions, and 29 turned out to be Hyalomma ticks.

The app won’t accept a report without a date, a place and a photo.

In the app’s first six months, people sent about as many reports through it as they had sent by email in the four and a half years before.

“Successfully involving the public in research can even help unravel problems like finding a needle in a haystack,” the authors wrote.

Industry observers note that thirteen of the 29 ticks were on horses. Five were on buffalo, two on dogs, one on a donkey and one on a cow, and reports came in between mid-June and the end of October.

Horse owners tend to check their animals closely and ride through grass and woods, which may help explain why horses topped the list, the researchers wrote.

News about the program may also have reached some groups of people better than others.

Even so, the authors concluded that owners of livestock and other large animals are likely more affected than other groups.

Recent findings suggest that three ticks came from people. Four more ticks were crawling with no host, including the one on the kitchen floor.

Most of the 29 were males, 21 in all. One possible reason, according to the authors, is that males may stay on a host longer while they look for mates.

At a buffalo farm near the village of Ágasegyháza, people found four Hyalomma ticks in 2022 and one more in 2023.

Two other finds came from within about 9 miles (15 kilometers) of the farm. One was on a cow in 2021, and the other turned up in a garden near the city of Kecskemét in 2023.

Industry observers note that all 18 ticks that people mailed in tested negative for the virus. The other 11 were thrown away or destroyed by the people who found them.

Earlier studies in Hungary found antibodies against the virus in 10 of 2,700 people tested between 2008 and 2017, and in 11 of 1,905 cattle and sheep tested in 2017.

Antibodies show past exposure, not a current infection, and these tests may also react to related viruses.

The biggest open question is whether these ticks are only passing through or starting to survive and breed in Hungary.

Recent findings suggest that answering that will take time. The team prepares to keep collecting reports, with close attention to livestock owners and to places where several ticks have already been found.

For now, the people in the best position to help are the ones already checking their horses and cattle.

Every tick they send in shows scientists a little more about where these ticks are turning up.

The full study was published in the journal Current Research in Parasitology and Vector-Borne Diseases.

Two stars in the Andromeda galaxy merged before astronomers’ eyes

💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • According to recent reports, for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter.
  • It has been revealed that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

According to recent reports, for seven years, a giant star in the Andromeda galaxy grew brighter. It swelled to more than twice its original size, even as its surface temperature barely changed. Then, in October 2025, it erupted. The slow brightening and sudden eruption tell a story of a smaller star orbiting inside of a massive star and what became of the pair, researchers report November 18 in Nature.

It has been revealed that in work published last year, after poring through nearly 30 years of telescope data, astronomers had found that the giant began brightening in 2018 and proposed that a smaller star was circling ever closer around a giant companion and had even slipped inside its outermost layers. Astronomers call this elusive phase of a binary star’s life common-envelope evolution.

Now, the astronomers have analyzed the system’s dramatic next developments, culminating in the October 2025 eruption. (The stars are nicknamed Little Bao and Big Bao as a nod to that event’s official designation, AT 2025abao.).

In a recent development, first, astrophysicist Viraj Karambelkar of Columbia University and colleagues revisited those years of brightening given the imminent eruption. One cause of the brightening could have been gas flowing away from the stars, giving off light as it slowed down. But even if all the energy of that moving gas turned into light, it still wouldn’t be enough to explain the glow.

Instead, the researchers determined that the binary hypothesis they had originally proposed fit better: As Little Bao orbited inside Substantial Bao’s gas outer layers, the gas pushed back against the little star. That drag made Little Bao spiral inward and transfer energy to the surrounding gas. Some of that energy escaped as light, making Big Bao shine brighter.

Sources indicate that then, it was time to dig into what caused the eruption. If the outburst threw enough of the shared gas into space, the individual stars could have survived in an even tighter orbit. But the team estimates that only about a tenth of the giant’s outer gas escaped. The energy carried by that fast-moving gas also suggests that Little Bao reached Big Bao’s core. Together, those clues point to a merger.

It has been revealed that still, too much dust clouds the system to directly see what remains. And it won’t settle for years or even decades, although Karambelkar and his colleagues will be watching.

They’ll be looking for more examples of this type of merger, too. “Now we can go and try to look for similar systems,” Karambelkar indicates, “and hopefully aim to catch more of these systems even before they erupt.”.

#77147. Extreme heat is killing more people, and scientists have estimated how much warming is to blame

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (950 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Extreme heat is killing more people, and scientists have estimated how much warming is to blame

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (950 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A Lancet Countdown report found that annual heat-related deaths rose 36% worldwide, with human-caused warming accounting for more than two-thirds of the recent toll.
  • The Paris Agreement took effect in 2016.
  • That was about 36% higher than the annual average from 2006 through 2015.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A Lancet Countdown report found that annual heat-related deaths rose 36% worldwide, with human-caused warming accounting for more than two-thirds of the recent toll.

The Paris Agreement took effect in 2016. From 2016 through 2023, an estimated 540,800 people died from heat worldwide each year, on average.

That was about 36% higher than the annual average from 2006 through 2015.

The share of heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose from 55% to 68%.

A project based at University College London, the Lancet Countdown, produced the figures in its tenth annual report, which tracks 54 measures of how climate change affects health.

According to recent reports, it was written by 146 researchers and produced with the World Health Organization. Every death count in it is an estimate from models, not a tally of death certificates.

In an interview with Earth.com, Jennifer Israelsson, a senior research fellow at the Lancet Countdown, remarked the finding that surprised her most was not a number from the heat data.

It was “the sharp decline in political engagement with the climate-health agenda, despite multiple years with record-breaking temperatures, deadly heatwaves and devastating flooding events across the globe, and the intensification of hurricanes,” Israelsson noted.

Between 2006 and 2015, heat was linked to an estimated 398,400 deaths a year. Between 2016 and 2023, it was linked to 540,800 a year, with a range of roughly 369,000 to 681,000.

Near the end of that stretch came the worst year. Heat was linked to a record 710,000 deaths in 2023, and the authors attributed 71.5% of them to human-caused warming.

The researchers attributed an estimated 2.96 million heat-related deaths to human-caused warming from 2016 through 2023.

According to recent reports, annual heat-related deaths attributed to human-caused warming rose by an average of 7,400 per year from 2006 through 2015. From 2016 through 2023, they rose by an average of 15,600 per year.

According to recent reports, the researchers used daily temperatures and death records reported at daily, weekly or monthly intervals across 129 countries. They then used models to estimate the global toll.

The second question was how many of those deaths would have occurred in a world with the same weather minus the warming humans have added.

Sources indicate that the authors call the gap between the two the attributable toll. The attribution step is latest to this year’s report, and the ranges around each figure are wide.

According to recent reports, heat also keeps people from working. The authors estimate 573 billion potential work hours were lost to heat in 2025, 35% above the average for 2006 to 2015.

The lost income came to $1.07 trillion, about 0.9% of global economic output.

The losses were equivalent to 5% of GDP in countries with a low Human Development Index and 0.5% in countries with a very high index.

The same decade brought real gains. Investment in clean energy reached a record $2.1 trillion in 2025, 82% more than went into fossil fuels.

Recent findings suggest that the share of electricity from modern renewables rose from 5.5% in 2016 to 13.5% in 2023. Fossil fuels still supplied 80.7% of the world’s energy in 2023.

In a recent development, where air pollution from fossil fuels fell, the authors counted the benefit. In 75 of 140 countries assessed, cleaner air prevented an estimated 323,000 deaths a year.

Air conditioning tells a mixed story. Its use grew from 32% of households in 2016 to 42% in 2024, and the authors estimate it prevented more than 360,000 heat deaths in each of 2022 and 2023.

In countries with a low Human Development Index, only 3% of households had air conditioning in 2024.

Israelsson told Earth.com the single change that would save the most lives from heat is a heat-health action plan.

That means a warning system that reaches hospitals and the public in time, plus measures for cooler buildings and safe working conditions.

She pointed to the Netherlands, which she stated has seen heat deaths fall since it adopted a heatwave plan.

Extreme drought covered 51.8% of the world’s land for at least a month in 2025, the second-highest extent on record after 2023.

Since 2016, the area in drought each year has grown about eight times as fast as it did in the previous decade.

Very heavy rainfall affected an average of 17.2% of the world’s land each year from 2016 through 2025, up from 14.8% in the previous decade.

Such downpours can increase the risk of floods, landslides and waterborne disease.

The number of people affected per storm or flood rose more slowly in countries with health early warning systems.

The annual increase was 8.6% smaller than in countries without those systems.

It has been revealed that whether the acceleration continues is the open question, and the authors wrote as much. The heat figures run only through 2023, and the drought and rainfall trends through 2025.

The authors’ answer is to have climate change formally declared a global health emergency.

Israelsson mentioned the WHO’s existing emergency mechanism was built for short, acute outbreaks like Ebola and “is not designed for long-term emergencies.”.

A latest instrument with the same kind of roles and responsibilities, aimed at long-term resilience, is needed, she remarked.

“A decade after the Paris Agreement, our findings are unambiguous: the health harms of climate change are growing faster than the world’s response to them, and in many cases even accelerating,” noted Marina Romanello, the Lancet Countdown’s executive director.

The report was published ahead of the COP31 climate talks.

The full study was published in the journal The Lancet.
