#77144. Webb looked at a giant black hole from the dawn of the universe and saw something unexpected beside it

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1126 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

Webb looked at a giant black hole from the dawn of the universe and saw something unexpected beside it

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1126 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Webb spotted a faint light beside a giant black hole just 900 million years after the Significant Bang, and astronomers think it may come from a second black hole.
  • In a recent development, giant black holes from the young universe still puzzle astronomers.
  • The pair, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, dates to just 900 million years after the Substantial Bang.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Webb spotted a faint light beside a giant black hole just 900 million years after the Significant Bang, and astronomers think it may come from a second black hole.

In a recent development, giant black holes from the young universe still puzzle astronomers. Now a team has found what looks like two of them, close together and both feeding.

The pair, nicknamed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua, dates to just 900 million years after the Substantial Bang.

If confirmed, it would be the closest-spaced quasar pair known from cosmic dawn.

Recent findings suggest that A quasar is the brilliant glow produced as gas falls toward a supermassive black hole. That glow can outshine all the stars in its galaxy combined.

Silvia Onorato, a postdoctoral research associate at NSF NOIRLab, led the study.

Her team thinks pairs like this one may mark places where young galaxies were crowding together, feeding new stars and fast-growing black holes at the same time.

The researchers lean toward two real quasars. They haven’t ruled out, though, that the fainter one is a copy of the brighter one, made when light bends around a galaxy in between.

“There is no definitive theoretical explanation for how a single one of these giant quasars exists so early in the age of our Universe, much less two,” Onorato said.

“We observed Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua at a time when the Universe was only a thirteenth of its age and astonishingly, its supermassive black holes are just as massive as those we see today.”.

The universe’s first billion years, a period astronomers call cosmic dawn, were busy.

Clumps of dark matter collapsed, galaxies made their first stars, and the first supermassive black holes took shape at the centers of the biggest galaxies.

Galaxies back then often ran into each other, and some merged completely.

Industry observers note that when galaxies collide, gas can funnel toward their central black holes. The gas heats up as it spirals inward, producing the light we see from a quasar.

Since galaxies collided so often, astronomers expect plenty of quasar pairs closer together than the width of a typical galaxy.

Industry observers note that so why have so few turned up? Part of the problem is timing, since a black hole shines as a quasar for only a short part of its life.

Distance is the other problem. Quasars from cosmic dawn are so far away that they look faint and are hard to detect from the ground. And when two of them are very close together, it’s hard to tell one from the other.

Those hurdles make Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua a rare find. If confirmed, it would be the third known quasar pair from cosmic dawn.

Recent findings suggest that the pair’s Hawaiian name was created through the A Hua He Inoa program at the ʻImiloa Astronomy Center of Hawaiʻi. The University of Hawaiʻi’s Hawaiian Language College, Ka Haka ʻUla O Keʻelikōlani, also took part.

In English, the name means “Two celestial bodies of fathomless powerful darkness in the brilliance of heat reincarnating energy into the Universe.”.

Astronomers found the pair in the Aether survey, a James Webb Space Telescope program that’s taking a census of objects in the early universe.

Emanuele Paolo Farina, an associate scientist at NSF NOIRLab/Gemini, leads the survey.

Farina’s team used Webb to split the light of 200 quasars into its colors, point by point. That’s 43% of all the quasars known from this stage of cosmic history.

Onorato’s team checked every one by eye. Next to J1602+4228A, a quasar first reported in 2004, they spotted a second, fainter source. No other quasar in the survey had a companion like it.

The faint one, J1602+4228B, is so dim and so close to its partner that seeing it from the ground should have been nearly impossible.

Earlier Gemini observations from a 2017 program had pointed only at the brighter quasar.

The team went back with Gemini North, a telescope on Maunakea, a dormant volcano in Hawaiʻi, and recorded each quasar’s light separately.

“The sky over Maunakea was so clean and sharp that we managed to collect the data in only two nights,” Onorato noted.

According to recent reports, the brighter quasar’s black hole weighs about 1.5 billion times as much as the Sun. Its partner’s comes in at about 400 million, roughly a quarter as heavy.

As seen from Earth, the two are about 18,100 light-years apart, or about one-fifth the width of the Milky Way.

The two quasars’ light was stretched by almost exactly the same amount on its way here, which means they’re at nearly the same distance from us.

Both black holes are pulling in matter near or slightly above the Eddington limit. At that point, light from the falling gas pushes outward about as hard as gravity pulls inward.

Feeding that fast is typical for quasars this early, the researchers wrote.

The fainter quasar also looks redder, a sign that more dust is blocking its light.

Sources indicate that could the second quasar be a copy of the first? A massive galaxy between Earth and a quasar can bend the quasar’s light and make two or more copies of it. Astronomers call this gravitational lensing.

To test the idea, the team looked at light from gas spread across hundreds of light-years around each black hole.

Stars inside a lensing galaxy can distort light from a small area near a black hole, but not from gas spread that widely.

Industry observers note that the light from the gas highlighted different patterns in the two spectra. The brighter source showed a stronger signature of gas flowing outward.

The researchers wrote that this difference favors two separate quasars.

It has been revealed that older Hubble images do show a galaxy near the line of sight to the fainter quasar, which could hold the extra dust or act as a lens. Its spread-out look suggests it’s fairly close to us, making strong lensing unlikely.

Even so, the team wrote, spectra alone can’t definitively rule out lensing.

Based on how quasars cluster over larger distances, a pair this close should be extremely rare.

Yet one turned up among the 199 quasars the team searched around. That’s roughly 100 to 1,000 times more clustering than the predictions suggest.

Predictions at such small distances are very uncertain, though, and one pair can’t show whether close pairs are really this common.

“Nāpōwawāʻenakaulua is a really unique environment,” Onorato stated.

“It’s a laboratory for astronomers to study how the very first massive galaxies and their central black holes assembled together through direct galaxy interactions during these early times.”.

The full study was published in the journal The Astrophysical Journal Letters.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

The future of Caribbean coral reefs may be hidden in their past

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Ancient coral fossils reveal more possible Caribbean reef habitat by 2100, but warming still threatens every species studied.
  • According to recent reports, predictions of coral survival in a warming Caribbean have generally been based on present-day reef records.
  • In a new study, mid-Holocene coral fossils dated to 5,000 to 7,000 years ago were incorporated into habitat forecasts.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ancient coral fossils reveal more possible Caribbean reef habitat by 2100, but warming still threatens every species studied.

According to recent reports, predictions of coral survival in a warming Caribbean have generally been based on present-day reef records. Evidence from fossil reefs now suggests this basis has been too narrow.

In a new study, mid-Holocene coral fossils dated to 5,000 to 7,000 years ago were incorporated into habitat forecasts.

Four reef-building species were examined: elkhorn, staghorn, boulder brain and mustard hill corals.

More potential habitat for 2100 was identified once the fossil records had been included in the models.

The overall decline was not reversed by this additional habitat. Losses of 45% to 100% of suitable habitat were still projected for each species by 2100.

The extent of loss varied by species and by the level of future carbon emissions.

The research was led by Claire Williams at the University of Texas at Austin’s Jackson School of Geosciences.

Two variables were used to build the computer models: sea surface temperature and sea surface salinity.

According to recent reports, water suitability for each coral was estimated by these models. Actual reef growth at any given site was not predicted by them.

In habitat modeling, every recorded location of a species is paired with the water conditions measured there.

Maps of the future ocean are then searched for matching conditions.

Two limitations of models trained on present-day records alone were described by the authors.

It has been revealed that only water conditions found on Earth today can be learned by such models. Locations where a species is presently absent for other reasons are also missed.

Recent findings suggest that records from a different ocean are supplied by fossils. Caribbean corals have persisted through hundreds of thousands of years of changing conditions.

The fossil period selected here is regarded by researchers as an analog for present-day warming.

Coral occurrence records were obtained from public sources including the Paleobiology Database. Published reef surveys provided further fossil records.

In a recent development, field observations collected in Jamaica between 2017 and 2024 were added by Williams’s team. At least 16 records per period were available for every species.

Fossil data are useful only if a species’ environmental tolerances have remained stable through time.

A closer match between past and present conditions than chance would produce was found for three species.

According to recent reports, elkhorn coral did not reach this statistical threshold. A large overlap between its past and present conditions was still seen.

Extra future habitat was picked up by the fossil-trained models for each of the four species.

As much as 44,200 square miles (114,559 square kilometers) of added habitat was projected for 2100. That is close to the size of Ohio.

No suitable habitat in 2100 was left for elkhorn or mustard hill coral by the modern-only models under high emissions.

Some habitat for both was kept once the fossil data were added. The authors flagged these estimates as highly uncertain.

The two sets of models were framed by the authors as the edges of a likely range.

Under high emissions, models based only on modern records found no suitable habitat for elkhorn or mustard hill coral in the study area by 2100.

Adding fossils revealed some potential habitat for both, though those estimates are highly uncertain.

Heat-stressed corals lose their color in a process called bleaching. Many of them die afterward.

The worst bleaching ever seen in the Northern Hemisphere came after record marine heatwaves in 2023.

Industry observers note that two emissions pathways were tested for each coral. Emissions level off near mid-century in one and keep climbing to 2100 in the other.

Habitat was lost by every species on both pathways. The losses grew under high emissions and from 2050 to 2100.

Boulder brain coral is a massive species that can live for a long time. Its losses were the steepest of all four.

Recent findings suggest that no suitable habitat was left for it by 2100 under high emissions. Elkhorn coral was left with very little.

This clashes with the official threat status that boulder brain coral currently holds.

The species is ranked as vulnerable by the IUCN, the body that tracks extinction risk worldwide.

Elkhorn and staghorn corals sit one level higher as critically endangered species. Boulder brain coral may be more threatened than once believed, the authors wrote.

According to recent reports, the largest share of habitat in 2100 was kept by mustard hill coral on both pathways. It is known as a weedy coral. It spreads easily but builds little reef structure.

Reefs made up mostly of this coral are expected to give less shelter to the sea life people rely on.

The models projected the heaviest habitat losses in the southern Caribbean.

All four species had lost their habitat near 10 degrees north by 2100 under high emissions.

Sources indicate that A small patch near 15 degrees north was held only by staghorn coral. Most leftover habitat sat close to 20 degrees north.

The Florida Keys, Cuba and the north coast of Mexico’s Yucatán Peninsula still held habitat.

It has been revealed that no real northward shift of the corals was detected. The southern habitat is simply lost and not moved.

Getting to the habitat that is left poses another problem for the corals.

Linked communities of mustard hill coral have been recorded more than 1,000 miles (1,700 kilometers) apart.

Elkhorn coral has been documented spreading only about 0.6 miles (1 kilometer).

Today, about 33% to 38% of modeled suitable habitat overlaps existing marine protected areas.

By 2100 under high emissions, the models projected that share would fall for mustard hill and elkhorn corals and rise for staghorn coral.

The models found no suitable habitat for boulder brain coral anywhere in the study area under that scenario.

Newly introduced protected areas in the northern Caribbean were called for by the authors.

Closer ties between existing reserves were also urged. Mexico’s Sian Ka’an and the Florida Keys National Marine Sanctuary were named as examples.

Reef-dependent regions such as Jamaica and the Lesser Antilles are likely to lose all suitable habitat for the four corals studied by 2100.

Recent findings suggest that rowan Martindale is a co-author and associate professor at the Jackson School. According to her, those places cannot simply be abandoned.

Local communities rely on reefs for fish and for protection from hurricanes, she added.

What Jamaica has already lost was examined in a second study by Williams and colleagues.

Fossil and living reefs in northeast Jamaica were compared in the companion study.

These fossil reefs formed 125,000 to 130,000 years ago and are now exposed above sea level.

The surveys were therefore carried out on foot. Corals were photographed at intervals along measured transect lines.

Staghorn coral made up roughly half of the fossil coral on the seaward reefs at Navy Island and Dragon Point.

Elkhorn coral accounted for about 40% of the fossil community at Dragon Point and about 10% at Navy Island.

According to recent reports, on nearby living reefs, the largely dead branching corals are now covered by algae. Mustard hill coral dominates the surviving coral cover.

Sources indicate that only sea surface temperature and salinity were included in the models. Conditions on the seafloor where corals grow may differ substantially.

Nutrient pollution, turbidity and ocean acidification were not considered in this analysis.

Coral disease and the decline of herbivorous reef animals were also excluded. Further habitat loss from these stresses was anticipated by the authors.

Future water conditions in the Florida Keys and along Cuba’s southern coast will be unlike any fossil or modern record.

Those areas are rated suitable by the models, yet corals may be unable to survive there. Future habitat is therefore likely overestimated.

In a recent development, newer climate projections became available only after the analysis had been completed. A warmer and more saline Caribbean is indicated by them.

Smaller changes are projected for the Yucatán, which may allow suitable habitat to persist there longer.

“Conservation needs to be adaptive and to keep learning newly introduced information,” Williams said.

Fossils from older warm periods could also be incorporated, according to the authors. Unmatched future conditions would then be reduced.

Future research could also apply this method to reefs in the Indian and Pacific oceans.

The full study was published in the journal Conservation Biology.

Tiny reptile found in Wyoming sandstone is a prehistoric ‘dragon’

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (995 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Neutron and X-ray scans revealed a tiny horned reptile inside Wyoming sandstone, offering a upcoming clue to where its extinct relatives fit on the reptile family tree.
  • Industry observers note that about 156 million years ago, the remains of a small horned reptile were buried in river sand in what is now Wyoming.
  • Its remains stayed hidden inside a slab of sandstone until scientists looked through the rock with neutrons.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Neutron and X-ray scans revealed a tiny horned reptile inside Wyoming sandstone, offering a upcoming clue to where its extinct relatives fit on the reptile family tree.

Industry observers note that about 156 million years ago, the remains of a small horned reptile were buried in river sand in what is now Wyoming. Its head and body were found apart.

Its remains stayed hidden inside a slab of sandstone until scientists looked through the rock with neutrons.

It has been revealed that inside, they found a species nobody had seen before. Its tiny, almost intact braincase may help settle a long-running argument about where an odd group of extinct reptiles belongs on the tree of life.

The animal also has a name worthy of a heavy metal album cover.

The research was led by the Paul Scherrer Institute (PSI) in Switzerland and the University of Zurich, together with the Aathal Dinosaur Museum and the Swiss materials research institute Empa.

In January 2023, PSI materials scientist Pavel Trtik took his three sons to the Aathal Dinosaur Museum near Zurich. The boys loved the teeth and armor.

Their father was more interested in the rock. Trtik works at the PSI Center for Neutron and Muon Sciences. He uses neutrons to see inside solid materials.

On a whim, he left his business card at the front desk with a note: “If you ever have something you want investigated, just get in touch.”.

Ten days later, the museum called. It had a fossil from the United States that nobody could identify.

A museum excavation team had found the fossil in August 2022 at the Meilyn Quarry in Wyoming.

That part of the American West has produced giants such as Diplodocus, Stegosaurus, and Allosaurus.

In a recent development, this find was much smaller. A row of tiny vertebrae showed in the sandstone, and the rest of the skeleton was still buried inside.

Recent findings suggest that it could have been an early snake, a crocodile relative, or a baby dinosaur. Nobody could say which.

Neutrons turned out to be the right tool for the job.

“Neutrons are particularly sensitive to hydrogen,” Trtik explained.

“And hydrogen is also present in hydroxyapatite, a mineral component of bones. This allows us to distinguish the fossilized remains from the surrounding sandstone.”.

The team also made X-ray scans at PSI, at Empa in Dübendorf and at the University of Zurich.

“The two techniques provide different kinds of information,” Trtik remarked. “Only by combining them can we get the clearest picture.”.

They then sorted, combined, and interpreted tens of thousands of cross-sectional images. Slowly, the animal took shape.

Sources indicate that they found pelvic bones, part of a hind leg and a tiny skull with an almost complete braincase. The skull turned out to be the real prize.

The reconstruction shows a reptile about 45 centimeters long with two horn-like spikes at the back of its head.

Its head and body were found apart, and fine sand buried both before the sand slowly turned to stone.

“It’s difficult to determine why the skull became detached from the torso,” explained Torsten Scheyer, the University of Zurich palaeontologist who co-led the study with Trtik.

“But we cannot rule out the possibility that a larger predator was involved.”.

If a predator did take the head off, it was lucky for science that the skull wasn’t eaten or carried away by the current.

The braincase is less than two centimeters across, and it holds the most notable evidence in the whole fossil.

In a recent development, the skull shows that the animal belonged to the choristoderes, a group of long-extinct reptiles. Later members of the group included long-snouted, crocodile-like river hunters, and some of them outlived the dinosaurs.

Paleontologists have argued for a long time about how choristoderes relate to other reptiles.

“The unusual shape of their skull bones has long made it difficult for palaeontologists to determine how they are related to other reptiles,” Scheyer said.

The newly introduced clue comes from the bones of the inner ear.

“They bear a striking resemblance to those of the so-called crown group of reptiles, which includes all living reptiles,” the palaeontologist explains.

“This could suggest that choristoderes are more closely related to living reptiles than previous fossil evidence indicated.”.

According to recent reports, the little reptile is also a fresh species. It is the most complete early member of the choristodere group found so far, and the oldest one known from North America.

Scheyer is a substantial fan of The Lord of the Rings and of hard rock, and both shaped the animal’s name.

“When I looked at the three-dimensional images of the little reptile, with its head possibly torn off, I knew straight away: such a spectacular creature deserves an equally spectacular name.”.

According to recent reports, he called it Meilynodraco amonamarthi. The first part means roughly “Dragon of Meilyn,” after the quarry and the horns on the back of the head.

The second part honors his favorite band, the Swedish melodic death metal group Amon Amarth.

The band took its name from Tolkien, since Amon Amarth is the Elvish name for Mount Doom, the volcano where the One Ring was made and finally destroyed.

The fossil will go on display in early 2027 in “Rock Fossils on Tour,” a traveling exhibition at the Aathal Dinosaur Museum.

“The little dragon will be in excellent company here, with other spectacular fossils named after famous metal musicians and rock bands,” remarked the museum director Yolanda Schicker-Siber.

PSI hopes to scan much bigger fossils in future. A proposed test facility called UFO, short for “UltraFast neutron irradiation for large Objects,” would fit objects up to a meter long.

It is being considered as part of a possible upgrade to PSI’s neutron source.

The study is published in the journal Royal Society Open Science.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov.
  • Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen.
  • The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Mississippi Democrat Scott Colom, here at a news conference in Jackson on Nov. 4, has defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images).

Democrat Scott Colom has unseated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith to become Mississippi’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.

The result is a stunning flip for Democrats in a deep-red state where they last won a Senate election in 1982, and it brings the Senate Democratic Caucus to at least 55 seats in the next Congress.

Recent findings suggest that colom was leading Hyde-Smith 49.2 percent to 48.7 percent — or by just over 4,600 votes out of more than 960,000 cast — when The Associated Press called the race Wednesday, a little over a week after Election Day. Ty Pinkins, the 2024 Democratic Senate nominee who ran as an independent this year, had 2 percent.

In recent days, as absentee and provisional ballots were counted, Colom had all but declared victory, repeatedly saying that Hyde-Smith had no path to victory.

“I'll work every day in the U.S. Senate to build a future that generations of Mississippians can be just as proud to call home,” he posted Monday on social media.

With his victory, Colom joins several other Democrats who flipped seats in deep-red states, including Texas’ James Talarico, Kansas’ Adam Hamilton and South Carolina’s Annie Andrews. Democrats have so far flipped eight Senate seats to win control of the chamber, overcoming a difficult Senate map and giving them their largest majority in the chamber since 2011.

It has been revealed that that majority could expand further if Democrats flip the Senate seat in Alaska, where former Rep. Mary Peltola narrowly leads Republican incumbent Dan Sullivan.

Recent findings suggest that republicans have dominated Senate elections in Mississippi in recent decades. The last Democrat to be elected senator in the Magnolia State was John C. Stennis, who won his sixth full and final term in 1982. Colom will be the third Black man to serve as a Mississippi senator after Republicans Hiram Revels and Blanche Bruce during Reconstruction.

While Revels and Bruce, who left office in 1881, were elected by the state Legislature, Colom will be the first Black senator elected directly by voters.

In a recent development, colom has served as a district attorney for four counties in northeast Mississippi since 2016. President Joe Biden nominated him for a federal district judgeship in 2022, but Hyde-Smith effectively blocked his nomination by not returning a so-called blue slip, a Senate Judiciary Committee tradition that lets senators derail district judge nominees in their home states.

In a recent development, senate Minority Leader Charles E. Schumer remarked last week that he’d had Colom in his sights for several years as a potential Senate candidate, including for a race against the state’s senior senator, Republican Roger Wicker.

Industry observers note that “I had Scott Colom and his father come to my house, and I served them a nice little brunch or something. I mentioned, ‘You got to run,’” the Fresh York Democrat recalled to MS NOW. “They were smarter than me. This was four years ago. They said, ‘We don’t want to run this time, but we know that Hyde-[Smith], the incumbent, is so weak, we could beat her.’”.

It has been revealed that still, the Mississippi race didn’t capture as much national attention as other Senate contests until the closing weeks of the campaign. A trio of Black senators, Angela Alsobrooks of Maryland, Lisa Blunt Rochester of Delaware and Cory Booker of Fresh Jersey, all campaigned with Colom throughout the summer and fall. Key national figures, including former President Bill Clinton, former Vice President Kamala Harris and former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, also stumped for him in October.

In a recent development, colom’s campaign engaged voters with quirky ads and unconventional forms of outreach, including meeting with people lining up to attend a Trump rally. One ad that went viral played on Hyde Smith saying earlier this year that people had “so many proteins to choose from” when asked about rising beef prices.

“Pick another protein?” notes a man in the ad. “I’d rather pick another senator instead.”.

Industry observers note that major Democratic outside groups made a late play in the state, with WinSenate, which is affiliated with Senate Democrats’ top super PAC, investing $2.2 million. The Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee spent $500,000 on a coordinated ad buy late last month.

The pro-Republican Senate Leadership Fund dropped $1.7 million on the race, and Trump headlined a rally for Hyde-Smith on Oct. 26.

You Can Build All the Power Plants You Want. Without This Overlooked Machine, None of Them Will Matter.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam.
  • It has been revealed that but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As humanity entered the 21st century and the ravages of climate change became more and more apparent, the push toward electrification (replacing gas-powered cars, furnaces, and stoves with electric versions) really gained steam. At the same time, the electricity supply itself has been getting cleaner. According to Pew Research, solar power accounted for only 0.01 percent of the world’s electricity production back then, but fast-forward a quarter of a century, and that number is now nine percent and rising.

It has been revealed that but building out an electrified future isn’t as easy as sticking wind turbines in the ocean and vast solar arrays in the desert and calling it a day. These latest forms of renewable energy also need to connect to the grid before they can supply us with that much-needed new power. Expanding the grid’s capacity to meet this ballooning demand was already going to be a tall order as more and more electric cars, ovens, and heat pumps came online. Now, the rise of power-hungry AI data centers has transformed that difficult task into a borderline impossible one for the simple reason that the U.S. may not have enough of the equipment—or the materials to make noted equipment—to build the required infrastructure.

In a upcoming study published in the journal Cell Reports Sustainability, researchers at Johns Hopkins University report that critical grid equipment, such as transformers and converters, could become the bottleneck in powering a rapidly electrifying society. According to the researchers, demand for electricity isn’t anything new. In fact, it’s been steadily rising since Thomas Edison flipped the switch on the Pearl Street Station in 1882. But due to the rise of AI data centers, the electricity industry has entered a whole new era of demand growth.

“When the demand for electricity started to grow faster than expected, it started to amplify all the cracks in the industry,” Yury Dvorkin, a Johns Hopkins researcher and co-author of the study, noted in a press statement. According to Dvorkin and co-author Boyu Yao, electricity demand historically ticked up a percent or two each year. But now, largely because of data centers, demand is projected to grow 21 percent overall by the end of the decade.

If this rapid demand growth persists, it will put considerable strain on supplies of specific materials, including copper, steel, nickel, aluminum, and manganese, needed to build the necessary transformers, which step up or step down the voltage of alternating current on the grid.

“This type of equipment was taken for granted, but without it, you can build a data center or a power plant but it won’t be powered because you cannot connect it to the grid,” Dvorkin mentioned. “By 2030 we’re likely to have transformer shortages even without the most aggressive power demand growth.”.

Sources indicate that according to their projections, copper will run short in 2027, followed soon by steel and nickel, which will affect not just grid utilities but wind power infrastructure and electric vehicle charging stations. This shortfall isn’t necessarily news: a study by S&P Global earlier this year found that copper could experience a 10 million metric ton deficit by 2040. This deficit isn’t caused by a lack of copper in the ground, since the planet holds abundant copper resources. Extraction is where the industry is facing a crucial bottleneck.

Sources indicate that “Copper is abundant in the ground, but there’s not enough being extracted to be able to meet the demand,” authors of a copper market analysis wrote for The Conversation earlier this year. That’s because investors want higher and more reliable returns than copper mines currently offer, and the industry faces complex permitting processes and can’t find enough workers.

This new study suggests that under its baseline scenario, the U.S. might be able to produce enough transformers yet still fall 16 percent short on other grid-related equipment. But with AI data centers supercharging demand, the study’s “high power demand” scenario is more likely. That scenario projects a 15 percent shortage of transformers and a 30 percent shortage of all other equipment. The authors also note that roughly two-thirds of this expected shortage can be attributed to AI data centers.

According to recent reports, “Utilities will compete for transformers with the data center industry,” Dvorkin noted. “Transformers will first be delivered to whoever can pay the highest premium. Will it be a mom-and-pop utility or a significant data center corporation?”.

I think we already know the answer to that question.

Hubble caught a spiral galaxy from an angle that hides its arms

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Hubble’s edge-on view of spiral galaxy NGC 1827 reveals dark dust lanes, a bright central bulge and blue patches where stars may be forming.
  • Today’s Image of the Day from Hubble indicates a ribbon of rust-colored dust cutting through a bright band of starlight.
  • The ribbon breaks into dark patches toward the edges, and it takes a moment to recognize what you’re looking at: a spiral galaxy seen from the side.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Hubble’s edge-on view of spiral galaxy NGC 1827 reveals dark dust lanes, a bright central bulge and blue patches where stars may be forming.

Today’s Image of the Day from Hubble indicates a ribbon of rust-colored dust cutting through a bright band of starlight.

The ribbon breaks into dark patches toward the edges, and it takes a moment to recognize what you’re looking at: a spiral galaxy seen from the side.

Recent findings suggest that the galaxy is NGC 1827. From this angle, the arms that would sweep around its center in a face-on view overlap along our line of sight.

What stands out instead is the structure of the disk itself, from its glowing central bulge to the uneven ribbon of dust that runs through it.

NGC 1827 lies about 37 million light-years away in the constellation Columba, also known as the Dove.

Hubble captured this view with its Advanced Camera for Surveys, and NASA released the image on October 16.

Industry observers note that A spiral galaxy’s disk is wide and relatively thin. Its arms curve through that disk, carrying stars, gas and dust.

When we see the disk nearly edge-on, much of that material appears in a narrow strip.

The central bulge, which extends above and below the disk, gives the galaxy its thicker middle.

That geometry also makes the dust especially easy to see. Along parts of the disk, we look through enough dust to dim the combined light of the stars behind it.

The resulting dark lane runs in front of the bright bulge, where the difference between the obscured and unobscured regions is easiest to make out.

Sources indicate that follow the dust lane away from the center and you’ll see bright blue patches scattered across the disk. NASA identifies them as places where upcoming stars are likely forming.

Hot, massive young stars give off intense blue light. They burn through their fuel rapidly by stellar standards, so a concentration of them can point to relatively recent star formation.

In NGC 1827, those blue patches sit among dark clouds, where gas and dust provide the raw material for future generations of stars.

The side view makes it difficult to tell which arm a particular patch belongs to.

A knot of blue light that appears close to the center in the image could sit farther out in the disk, somewhere along the same line of sight.

Hubble indicates where each feature appears in the image, but its true distance from the galaxy’s center is harder to pin down.

Just left of the galaxy’s bright middle, a star stands out with four sharp spikes.

It has been revealed that it looks close enough to belong to NGC 1827, but it lies between Earth and the galaxy. Its apparent position is a chance alignment.

Those four spikes offer a clue to another kind of structure, this time inside the telescope. They appear when light from a bright point source bends around the supports that hold Hubble’s secondary mirror in place.

The pattern is especially obvious on this star because so much of its light comes from one tiny point in the image.

Industry observers note that other objects sit much farther away. Look into the dark sky beyond the disk and you’ll find small, faint smudges, some of them distant galaxies.

A single frame brings together a foreground star, a nearby spiral and galaxies deeper in the background.

The portrait came from a Hubble program targeting 260 satellite galaxies around 22 hosts similar to the Milky Way.

These smaller galaxies give astronomers a way to test how well models of the universe describe what happens on the scale of individual galaxies and their neighbors.

Computer models can reproduce many of the broad patterns astronomers see across the universe.

The details get harder to match on smaller scales, where the growth of galaxies depends in part on how gas gathers and how stars affect the material around them.

Looking at many satellite systems gives researchers a broader sample for those comparisons.

Hubble’s sharp view is useful because a galaxy’s overall brightness tells only part of its story.

In this image, the narrow dust lane, bright central bulge and scattered blue patches each give a different view of how its material is arranged.

From another vantage point, the spiral arms might be the first thing we’d notice.

From Earth, the most striking feature is the dark streak down the middle, visible because the galaxy’s own stars light it from behind.

#77135. American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 17m • 📚 Deep Dive (3440 w)

American science is broken. Meet the people fixing it

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencenews

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This is a human-written story voiced by AI.
  • The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes.
  • Industry observers note that “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .).

The February sun was setting outside her family’s West Virginia home when Rebecca Lindsey found out she was being fired in 75 minutes. Lindsey, who until early 2025 managed the federal government’s climate.gov website, had just begun to think her job might be safe during the second Trump administration.

Industry observers note that “Every week, it was like, ‘This is the week we’re all going to get fired,’ ” says Lindsey, who had worked as a contractor and later a civil servant at the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration for nearly 15 years. “Every time you would hear the rumor and then it wouldn’t happen, you would think … maybe this is all just talk.”.

But at 3:45 p.m. on February 27, 2025, Lindsey and around 800 of her NOAA colleagues received a mass termination email saying they no longer “fit the Agency’s current needs.” In June, Lindsey’s sister and the data visualization lead for the project, Mary Lindsey, was fired alongside the remaining climate.gov contractors. The website URL was redirected, hiding the site — and its decades’ worth of climate visualizations, educational tools and extreme weather trackers — from the public.

The Lindsey sisters decided to fight back. Along with another terminated NOAA employee, they split a $65,000 grant from the nonprofit Surge Climate Talent and launched a crowdfunding campaign to rebuild and enhancement climate.gov. The site, now called climate.us, notched one million views in its first month.

It has been revealed that but as proud as they are of their work, the project is a patch, not a fix. Rebecca Lindsey predicts it would take at least seven employees and $1.8 million annually to resume 80 percent of the old site’s work. “Climate.gov was more than just a website; it was a climate literacy program,” she notes. To rescue the full mission, they still have a long way to go.

Courtesy of M. Lindsey and R. Lindsey.

The Lindsey sisters are far from the only tale of makeshift resilience. Over the last year, untold numbers of U.S. scientists and their supporters have rebuilt data dashboards, formed recommendation groups for childhood vaccines and screenings, and doled out research funds for hundreds of stranded early-career scientists. They’ve reconstituted committees to advise space missions, rehomed key reports on climate and Arctic science, and even turned to social media to spread public health alerts in the wake of a massive realignment of the federal science enterprise.

“I don’t think anyone could have foreseen the amount of destruction and deliberate breaking down of norms and infrastructure” over the last two years, notes Christina Madison, a clinical pharmacist and public health communicator known on social media as The Public Health Pharmacist.

It has been revealed that since January 2025, the second Trump administration has frozen or rescinded billions of dollars in research funding on topics from climate change to vaccine hesitancy and is trying to redirect it — often without congressional approval — to administration priorities such as artificial intelligence and quantum computing. During deliberations for the FY2026 and FY2027 budgets, the White House proposed slashing future science funding by one-third.

In a recent development, “When this was first starting, it really, truly felt like an alternate universe,” says Sean O’Leary, a pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. “The science was always what drove the decision making, and now we’re at a place where it’s not.”.

Recent findings suggest that in 2025 alone, the federal government shed some 20 percentof its science workforce. And in May 2026, the Office of Management and Budget proposed a sweeping set of rules to expand the authority of federal political appointees in selecting science grants.

Approximate proportion of the scientific workforce who left federal service in 2025.

Industry observers note that yet some researchers see the destruction as an opportunity to rebuild their corners of U.S. science — or even reimagine it, says Michael Osterholm, an epidemiologist at the University of Minnesota in Minneapolis. “If there’s any good that can come out of what has been a horrible situation, it’s that it’s given us time and provided a pause to think through clearly: Is this the way we want to continue?”.

University of Ottawa ecologist Julien Martin spent a decade building a respected lab that probed how social behaviors affect the evolution of bushy-tailed, cat-sized rodents called marmots. So when the National Science Foundation began its sweeping grant cuts, Martin found himself doing something unexpected: uploading cute marmot videos to OnlyFans, an online video subscription platform better known for hosting pornography.

Recent findings suggest that the effort, called OnlyMarms, netted $6,000 — a mere drop in the funding bucket. But the project went viral, leading outside supporters to launch a cryptocurrency token that earned the lab an additional $150,000. And direct donations, including an anonymous $300,000 gift, gave the lab enough to fund one Ph.D. student’s entire degree.

“When you see that so much money could be obtained by doing essentially nothing about science, it’s quite shocking,” Martin indicates. He welcomes the support, but having to spend so much time on non-research tasks has also felt demeaning. “Sometimes, you have to question: Is the science funding broken? Are we just competing for pennies?”.

In 2025, the National Institutes of Health and the NSF canceled or suspended more than 7,800 existing grants, totaling billions of dollars. (Some 5,200 grants were later reinstated.) Each agency issued roughly a quarter fewer grants in 2025 than their previous 10-year averages.

Industry observers note that universities and research centers were hit hard. “It was really dire,” indicates Emily Young, who leads medical research grantmaking at the San Diego-based Prebys Foundation. In phone calls with researchers, many told her they had halted ongoing experiments, such as developing measles vaccines for people with autoimmune disorders.

But the thing that really stood out, Young indicates, was how the sudden drop in funding was affecting postdocs and early-career researchers. “Young people were going from feeling like they had an avenue for a really promising career … to feeling like they were in a worthless career.”.

It has been revealed that so, in May 2025, the foundation awarded $7 million total in emergency grants to seven local institutions, including San Diego State University, the University of California, San Diego and Scripps Research. The grants targeted more than 80 research programs involving early- and mid-career scientists that were facing hundreds of millions of dollars in lost federal funding.

Industry observers note that larger science philanthropies also stepped into the breach. The Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation gave $55 million total to 30 universities to support 400 postdoctoral researchers. The Alfred P. Sloan and Spencer foundations, among others, partnered to provide 83 quick-turnaround grants of around $25,000 each to researchers whose NSF education grants had been canceled.

Some wealthy universities also offered bridge funding to their researchers; Johns Hopkins University gave awards up to $250,000 to individuals with unexpected funding gaps, and the Yale School of Medicine arranged to fund up to 90 percent of terminated or frozen NIH grants.

After the first bout of funding chaos, science philanthropy Schmidt Sciences announced a more ambitious approach: to develop the science themselves. In January 2026, they revealed plans to construct three ground-based observatories and a space telescope larger than NASA’s Hubble by the end of the decade. The space telescope alone will cost hundreds of millions of dollars and provide open-access data to scientists worldwide, with a special focus on exoplanets and transient events like supernovas.

In November 2026, the philanthropy opened its first round of funding for early-career scientists using the observatory system; individual awards will total up to $2.5 million each.

Recent findings suggest that “Originally, the hope was we would play a more classic philanthropic role,” indicates Arpita Roy, an astronomer who directs the Astrophysics & Space Center at Schmidt Sciences. But given the federal funding landscape, she says, “it became pretty clear to us, if we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

Industry observers note that while private funding can be a lifeline, Young indicates, it’s still a temporary measure at best. “We are not going to fill the vacuum of federal funding,” she says. “There is simply not enough philanthropic resource out there to do that.”.

In 1995, the American Academy of Pediatrics and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention made a consequential decision: Rather than publish independent recommendations for childhood vaccines, as they had since the 1960s, they would issue one set jointly. Over the next 30 years, a group called the Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices advised the CDC, with academy input, to expand its recommendations to include chickenpox, hepatitis A and pneumococcal infections. Cases of the three dropped by more than 90 percent, saving thousands of lives.

But in June 2025, Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr., an outspoken vaccine critic, fired all 17 members of ACIP and replaced many with vaccine skeptics. Kennedy also dismissed the academy representatives that informed the group.

Sources indicate that “Essentially, we had no voice anymore,” recalls O’Leary, the pediatric infectious disease researcher at the University of Colorado Anschutz. He also serves as the AAP’s immunization schedule editor. “So we made a decision to not participate until we could say, ‘OK, this is a body that can be trusted.’ ”.

Recent findings suggest that in July 2025, the academy and other public health groups sued over the ACIP firings. The committee was unable to meet due to the lawsuit, and over the next six months, the CDC removed recommendations from its childhood vaccination schedule including hepatitis A and B, COVID-19 and meningococcal disease. The American Academy of Pediatrics issued its own schedule including those vaccines in January 2026.

Svetlana Repnitskaya/Getty Images Plus.

In a recent development, the loss of trustworthy federal recommendations leaves “an impossible gap to fill,” O’Leary claims. But when it came to stepping in, “from my perspective, there was not an alternative.” The academy has since collaborated with the Vaccine Integrity Project, a new group led by Osterholm, to conduct the scientific reviews that inform vaccine recommendations.

Industry observers note that vaccines weren’t the only childhood health matter to get a shakeup. In April 2025, HHS terminated the Advisory Committee on Heritable Disorders in Newborns and Children, which formulates newborn screening recommendations for genetic disorders, many of which can be deadly or disabling. Currently, some 98 percent of U.S.-born infants are screened at birth.

In a recent development, when the genetics community raised concerns, Cynthia Powell, a retired pediatric geneticist at the University of North Carolina School of Medicine in Chapel Hill, gathered around 15 representatives of professional medical societies to create the Newborn Screening Collaborative. With support from the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics, the group began meeting in early 2026.

While the collaborative cannot give direct recommendations to HHS, it hopes to conduct evidence reviews for states and the small, parent-led advocacy groups that form around rare diseases, Powell says. It looks to focus on conditions that already have treatments under development, like a rare metabolic disorder known as Sanfilippo syndrome type A.

Approximate number of NIH and NSF grants canceled or suspended in 2025. Some 5,200 have since been reinstated.

“This Newborn Screening Collaborative is another effort not to leave a complete void,” notes Jewel Mullen, an epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin who was lead editor on a May 2025 newborn screening report for the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering and Medicine.

Other researchers are filling gaps in awareness about public health threats. A philanthropy-backed group called the Evidence Collective posted about the diarrhea-causing cyclosporiasis outbreak before the CDC’s Health Alert Network did. The collective, made up of more than 30 medical communicators, has more than 10 million followers across social media and notched 11 billion impressions in 2025.

It has been revealed that “I don’t think that we will ever be able to fully replace the infrastructure that was there through the federal government,” says Madison, a founding member of the collective. But “there is a concerted effort now to look at: How do we take the momentum that we have with these organizations, and then make it sustainable?”.

Although stopgap measures are succeeding so far, scientists see them as Band-Aids at best. “We’re going to do it for as long as we’re needed,” Osterholm states. But “I look forward to the day when we’re not going to be needed anymore.”.

In a recent development, in April 2025, nearly 400 scientists working on the National Climate Assessment, a recurring, congressionally mandated report, received an email that it was being reevaluated and they were being released from their work. One of them — Rutgers University climate scientist Bob Kopp — wasn’t surprised. “I don’t think you have to speculate very far” to know why, Kopp says. He cites a directive in the White House’s 2027 budget request to “stop wasting biological and environmental research resources on climate change.”.

However, “there was an immediate and deep sentiment by the science community to continue the work,” claims environmental engineer Costa Samaras of Carnegie Mellon University in Pittsburgh, who had also been involved with the climate report. He and colleagues asked the American Geophysical Union and the American Meteorological Society to help organize the U.S. Climate Collection, a new set of papers from scientists about climate research, risks and solutions that will keep the public informed until federal assessments resume.

While the work is promising, “a volunteer effort of 170 scientists cannot substitute for a $30 million effort of 600 people,” Kopp indicates.

Sources indicate that the American Geophysical Union similarly stepped in with crucial financing for the Arctic Report Card, an annual report from NOAA that has provided information about the changing Arctic since 2006. Its editors were blindsided when they found out during a routine meeting in August 2026 that NOAA was withdrawing its support.

It has been revealed that AGU’s in-kind offer to support the project just one month later was “tremendous,” says Twila Moon, a glaciologist at the National Snow and Ice Data Center in Boulder, Colo., who edits the report card. “But [it] is not a kind of model that is sustainable into the future.”.

According to recent reports, AGU President Brandon Jones agrees. Nevertheless, at the time, the organization “had this sense of what was moral, what was right, what was ethical,” Jones claims. And given AGU’s resources, “it seemed like it was our turn to show up and step up and act like the union that we’ve always been.”.

The Planetary Society, a nonprofit space advocacy organization based in Pasadena, Calif., took the lead on several committees that NASA dropped. In January, the agency cited executive orders as it withdrew financial and logistical support from eight groups of space scientists and experts that advised NASA’s planning teams on exploring asteroids, comets and planets.

“It was pretty well-managed and organized [before], and then really fell apart because of the intrusion of the executive orders,” indicates Jack Kiraly, chief of advocacy at the Planetary Society. The organization now hosts the advisory groups’ websites, documents and meetings. “We’ve basically been having to reinvent this whole system.”.

Chris Gunn, Courtesy of Schmidt Sciences.

In a recent development, climate.us isn’t the only site saving federal data. In November 2024, many environmental organizations “started preparing for the worst,” says Brittany Janis, executive director of the Open Environmental Data Project. Her group and nine others banded together to create the Public Environmental Data Partners, a network of 400 volunteers that archive environmental data and tools they suspected “would probably be on the chopping block.”.

In February 2025, the Environmental Protection Agency deleted a tool called EJScreen, which maps places where people face high levels of risk from environmental burdens such as hazardous waste and ozone. Within 48 hours, the partnership had stood up EJScreen on a newly introduced website, using open-source files to reverse engineer and refine the data pipelines. It has since received 1,000 views a month, Janis says.

Nearly $2 million in philanthropic funding has helped the project pay staff, host data and hire engineers. It has restored the Federal Emergency Management Agency’s Future Risk Index, which projects county-level economic losses from climate change; the White House Council on Environmental Quality’s Climate and Economic Justice Screening Tool, which identifies communities overburdened by pollution; and the Department of Homeland Security’s Homeland Infrastructure Foundation-Level Data tool, which maps infrastructure at risk of natural disasters.

“We should not misunderstand the administration’s closing off of this data [to mean] that they don’t think data is vital,” Janis states. “They recognize how important it is — and how valuable it is to causes that they disagree with.”.

At the University of Chicago, the Data Mirror Project preserves datasets larger than one terabyte, including those from the U.S. Census Bureau and the National Park Service. The project has a guiding principle: LOCKSS, which stands for lots of copies keeps stuff safe, states colead Lisa Chinn, who is head of research data services at the university library. An agency doesn’t have to delete its data to create problems, she adds. Firing website staff can lead to wonky links, corrupted files and pages that degrade into Wingdings gibberish.

The thought of losing all that data can be stressful, Janis says, but “there’s a lot of parachutes that have gone out.”.

In a recent development, even as researchers, volunteers and scientific organizations pick up the pieces of the federal science enterprise, some are already imagining newly introduced ways of shaping it. “The world was not perfect in 2024,” says Rutgers’ Kopp. “Reconstruction is an opportunity to improve upon the way things are done.”.

Recent findings suggest that to Mullen, the epidemiologist at the University of Texas at Austin, transparency is key. Newly introduced bodies like the Vaccine Integrity Project and the Newborn Screening Collaborative should make their meetings and deliberations as open as possible, she says, especially when “people think that those with the loudest voices or the biggest wallets are going to be the ones that have the greatest influence behind the scenes.”.

According to recent reports, powell, of the Newborn Screening Collaborative, is hoping for greater efficiency in the disease recommendation process. Previously, it could take as long as three years to bring a condition from an initial vote to a final recommendation; with the collaborative, she hopes it could take one to three months.

Janis, of the Open Environmental Data Project, hopes to develop more creative and flexible data tools for researchers based on their needs. And Madison from the Evidence Collective and Martin of OnlyMarms believe that the science infrastructure needs to diversify its funding sources to prevent future shocks.

“If we really think these things need to exist in the world … then we need to build them out.”.

According to recent reports, however, Janis notes that there are inherent risks in having the private sector support public goods such as open information. And Kopp warns that “attempts to replace something that was well-functioning … are not going to necessarily end up with something that is better or even as good as what was there before.”.

At the end of the day, one of the key elements in establishing a fresh science system is “faith that you will still exist in a year or 10 years or maybe even 20 years,” indicates Katharine Jacobs, an environmental scientist who directed a previous National Climate Assessment under President Obama. Without stable institutional funding, “we are all essentially wasting our time, bashing our heads against the wall, trying to create a system that we can’t support,” Jacobs says.

For the Lindsey sisters, being involved in public service — even outside the government aegis — has been empowering, especially during what they see as an otherwise dark period for science.

Industry observers note that they have raised more than $600,000 from individual donations since August 2025. And in February, they received a one-time grant from the Doris Duke Foundation and others that will cover their salaries and benefits until February 2027.

“If we can get the money, I can see us doing this indefinitely,” Rebecca Lindsey says. She still hopes to retire one day, and she fights off worries that the government might come knocking about their unsanctioned work. But “we had a public that trusted us,” she says about jumping into the fray. “It was a risk worth taking.”.

#77134. When AI causes harm, who should be held responsible?

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (822 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Earth ↗ Open Full Page

When AI causes harm, who should be held responsible?

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (822 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • When AI causes harm, a proposed legal framework would trace responsibility through the decisions people made while building, training, and deploying it.
  • Sources indicate that when an AI system causes harm, there is often no obvious person to blame.
  • A proposed legal framework argues that courts can use existing law to trace AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and ran the system.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When AI causes harm, a proposed legal framework would trace responsibility through the decisions people made while building, training, and deploying it.

Sources indicate that when an AI system causes harm, there is often no obvious person to blame. Nobody typed the harmful words, and nobody gave the order.

A proposed legal framework argues that courts can use existing law to trace AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and ran the system.

It would assign responsibility based on the decisions that contributed to the harm.

The proposal comes from Martin Hilbert, a professor of communication at the University of California, Davis.

AI agents now trade stocks, proposal holidays, and write complex software. When they go wrong, the damage can be serious.

Earlier this year, OpenAI reported that AI models it was testing gained access to systems at the machine-learning firm Hugging Face.

AI chatbots have also been linked to suicides among young people.

It has been revealed that cases like these don’t fit the law neatly. If a chatbot persuades a child to hurt himself, no single person noted those words or even chose them.

In cases like these, Hilbert argues, courts could examine which human decisions contributed to the outcome and who could reasonably have foreseen the risk.

Hilbert identifies two approaches that he says are a poor fit for AI.

In a recent development, product liability law points at the manufacturer that built the model. But AI models learn from enormous amounts of data that the company didn’t create.

Millions of users also shape how the systems behave. Putting all the blame on the developer ignores most of the people who contributed.

The other route comes from free speech protections and the immunity laws that shield social media platforms.

Hilbert argues that applying those protections to AI-generated output could lead courts to treat the system as if it were an independent speaker, raising questions about whether it should have rights of its own.

Industry observers note that “Courts adapt tools to regulate earlier technologies, but many of these tools were never designed to address AI,” Hilbert remarked. “The result is a corridor of precedents that might narrow with every ruling.”.

In other words, every ruling made with these ill-fitting tools becomes a precedent, and the legal options may get narrower each time.

Hilbert argues that existing law gives courts a starting point for tracing AI-related harm back to the people and organizations that built, trained, and deployed the system.

“Every AI, without exception, starts with goals that a human defines, and every subsequent step in the AI’s development involves a chain of deliberate human choices,” he explained.

Industry observers note that because people are involved at every step, tracing their choices demonstrates how much each contributed to a given harm. Liability can then be shared out to match.

The test is foreseeability, meaning whether a person knew, or reasonably should have known, that their decision could cause harm.

Hilbert draws on tools from environmental, vaccine, and financial regulation to show how courts might apply this approach.

Hilbert also points out four further gaps in how the law handles AI, and suggests a fix for each.

The first is the tangled supply chain. A model’s developer can blame the tech giant that deployed it, and the deploying company can blame the developer.

US environmental law faced the same problem with polluted land. Under the “Superfund” program, responsibility for cleanup costs can extend to many parties at once.

Hilbert suggests a similar approach for AI.

The second gap is the burden of proof. Sometimes a harmful outcome can’t be linked to any single decision about how a system was set up.

In those cases, Hilbert suggests that the tech giant should have to show it acted responsibly, and that no reasonable alternative design would have lowered the risk.

That would reverse the usual arrangement, in which an injured person has to prove what went wrong inside a system they can’t see.

The third gap concerns what happens after release. Product liability assumes that a defect existed when the product was sold.

An AI system’s behavior can change after release as developers update it or people deploy it in new settings.

Hilbert argues that this calls for ongoing monitoring and a clear definition of what good-faith compliance looks like over a model’s lifetime.

The last gap is speed. Lawsuits take years, and AI changes in months. Dealing with this requires public governance that can keep pace with the technology.

A first step could be to give the industry’s current voluntary safety standards real enforcement.

“It takes a village to raise an AI, and everyone in that village bears a duty of care,” Hilbert concluded.

The study is published in the journal Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.

Latest Update: Some Democrats doubt Trump is serious about cutting deals in latest Congress

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1056 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Rollcall

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that president Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct.
  • President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.
  • According to recent reports, on the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that president Donald Trump speaks with reporters on the South Lawn of the White House on Oct. 13 before leaving for a campaign rally in Alaska. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

President Donald Trump’s postelection statements about working with Democrats have presented the incoming majority with a kaleidoscope to decipher, but some Democratic lawmakers have their doubts.

According to recent reports, on the one hand, the Republican president has contended that he can work with House and Senate Democrats after the new Congress is seated in January, even floating a bipartisan immigration bill. But on the other, he promoted his hard-line aide Stephen Miller to White House chief of staff, raising doubts about any cooling of the political environment.

Sources indicate that at every stop along his October campaign rally blitz before Republicans suffered massive losses on Nov. 3, Trump railed against “Dumbocrats” and their “bad” policies. He mocked their candidates as too extreme, too corrupt and too beholden to the most progressive wing of their party. He even warned that, if voters handed them control of the House and Senate, it would set off “a 1929-style economic depression.”.

According to recent reports, voters ignored him. They handed House Democrats over 250 seats at least come January, and the party will have at least 54 seats in the Senate.

Industry observers note that trump was asked during a “60 Minutes” interview taped Friday afternoon at the White House if he could resist insulting Democratic lawmakers for six months if that’s how long it took to reach a deal on major legislation. “Very easily,” he responded.

But several Democrats are so sure about getting to a “Kumbaya” moment with Trump during his final two years.

Recent findings suggest that virginia Sen. Tim Kaine said it was hard to take the president at his word because he is “so unpredictable.”.

“But I'm certainly telling my colleagues we should try to put as many bills as we can on his desk that do good things for the American public, and then see how he behaves,” he said Tuesday.

Sources indicate that "We're gonna put bills in front of the president on affordability starting Day One,” California Rep. Robert Garcia, the likely incoming House Oversight and Government Reform chair, noted Tuesday. “We'll have to see if he's serious, but I don't trust Donald Trump for a second.”.

Cannabis use disorder is linked to higher odds of suicidal thoughts

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Adults with cannabis use disorder reported suicidal thoughts far more often than other adults, and the gap held steady for a decade.
  • Adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting serious suicidal thoughts in the past year than adults without the disorder, even after researchers accounted for depression and other factors.
  • In a recent development, across U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Adults with cannabis use disorder reported suicidal thoughts far more often than other adults, and the gap held steady for a decade.

Adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting serious suicidal thoughts in the past year than adults without the disorder, even after researchers accounted for depression and other factors.

In a recent development, across U.S. surveys from 2014 through 2023, researchers found no clear evidence that the link grew stronger.

Sources indicate that cannabis use disorder is not the same as using cannabis. It means having trouble controlling the habit even when it is clearly causing harm.

The survey measured it with nine yes-or-no questions about the past year.

Tosin Philip Oyetunji, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced, led the study with three colleagues there.

The team pooled ten years of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health, which the federal government runs every year. After minors and incomplete answers were set aside, 415,861 adults were left.

Among them, 4.0% met the criteria for the disorder. And 4.6% said that in the past 12 months they had seriously thought about killing themselves.

“What we would most like people to understand is that struggling with cannabis use can go hand in hand with mental health challenges that are not always visible,” Oyetunji said in an interview with Earth.com.

Adults with the disorder had 1.57 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts. The range around that figure runs from 1.44 to 1.72.

The comparison is adjusted, which matters more than usual here. The model accounted for depression, serious psychological distress and heavier drinking that met the criteria for alcohol use disorder.

The team also controlled for income, education, insurance, self-rated health, religious attendance and whether a person’s state had legalized recreational cannabis.

Recent findings suggest that so the gap isn’t just depression showing up in a different column. Nobody was followed over time, though, so the survey can’t say which came first.

The team expected the link to strengthen. Cannabis potency has risen sharply since legalization began, and Canadian data had suggested a tightening link.

An earlier national study had also tied cannabis use to suicidal thoughts, plans and attempts.

The researchers found no clear evidence that the link strengthened. In the 2016 and 2022 surveys, the odds ran higher than in the first survey year.

Neither of those two survived the correction the team applied for testing ten years at once. Across the decade, the differences from one survey to the next were too small to rule out chance.

“A public health concern does not have to be getting worse to deserve attention,” Oyetunji said when Earth.com asked why the link had held while the drug changed.

Sidra Goldman-Mellor, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study’s senior author, put the other half of it plainly.

“People with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that’s not something that is widely understood,” she noted.

The disorder was not the only measure that highlighted the pattern. The survey’s criteria changed partway through the decade, so the team ran the analysis again using how often people used cannabis.

Nondaily users had 1.39 times the odds of reporting suicidal thoughts, compared with people who had not used cannabis at all. Daily or near-daily users had 1.65 times the odds.

“This suggests that patterns of cannabis use may also be notable to consider when examining mental health, and it raises questions about how the frequency of use relates to suicidal thoughts,” Oyetunji told Earth.com.

The team also split the sample by sex, by age and by race and ethnicity.

Adults with the disorder had higher odds in every one of those groups, and the differences between the groups were too small to call real.

According to recent reports, everyone answered once, so nobody can say which came first. Every answer was also the person’s own account of a year they were remembering.

The study focused on serious suicidal thoughts. The link with cannabis use disorder may differ for suicide looks, attempts or deaths.

It has been revealed that the survey also records nothing about what people were using. Potency, product type and whether someone vaped concentrates are all missing, so the study cannot test the potency question it raises.

Industry observers note that studies of high-THC products disagree anyway. A recent review found strong links between high-THC cannabis and the disorder itself or psychosis, and weaker ones for depression and anxiety.

Craving and withdrawal were left out of the disorder measure so the questions would match across years, which probably undercounts it.

The survey excluded people living in institutions and people experiencing homelessness who were outside shelters.

The authors raise one more possibility. As cannabis use spread, the group meeting the criteria may have shifted toward milder cases.

A shift like that would hold the average down even if nothing had changed for the most severe cases.

It has been revealed that two people can give this survey the same answers. In one of them, cannabis use deepened a crisis. In the other, a crisis drove heavier use.

A single round of questions cannot tell them apart. Researchers would have to follow the same people for years, with the potency and the products written down.

Oyetunji is widening the question rather than narrowing it.

“I want to better understand how these risks overlap, what drives them, and where we may be missing opportunities to help people before they experience serious harm,” he said.

Clinics don’t have to wait for that. Someone asking for help with cannabis may be carrying something they have not mentioned, and the authors argue that the right response is to ask.

The full study was published in the journal Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs.

The 6 Best Metal Detectors for Treasure Hunters and Experts Alike
