  • That stated, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

You've probably seen a metal detectorist hard at work at a beach or park with their funky-looking gadget and thought, "I wish I had one of those." It's easy to fantasize about stumbling upon a hoard of buried pirate gold or, more realistically, a lost piece of jewelry, but the reality of metal detecting is this: It's more about the process of searching than the actual find itself.

That stated, metal detecting can be a fun and relaxing hobby for anyone to try, especially with friends, and the barrier to entry is low. It’s an activity that gives you an excuse to spend a few hours outside, scouring the sand or dirt for coins or who-knows-what, and you might even find something that really makes it worth your while, though it's best if you don't expect to.

To determine the best metal detectors for newbies and experts alike, I tested a number of different models on the beaches and in the parks of South Florida, rating their performance, handling, and overall usability across several different terrains. I also consulted with an expert detectorist who helped me understand what factors to consider when making my choices. No matter which of these machines works best for your use case, all of them are great gets.

I selected the best metal detectors after trying a handful of options that came recommended to me by Jeff Lubbert, an expert detectorist who has been tracking down treasures and finding lost rings since the mid-1980s, and a handful of other expert detectorists.

Lubbert has used his metal detector in 28 states, one United States territory, five foreign countries, and three foreign territories, where he has recovered items adding up to approximately $980,000. He is president of the Eureka Treasure Hunters Club in Denver, Colorado, and has written articles about metal detectors for outlets like American Diggers. He's also appeared on the TV show Forensic Files.

To test accuracy, I buried an old spoon and two different coins—a quarter and a penny—8 inches underground to check their level of discrimination and pinpointing. I also used each detector for several hours in a variety of conditions, including in a grassy park and at the beach, in both dry sand and wet sand, and under several inches of surf.

Industry observers note that the Minelab Vanquish 560 is a dynamic metal detector that works well on every terrain, including wet sand, and is incredibly intuitive to use. Unlike the slightly cheaper Vanquish 440, my previous top recommendation, the 560 is waterproof to 16 feet, which makes it suitable for wading and underwater use. It also includes a rechargeable battery, a flashlight, and Bluetooth headphone support, making it one of the most fully-featured detectors in this guide, and especially for this price.

While it only has four find modes (including an adjustable “custom” option). That’s are far fewer than you will find on professional-grade detectors like the Minelab Equinox 900, but it's still much more than enough for most amateur metal detectorists.

Industry observers note that the Vanquish 560 punches well above its weight, and value-wise, it's the best detector we tested on a per-dollar basis. It may feel like a splurge for first-timers, but you’re getting what you pay for. And it’s an incredibly handsome upgrade for folks looking strong accuracy and some quality-of-life improvements.

It has been revealed that since I primarily spoke with experts and enthusiasts, the Nokta FindX Pro was not remotely on my radar when I first began my research. But it may just be the best option for fresh detectorists looking to dip a toe into the hobbyist pool. It’s an all-in-one kit, complete with an effective digging tool, a nice duffel bag, and decent headphones—all for less than $200.

While it is not as accurate as my other recommendations, it’s a more than capable VLF detector. I was able to find items at both parks and beaches, though I noticed that its performance really suffered on wet sand and underwater. Its compact frame and adjustable handle make it accommodating to a wider-than-average range of newcomers, including kids and adults.

If you’re interested in the hobby and don’t want to spend too much to try it, the FindX Pro is a great fit for beginners.

It has been revealed that while I wasn’t able to get this detector in for my current round of tests, Lubbert recommended the Minelab Manticore for expert detectorists who want the ultimate metal detector experience. He says it can visualize the ground beneath it in a 2D map, directing you to finds with depths and ID targets. It should work well in any terrain, including underwater, and has the most advanced backlight of any Minelab machine. Plus, with 10 search modes, there are many options for veteran detectorists looking to optimize for a specific type of search.

The price is substantial, but if you’re willing to spend this much money on a detector, I’m confident that it will be worth it.

Sources indicate that the Simplex line is often recommended by experts as a good entry point for new detectorists. Nokta is one of the two biggest brands in the metal detecting game—the other is Minelab—and the Simplex Lite is a strong, basic VLF detector. I found it had top-notch discrimination, plenty of find modes, and a good coil size that easily found my testing materials and led me to beer cans, aluminum foil, and plenty of other objects on the beach.

Because this is a single-frequency VLF detector, it doesn’t perform as well as the Vanquish 440, especially on the mineralized sand at saltwater beaches. It’s still a very capable machine, though—even more so if you’re searching for a specific type of item, particularly coins and jewelry. Though it offers fewer customization options than its more expensive multi-frequency counterparts, it’s also much easier to pick up and use as a newcomer.

For those who are looking to spend a bit more, you can upgrade to the Simplex Ultra, which adds Bluetooth support and gives you precision detector tools like target ID scale and depth.

Underwater metal detecting is typically the domain of serious enthusiasts, especially if it’s in seawater. If this sounds intriguing, two different experts for metal detector recommendations (including Lubbert) suggest the XP Deus II, a high-end machine that specializes in just that. Expert Stanley Ross, known as the Metal Detector Man, who we spoke with for this article previously, notes that he uses his Deus II to search for lost rings and other jewelry on the beach all the time.

In a recent development, the Deus II has something called "fast multi-frequency" technology, which allows for superior multi-frequency detection in a variety of conditions, and it's rated for up to 20 meters of water, a massive upgrade compared to our other picks that top out at 5 meters of water resistance. Our other multi-frequency picks use similar technology, but the Deus II offers better and faster response in saltwater conditions, making it easier to pinpoint buried targets without having to pass over the same spot multiple times, especially underwater.In order to use the Deus II underwater, however, you'll need a few accessories, including its waterproof wireless headphones and an underwater remote control. While these upgrades are technically “optional” in the sense that you can easily use the Deus II on land without them, they are virtually required for anything beyond getting your ankles wet.

Recent findings suggest that both of these additions will increase the price of the overall package considerably, depending on which exact model of headphones you choose. Both the $280 WS6 headphones (which can control the detector, but are not recommended for underwater use) and the $749 remote control have slightly different interfaces, but the remote control is generally recommended for both ease of use and underwater functionality. Because of its high customizability and 12 preset modes, the Deus II isn't quite as beginner-friendly as some of our other picks.

While I haven't yet tested the Deus II for myself, it’s highly regarded among enthusiasts. If you're interested in underwater detecting—whether that's wading around or even diving down—this choice will not disappoint.

In a recent development, the Minelab Equinox 900 is the most feature-rich metal detector I tested. From the second I picked it up, I could tell that it would be a cut above the rest. The build quality is noticeably better than that of other, less expensive models I tested—it just feels more substantial.

Recent findings suggest that its features and performance back up that first impression. The Equinox 900 consistently performed better than its less expensive counterparts as well, pinpointing targets precisely and identifying both their depth and target ID. Though I was able to find my planted targets with every detector, the Equinox 900 directed me precisely to all three, making the process quicker and easier in both dry and wet sand.

Recent findings suggest that it also features a number of settings and tools that improve the detecting experience, including six customizable frequency settings, an easy-adjust handle, and Bluetooth support so you can use wireless headphones. All that customization is incredible if you’re an expert. I personally had more success using the premade settings, but I can see detectorists like Lubbert fine-tuning searches to great effect.

In a recent development, I was especially taken with its handgrip vibration feature, which gives you a rumbling haptic response when the Equinox picks up a target. It’s a great way to get your attention in a loud area, if you’re hearing-impaired, or if you’re just on a long walk and not paying close attention. Personally, I found it very helpful while roaming some very popular stretches of Miami’s beaches.

It’s worth noting that Minelab lists the Equinox 900 as a bit heavier than the other models we tested, though I personally didn’t notice a difference, even after several hours of sweeping. At more than triple the price of my best overall pick, it’s fair to say that the Equinox 900 is an investment for serious hobbyists. But it is far and away the most effective choice I tested and a worthy upgrade.

In a recent development, in addition to a decent pair of headphones, it helps to carry a pinpointer when using your metal detector. These precise, short-range auxiliary detectors assist you with determining the exact location of a find after picking something up with your detector’s large coil.

Industry observers note that this one, from Minelab, is relatively expensive, but fully waterproof with five sensitivity levels, and it works very well. It also features ferrous discrimination, which allows it to tell if a target is made of ferrous metals like iron or non-ferrous metals like gold, silver, or copper. It isn’t strictly necessary but is an extra feature you’ll enjoy using in trash-filled parks.

We tested and loved the Minelab Vanquish 440, a slightly cheaper version of our current best overall pick, the Vanquish 560. It was recently replaced with a upcoming and improved model, the Minelab Vanquish 460, which is also a strong choice. We ultimately chose to recommend the 560 because it offers a more robust set of features and works well over more types of terrain.

Recent findings suggest that while shopping for a metal detector, you need to take into account a number of key factors, particularly the type, coil size, weight, and extra features like backlight and frequency customization. Weight and build quality also make a significant difference, especially when you use these devices for hours at a time. It was initially hard to weigh these distinct traits, but after testing these machines myself, the features worth springing for became clear.

If you’re going to shop for a hobby-grade metal detector, it’s notable to understand how they work. This is fairly technical equipment, so manufacturers will cater their products primarily to veterans who already have a bit of knowledge, which may be intimidating to upcoming people.

Industry observers note that most metal detectors have a round head called the “search coil,” which is the actual detector itself. It has two parts, the transmitter coil and the receiver coil, which work in tandem to produce an electromagnetic field that shoots down into the ground wherever you wave it. When the field hits metal, it triggers another magnetic effect in response, which the coil picks up. Depending on the device, that signal may be able to tell you how deep an object is buried, based on the strength of the response.

Industry observers note that most of the detectors I recommend can determine what kind of metal they’re reading by measuring the object’s “phase shift,” or the time it takes for the object to react when the coil changes its magnetic current. This function, called “discrimination,” can sometimes help you figure out if your quarry is worth digging up before you go to the trouble of getting your digging tools out. However, as Lubbert notes, discrimination is not always reliable, and it’s generally best to err on the side of digging if you think you’ve found something worthwhile.

Sources indicate that the first thing to look at before buying a metal detector is where you plan to use it, as some detectors are better equipped to scan specific types of terrain. For example, if you live near the coast and plan to sweep your local beach, you may want a different model than someone looking under hard soil in local parks. Though there are many kinds of detectors, I focused on the two most frequently used by novices and veteran hobbyists.

The physical size of the metal detector coil is important, too. If you don’t sweep the coil over an object, you aren’t going to get a ping, so bigger is better. Under most conditions, Lubbert recommends looking for a coil that’s at least 11 inches in diameter.

Industry observers note that that said, Lubbert advises that smaller coils have their uses, especially in wooded areas, since it’s easier to get between twigs, grass, and weeds with a more compact head. Larger coils can theoretically detect objects that are deeper underground, but they’re also more susceptible to electromagnetic interference from the environment. He recommends having both a compact coil and a large coil option if you plan to scan a wide range of environments.

Recent findings suggest that in general, all of my recommendations here seem relatively light on paper—the heaviest weighs only a few pounds. Keep in mind, though, that you could be waving this device around with one arm for hours at a time. Even a few ounces can greatly impact how rapidly you tire out.

Mid-range and high-end metal detectors tend to feature backlit displays, which come in handy when searching in low-light conditions. (Some high-end models even come with flashlight functions). Though not a universal feature, I consider this essential for all but the cheapest options.

High-end metal detectors grant you a degree of customization through advanced settings, allowing you to set a specific level of discrimination that, when properly used, can help you identify relics and coins in a variety of environments. You need to know what you’re doing to take full advantage of these do-it-yourself search modes, but there are guides online to help you learn as you go.

It has been revealed that lastly, most metal detectors I researched and/or tested feature built-in batteries that last for hours on a full charge. That noted, some models—including one of my picks—use disposable batteries instead. There are advantages and disadvantages to both: Disposable batteries can be replaced rapidly, but you need to keep spare cells on you. It comes down to your preference, so go with what feels right.

It has been revealed that “Make each swing of the detector take about 2 seconds and overlap your swings so that the coil covers all of the ground,” Lubbert says. “Wear headphones, as it helps you hear those deep target whispers.”.

Lubbert also said that detectorists should be happy with what they find, and that you should expect 95 percent of your digs to result in trash. When that happens, be cool, and make sure to dispose of it properly.

According to Lubbert, a dedicated detectorist should have a pinpointer, proper recovery tools like a shovel, and a pouch to store trash and treasure separately.

Based on my testing experience and to echo his point above, I found headphones to be a must-have when using a metal detector, as the built-in speakers are difficult to hear, especially on a crowded beach.

Finding a legal place to use your metal detector is not as easy as you might think. It’s illegal to use a detector in U.S. National Parks and historic battlefields. Many cities ban using them on public property or require you to apply for a permit beforehand. Make sure to check your local city and county laws to determine if and where you may be allowed to use a metal detector and if you’ll need a permit to do so.

And, of course, if you plan to use your detector on private property, you should obtain permission from the owner, or else you might dig up a lawsuit instead of treasure.

He has been a full-time writer of various things for around a decade, especially long-form features about tech and digital culture. Latest Update: Movement can change how swiftly you learn from the same visual clues

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1044 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a virtual reality study, swinging a lightsaber or throwing a punch helped volunteers learn visual patterns that required combining two features.
  • In the textbook account, learning happens in the head, and the hands do nothing more than report the answer.
  • Volunteers learned to sort striped discs more accurately when they answered by swinging a virtual lightsaber or punching a virtual target.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a virtual reality study, swinging a lightsaber or throwing a punch helped volunteers learn visual patterns that required combining two features.

In the textbook account, learning happens in the head, and the hands do nothing more than report the answer.

Volunteers learned to sort striped discs more accurately when they answered by swinging a virtual lightsaber or punching a virtual target.

The advantage appeared when they had to judge the angle and thickness of the stripes together.

In the punching experiment, volunteers kept their lead when they switched to button presses immediately after training.

For sorting tasks that could be solved with explicit rules, bigger movements gave volunteers no clear advantage.

Luke Rosedahl is an assistant professor of biomedical engineering in Florida Atlantic University‘s College of Engineering and Computer Science.

Professor Rosedahl conducted the experiments at Brown University with Yuka Sasaki and Takeo Watanabe.

The 160 participants were young adults recruited around Brown, sorting striped discs in a headset, so how far the result reaches outside a lab is still open.

“We found that larger movements substantially improved learning when people had to recognize patterns by integrating multiple features, but provided no meaningful benefit when people learned categories using explicit rules,” Rosedahl said.

Industry observers note that “Even more intriguing, the benefit occurred whether participants swung at the target or punched a separate response box. The movement itself appeared to matter, not whether it directly interacted with what they were learning.”.

Recent findings suggest that some categories come with a rule. If it has whiskers and meows, it’s a cat. Psychologists call these rule-based categories, and people learn them by testing hypotheses, which is thought to lean on the front of the brain.

Other categories can’t be put into words. A radiologist’s sense that a lesion looks aggressive comes from weighing several features at once, and so does a driver’s read on whether a road is icy.

People learn these by comparing each upcoming case with ones they’ve seen.

That kind of learning is thought to run through the striatum, a deep brain structure tied to movement and habits.

Both kinds were tested with the same material: gray discs striped at different angles and thicknesses, shown one at a time in a virtual reality hallway.

Sources indicate that for the rule-based version, thickness and angle could be judged separately. For the other version, the dividing line ran diagonally through both, so no single feature gave the answer.

In the first experiment, 80 people each sorted 600 discs into two groups over 12 blocks, with the disc flashing green or red after every answer. Half answered by pulling a controller trigger.

The other half swung a virtual lightsaber and hit the disc.

On the hard, no-rule categories, the swingers pulled ahead by the second block and stayed ahead for most of the session.

On the rule-based categories, the swingers did very slightly worse, by an amount that could have been chance.

Industry observers note that A swing takes longer than a button press, and it touches the thing being judged. Either could have been the real cause.

In a second experiment with 80 newly introduced volunteers, some punched a virtual response box separate from the disc, while others pulled a controller trigger.

Every disc stayed on screen for 2.5 seconds, however quickly they answered.

The rule-based task was also made harder, with two rules to discover instead of one, in case the first version had simply been too easy to show a difference.

Punching still helped on the no-rule categories and still did nothing for the rule-based ones. Slower answers went with worse accuracy, not better, so taking extra time wasn’t the reason.

In the final 100 training trials of the task that required combining both features, volunteers who punched got 90.7% of answers right, compared with 81.0% for those who pressed a button.

Then everyone switched. The punchers moved to buttons and scored 89.5%, almost unchanged. The button group moved to punching and scored 83.1%.

Whatever the major movements had built was still there when the movement stopped, which points to better learning rather than a boost at the moment of answering.

The authors can’t say what the arm is doing for the brain, and they remarked so. They offered two possibilities.

One possibility is that more effortful movements increase dopamine release in the striatum, which could help reinforce learning.

Effortful actions have also been shown to steer attention toward the features that matter. And movement has helped in other corners of learning, the authors wrote, such as writing by hand to learn to recognize letters.

In a recent development, the selectivity is the clue. If swinging had simply made people more engaged, Rosedahl’s team wrote, both kinds of categories should have improved.

The benefit appeared only when people had to combine visual features, a kind of learning thought to involve motor circuits.

The result also raises a question about decades of earlier work, nearly all of it done with button presses.

Those studies found that no-rule categories are learned slowly and that written instructions on how to perform them don’t help.

The authors suggested that the buttons themselves may have been holding that learning back.

The team didn’t record which hand participants favored, and controllers were handed out in no particular order, so the role of handedness and motor experience is unmeasured.

Industry observers note that other category types, such as rules with exceptions, may respond differently. And everything happened with participants seated and a headset on.

The team wrote that the next studies should test the effect in real training, in fields such as radiology and aviation.

Sources indicate that there, the judgments that can’t be put into words are the ones that take years to learn. Rosedahl framed the stakes in one line.

“Incorporating movement could offer a simple way to improve learning in situations where conventional approaches fall short,” he noted.

Whether a bigger swing of the arm can speed up a radiologist’s eye, and not only a student’s sorting of striped discs, is the test that comes next.

The full study was published in the journal Science Advances.

Breaking: Prickly pear cacti generate electricity, and sunlight changes their voltage

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1047 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Prickly pear cacti generate a small voltage that varies with sunlight, and researchers are exploring whether it could power field sensors.
  • Sources indicate that in a California greenhouse, a row of prickly pear cacti is quietly generating electricity.
  • When eight stems were wired together, they reached 4.5 volts, three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Prickly pear cacti generate a small voltage that varies with sunlight, and researchers are exploring whether it could power field sensors.

Sources indicate that in a California greenhouse, a row of prickly pear cacti is quietly generating electricity. A single stem can produce about half a volt.

When eight stems were wired together, they reached 4.5 volts, three times the voltage of a standard AA battery.

Industry observers note that the trick depends on the unusual way cacti photosynthesize. They store up acid overnight and use it up in daylight.

That turns each stem into something like a small living solar panel.

The work was led by the University of California, Santa Cruz (UCSC).

Most plants take in carbon dioxide during the day. They open tiny pores in their leaves, let the gas in and use sunlight to turn it into sugar.

The downside is that water escapes through those open pores. In a desert, that’s a costly trade.

Prickly pears and some of their relatives work around this problem. Aloe, pineapple, and dragon fruit use a system called crassulacean acid metabolism, or CAM for short.

According to recent reports, these plants keep their pores closed in the heat of the day and open them in the cool of the night. They pull in carbon dioxide while it’s dark and store it as malic acid, the same acid that makes green apples sour.

When the sun comes up, they break the acid down and finish making sugar.

Recent findings suggest that the cactus’s shape provides the second part of the trick. Prickly pear stems are thick and opaque, another way of holding on to water, so photosynthesis happens only in the outer two millimeters or so.

When morning light hits one side of a stem, that side starts using up its stored acid. The shaded side keeps its acid.

The result is a difference in acidity across the stem, from one face to the other. That difference creates a voltage, and the researchers tap into it with a wired electrode inserted into the plant.

In effect, the cactus charges overnight and releases the energy during the day.

The idea came from Michael Loik, a professor of environmental studies who has studied cactus physiology and ecology for about 40 years.

“I’ve been obsessed with the plant since forever, it seems,” Loik stated.

He suspected the cacti could produce electricity. He and Charlie Chesney, then a PhD student in environmental studies, set out to prove it and measure it.

It has been revealed that they used cacti in field plots at the UCSC Farm, in greenhouses, and in the lab. Chesney recruited a large group of undergraduates from engineering, the sciences, and the social sciences, and seven of them are now authors on the paper.

“The undergraduate students told me they liked this project so much because it felt whimsical, and like a light-hearted approach to something that is so serious,” mentioned Chesney, who led the project.

“It was a fun way to explore climate solutions that put creativity first.”.

When researchers wired eight stems together, they measured 4.5 volts, three times the nominal voltage of a standard AA battery.

It has been revealed that the researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors. The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

Chesney has since graduated. Colleen Josephson, an assistant professor of electrical and computer engineering, is continuing the work with her PhD student John Madden, and they are looking for ways to strengthen the signal.

In a recent development, the team also wanted to know how weather and growing conditions affect the voltage. The cacti behaved very much like solar panels.

Voltage was much higher in summer than in winter, and through the day it tracked the amount of sunlight.

“Just how closely the voltage aligned with the sunlight conditions was really surprising,” Chesney noted.

“Comparing winter to summer voltage, the voltage really follows the same pattern of the amount of sunlight throughout the day.”.

Industry observers note that there is an upper limit. Too much sunlight and the cactus goes into self-protection mode.

It has been revealed that “If it’s too high, then the cactus will start trying to protect itself from a sunburn, which will also decrease the voltage,” Chesney said. “There’s a balance, a mid-range of light that causes the voltage to be higher.”.

Then came the drought test. The team stopped watering some cacti for 15 months.

Industry observers note that the plants survived and kept photosynthesizing. Sometimes, they even produced more voltage than cacti that had been watered normally.

“This was a really surprising result, but also showed how resilient a cactus is – it could still produce electricity even when it seems, to us, like it’s near death,” Chesney said.

A separate experiment led by undergraduate Erin Langness looked at nitrogen, a common fertilizer ingredient.

Nitrogen increased the cacti’s store of malic acid, so they kept photosynthesizing and producing voltage later into the day.

The team isn’t trying to run homes on cacti. They have something smaller in mind.

The researchers are exploring whether prickly pears could power low-energy field sensors.

As climate change puts more pressure on crops, farmers increasingly use low-power sensors to monitor their fields.

The voltage may also help growers monitor how the plants respond to changing conditions.

That could be useful on farms that grow prickly pears for their edible pads, called nopales, and their fruit, called tunas.

“There are many commercial applications of cacti where monitoring their health using a low-power system like ours, that is just operating off on the side and is self-powered,” Loik said.

It has been revealed that “This could be a really interesting avenue to pursue. It could be connected to a plant that acts as sentinel, measuring conditions and sending it back to the base station at the farmer’s office.”.

Other CAM plants, such as agave and pineapple, might work too. The researchers note, however, that some of them may not tolerate the wires as well as the prickly pear does.

The study is published in the journal Plants, People, Planet.

In a recent development, more U.S. women are taking menopause hormone therapy, fresh prescription data suggest.

In a recent development, monthly dispensing of hormone therapy for women aged 40 to 74 more than doubled since 2023, growing from 2 million to 4.9 million, researchers report November 19 in JAMA. The analysis of U.S. pharmacy dispensing data revealed that this increase began in 2024. The rise continued in 2025, before and after the Food and Drug Administration’s November removal of the black box warning from packaging, and into 2026.

Although the data in the new study are aggregate, the researchers used population data to estimate the dispensing rate for this age group, which jumped from 28 prescriptions per 1,000 women to 67 prescriptions per 1,000 over the period studied.

In a recent development, the newly introduced study wasn’t designed to determine what’s behind the increase. It’s possible that the evidence regarding hormone therapy’s safety and effectiveness for the treatment of menopause symptoms, such as hot flashes, is reaching more women. Medical groups such as the Menopause Society have recommended menopause hormone therapy for women with symptoms who are younger than 60 or within 10 years of the start of menopause, absent certain risk factors including prior breast cancer and stroke.

“Greater attention to women’s health, updated medical guidance supporting individualized menopause hormone therapy and social media may all be contributing to increased interest,” states Dana Sarnak, who studies sexual and reproductive health at Johns Hopkins School of Medicine. Anecdotally, her clinician colleagues report more patients seeking menopause care, she says.

Many women and physicians turned away from hormone therapy in the early 2000s after a large study called the Women’s Health Initiative raised safety concerns, which were later considered overblown. Research since then has provided a more nuanced understanding of the benefits and risks of menopause hormone therapy at different ages.

It has been revealed that there are safer formulations, including patches and gels, of estrogen today then at the time of the Women’s Health Initiative, for which participants took a pill. The latest study found that product use increased for transdermal and vaginal estrogen and for progesterone products — women who have their uterus need to take progesterone along with estrogen. The use of oral formulations remained stable. There has been a shortage of estrogen patches in the United States this year, which the U.S. Food and Drug Administration attributes to increasing demand.

Breaking: Scientists may have found a way to track one of North America’s most elusive turtles

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1118 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.
  • Industry observers note that diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count.
  • By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A tiny flatworm found in diamondback terrapins and the snails they eat may help scientists understand how turtle populations are connected.

Industry observers note that diamondback terrapins are hard to find and harder to count. A new study suggests that one of the best ways to follow them may be through a tiny flatworm that lives in their intestines and in the snails they eat.

By reading this parasite’s genes along the US Atlantic coast, scientists found that its populations split into distinct groups.

They also found a genetic dividing line about 300 kilometers south of where turtle experts had drawn the boundary between two terrapin subspecies.

The study was carried out by researchers from Florida Atlantic University’s Harbor Branch Oceanographic Institute and East Carolina University.

The diamondback terrapin is the only North American turtle that lives exclusively in brackish water, in salt marshes and estuaries along the coast. For a long time, people mostly ate it.

Recent findings suggest that turtle soup was a fashionable dish, and hunting for it drove the species into steep decline until the early 20th century. Then, in 1920, Prohibition banned sherry, a key ingredient in most turtle soup recipes.

Demand collapsed, and so did the hunting.

In a recent development, that wasn’t a happy ending, though. Terrapins kept declining because of habitat loss, coastal development, and drowning in crab pots.

Industry observers note that the species is now listed as “vulnerable” on the IUCN Red List. Conservationists want better data on where terrapin populations live and how they’re connected.

But the turtles are secretive and spread out, and catching enough to answer those questions is slow, expensive work.

The parasite is a fluke called Pleurogonius malaclemys. It can’t complete its life without two hosts.

According to recent reports, its eggs pass out in terrapin droppings and are eaten by eastern mudsnails. Inside the snail, the fluke multiplies by cloning itself.

Its larvae then leave the snail’s soft body and form small pearly cysts on the hard plate the snail uses to seal its shell.

When a terrapin eats an infected snail, the fluke grows into an adult in the turtle’s gut and reproduces sexually there.

Sources indicate that this arrangement is what makes the fluke useful. Mudsnails are abundant and easy to collect, and they barely move.

According to recent reports, terrapins are the ones that carry the parasite from marsh to marsh. If the turtles don’t travel, the fluke’s genes don’t travel either. In principle, the parasite’s family tree should trace the turtle’s movements.

“One of the biggest challenges in conserving vulnerable species is understanding how populations are distributed and connected without having to capture and handle large numbers of animals,” said senior author Michael McCoy from FAU Harbor Branch.

“Our findings show that this parasite may provide an notable window into the ecology of diamondback terrapins.”.

The team collected mudsnails from Cape Cod in Massachusetts to St. Augustine in Florida and dissected more than 4,000 of them. Infections inside the snails were rare, never reaching 4% at any site.

The cysts outside were far more common, appearing on as many as 74% of snails at some marshes. Altogether, the fluke turned up at 23 of the 29 marshes sampled.

Finds on Cape Cod and in northeast Florida pushed its known range further north and south.

The Wetlands Institute provided the researchers with 38 female terrapins that had been killed by cars in Latest Jersey.

Seventeen of them carried adult flukes, with up to seven worms per turtle.

Sources indicate that from 476 genetic sequences, the team found 102 distinct versions of a stretch of the fluke’s mitochondrial DNA. More than three-quarters of these versions turned up at only one location.

One version dominated the northern marshes, and another dominated the south. The farther apart two marshes were, the more their flukes differed genetically.

It has been revealed that that fits what is known about terrapins. The most mobile of them, adult females, have been recorded traveling no more than 8.5 kilometers. If the hosts stay close to home, their parasites become local too.

The most striking result was where the sharpest split fell. Biologists have traditionally drawn the line between the northern diamondback terrapin and the Carolina terrapin at Cape Hatteras in North Carolina.

The fluke’s genetic break falls instead between Wilmington, North Carolina, and Charleston, South Carolina, near the state border. That’s about 300 kilometers further south.

Terrapin subspecies were originally defined by their appearance, before genetic tools existed, so the parasite’s data adds to growing questions about where the real boundaries lie.

It has been revealed that the study also turned up something nobody had described before. Most fluke cysts are pearly white, but some had a faint blush or a pink ring around the edge, while others were bright fuchsia.

In a recent development, they first appeared in North Carolina in 2023 and later in Massachusetts and Newly introduced Jersey, sometimes on the same snail as ordinary cysts. The color is in the cyst wall, not in the larva inside.

Recent findings suggest that the pink cysts didn’t match any genetic group, and the researchers don’t yet know what causes them. One possibility is that they are simply older.

In a recent development, the authors make a broader point. Parasites account for nearly half of all known species, yet they are rarely studied and almost never protected.

According to recent reports, when a host declines, its parasites decline with it. Scientists recently formed an IUCN group dedicated to parasite conservation, and this study adds basic range and diversity data for a parasite that has been almost entirely ignored.

The team is careful not to overstate the results. The analysis used a single genetic marker, which is inherited only through the mother.

No one has yet compared fluke genetics directly with terrapin genetics from the same marshes, and that test will decide whether the fluke truly mirrors its host.

In a recent development, counting cysts is also not a straightforward way to count turtles. One earlier study found that cyst numbers explained less than 8% of the variation in terrapin abundance.

“Our results point to an opportunity to look at conservation from a different perspective,” McCoy remarked.

“Rather than relying exclusively on direct observations of terrapins, we can investigate the organisms that depend on them.”.

“Understanding where these parasites occur and how their populations are genetically connected could help scientists identify key geographic divisions and develop better questions about how terrapin populations should be monitored and managed.”.

The study is published in the journal Ecology and Evolution.

  • In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug.
  • Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.
  • A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In an aerial view, a fire truck sits parked in a neighborhood destroyed by a wildfire on Aug. 11, 2023 in Lahaina, Hawaii. The performance of the FirstNet network during the Maui fires has partially led to calls for a revamp of its structure. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images).

Supporters of the FirstNet program that provides emergency communications for first-responders still see hope for reauthorization this year, despite continued disagreements over what changes, if any, should be made to how the program is governed.

A House-passed reauthorization bill would shift authority toward the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and away from the FirstNet board, which is made up in part by first-responders.

The potential change is opposed by the influential Fraternal Order of Police, but any upcoming bill or amendment would require floor votes in both the House and Senate, a potentially tall order as the 119th Congress draws to a close.

Authority for FirstNet, a program developed in the wake of 9/11, is set to expire in February of 2027 unless lawmakers pass an extension.

The program’s governing entity, the First Responder Network Authority, was created in 2012 in response to recommendations after the terrorist attacks, during which public safety agencies using different radio systems and overloaded phone lines struggled to adequately communicate.

The House passed its bipartisan reauthorization bill in April via voice vote. Senators have not yet taken up that legislation or introduced their own. In January, the Senate Commerce Committee’s Telecommunications and Media Subcommittee held a hearing on the program.

Related: First-responder network reauthorization advances.

Craig Wheeler, a spokesman for subcommittee Chair Deb Fischer, R-Neb., noted in a statement this week that reauthorization is still a priority.

It has been revealed that “Sen. Fischer has been working closely with Chair Cruz on a bill and is having bipartisan discussions with Ranking Member Cantwell,” Wheeler said, referring to Sens. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, and Maria Cantwell, D-Wash.

According to recent reports, “Moving a bill as soon as possible remains a top priority for Sen. Fischer, including getting it through both chambers and signed into law by President Trump.”.

The House bill would extend authority for FirstNet through fiscal 2037, stagger terms on the authority’s board and require five members of the board with public safety backgrounds, rather than three as needed under current law.

At concern in the reauthorization debate, in part, is control of the First Responder Network Authority.

The House bill would eliminate language in current law that established FirstNet as an “independent” authority within the Commerce Department’s National Telecommunications and Information Administration and would require the administration’s approval for most non-planning or emergency actions, though the bill was amended to include a list of actions the network can take without NTIA approval.

The changes are meant to respond to reports from the Commerce Department's Office of Inspector General that found that the AT&T-run service was not sufficiently available during the Maui wildfires in 2023 and that senior officials of the FirstNet Authority attempted to interfere with audits.

Industry observers note that the Maui report noted the small number of FirstNet subscriptions among state and local first responders in the area and in an op-ed earlier this year, Maui Fire Chief Brad Ventura mentioned his department was “not using FirstNet devices” at the time of the fires but is now adopting them. He also supported reauthorization in the op-ed.

Related: First-responders network faced with calls for change.

But the shifting of control drew opposition from the Fraternal Order of Police, which prior to the bill’s committee markup urged its members to instead support a “clean reauthorization” of the program.

In a recent development, jim Pasco, executive director of the FOP, emphasized his group’s desire to see decisions made by the FirstNet board, rather than by NTIA. He noted that moving authority away from a group that is required to include first-responders would be “a threat to officer and public safety.”.

Yucel Ors, legislative director for public safety and crime prevention at the National League of Cities, noted that his group, along with the International Association of Fire Chiefs and other state and local government and public safety groups, worked closely with the House, including on the changes to put some “everyday controls and functions” back directly under the board’s control.

He said the National League of Cities supported the House bill, but that they hope that any changes made to FirstNet’s governance are “not going to impact the day-to-day operations that public safety depend on, rely on, and expect.”.

Ors remarked he expects the Senate would make changes to the House-passed bill, but he doesn’t know if those changes would come in the form of an amendment or an entirely newly introduced bill.

No proposed Senate amendment to the House bill, or alternative Senate bill, has yet to emerge.

He expressed concern over the timeline for reauthorization, especially if the Senate doesn’t take up the House bill as is.

A new Senate bill or amendment would require votes in both the House and Senate, with floor time dwindling as both chambers work through must-pass legislation before the end of the year.

It has been revealed that congress could potentially pass a short-term reauthorization of FirstNet. Ors expressed worry that option could jeopardize the public-private relationship with contractor AT&T.

Pasco stated he would prefer a short reauthorization over the House-passed bill, but said he hopes a full reauthorization could still pass this Congress.

The House bill has strong bipartisan support and the Senate’s negotiations are also bipartisan. Both Ors and Pasco expressed confidence that if time runs out this year for a reauthorization bill, a latest version of the legislation would still have strong prospects under a Democratic Congress.

Additional context regarding the role of FirstNet during the Maui fires was added to this report.

#77120. In 1988, ice covered 1.66 square miles near the summit of Indonesia’s Puncak Jaya, and now what is left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (801 w)

In 1988, ice covered 1.66 square miles near the summit of Indonesia’s Puncak Jaya, and now what is left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (801 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Landsat images show the ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya in Indonesia has dwindled to small patches that no longer flow like glaciers.
  • Industry observers note that in 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of New Guinea.
  • Sources indicate that that’s roughly 2 percent.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Landsat images show the ice near the summit of Puncak Jaya in Indonesia has dwindled to small patches that no longer flow like glaciers.

Industry observers note that in 1988, glaciers covered about 1.66 square miles (4.31 square kilometers) near the summit of Puncak Jaya, on the island of New Guinea. By September 2025, about 0.03 square miles (0.09 square kilometers) were left.

Sources indicate that that’s roughly 2 percent. What’s left would fit on about a dozen soccer fields.

It also no longer moves. The patches are too thin and too broken up to behave like a glacier, NASA Earth Observatory reported on November 16.

Puncak Jaya stands in the Sudirman Range, in the Indonesian part of New Guinea. Very few places this close to the equator have held ice all year round.

Next door is the largest stretch of warm ocean water on the planet. So the glaciers here sit near the warmest conditions in which year-round ice can survive at all.

It has been revealed that scientists have called them high-altitude canaries in the coal mine. Other members of that small club are what’s left of Humboldt Glacier in Venezuela, the ice fields of Kilimanjaro in Tanzania and the Quelccaya Ice Cap in Peru, a country that has lost more than half of its glaciers in six decades.

According to recent reports, NASA compared two false-color pictures of the range. Landsat 5 took one on November 3, 1988. Landsat 9 took the other on October 19, 2026.

Industry observers note that ice shows up light blue, bare rock brown, clouds white and plants green. In 1988, blue caps several of the highest ridges. In 2026 there are only a few small blue fragments, and brown rock covers most of the old icy ridgetops.

The area figures come from Donaldi Permana, a climate scientist at Indonesia’s Agency for Meteorology, Climatology, and Geophysics (BMKG). The 2025 number is based on satellite and aerial data.

An aerial survey is planned for December. It should show how much ice is left in 2026, Permana remarked.

The ice got thinner, too. At the main monitoring site, on the East Northwall Firn, it was 105 feet (32 meters) thick in 2010, Permana remarked.

In 2023 it measured 13 feet (4 meters). By November 2024 there was no ice there at all.

According to recent reports, thinning ice also cracks apart. Each new piece has fresh edges where it can melt, and so the losses feed on themselves.

Sources indicate that in the 2026 image, newly bared rock sits between the remnants. Snow still falls on the mountain. It just doesn’t stay on the bare rock long enough to turn into new ice.

“It’s a house of cards problem,” noted Chris Shuman, a retired University of Maryland glaciologist who has followed Puncak Jaya’s glaciers in satellite images. “Once this process gets going, there’s really no turning back.”.

To count as a glacier, a body of ice generally has to do two things. It has to be thick enough to creep downhill under its own weight. And it needs a zone where snow piles up faster than it melts.

On Puncak Jaya, the ice is now so thin, and so split into small, stagnant patches, that it has stopped flowing.

“While small ice remnants persist in high-altitude crevices around Puncak Jaya, their functional life as active glaciers is effectively over,” Permana stated.

El Niño years are especially rough on these glaciers. Warmer air pushes the freezing level above the summit, so rain falls instead of snow.

According to recent reports, fresh snow is white. It bounces sunlight away and protects the ice underneath. Without it, the darker surface soaks up heat and melts faster.

Recent findings suggest that during the 2015-2016 El Niño, the ice thinned about five times faster than normal, a finding NASA links to a study in PNAS. In one year it lost roughly 17 feet (5.3 meters) of thickness.

Industry observers note that then came the 2023-2024 El Niño. The ice thinned again, by about 7 to 13 feet (2 to 4 meters) a year.

Recent satellite studies suggest the main ice areas could be gone completely around 2030. For this, NASA links a study published in The Cryosphere.

Recent findings suggest that BMKG’s own estimates suggest the ice could disappear much sooner, Permana noted, with the current El Niño speeding things up. Either way, Puncak Jaya’s ice looks set to vanish well before Africa’s remaining glaciers, which may be gone by 2040.

NASA links the 2 percent figure to a World Meteorological Organization report, State of the Climate in the South-West Pacific 2025.

The information was obtained from NASA Earth Observatory.

#77118. Swordfish hunt about 2,000 feet down, but every so often one plunges as deep as a mile, and scientists suspect it is reading the ocean

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1083 w)
📖 Baca

Swordfish hunt about 2,000 feet down, but every so often one plunges as deep as a mile, and scientists suspect it is reading the ocean

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1083 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Earth

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet.
  • Swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface.
  • Sources indicate that satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Satellite tags on 34 North Atlantic swordfish caught rare dives past 3,280 feet. They were short and came near eddies and fronts, hinting the fish check the ocean.

Swordfish spend their days hunting in the dark, about 2,000 feet (600 meters) below the surface. Every so often, one keeps going.

Sources indicate that satellite tags on North Atlantic swordfish have caught these rare plunges past 3,280 feet (1,000 meters). Nobody knows why the fish make them.

It has been revealed that A team from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution (WHOI) has now looked at years of tagging data in search of an answer. The dives were short, fairly steady, and most common where surface temperatures varied and the sea surface stood higher. The authors think the fish may be sampling the water column, possibly to help them find their way. The study was published in Marine Biology.

It has been revealed that swordfish live in open oceans around the world, from about 45 degrees north to 45 degrees south. They follow a daily rhythm. By day they stay deep, usually between about 1,300 and 2,300 feet (400 and 700 meters), and at night they rise toward the surface.

Recent findings suggest that that routine follows their food. Huge numbers of small animals live in the ocean’s twilight zone and move up and down each day, and swordfish track them. Like other large predators of the open sea, tuna and swordfish get much of their food from that dim layer.

Swordfish can handle water from about 36 to 88 degrees Fahrenheit (2 to 31 degrees Celsius). They keep their eyes and parts of their body warmer than the surrounding water, which helps them stay deep for long periods.

In a recent development, the researchers combined data from 34 pop-up satellite tags placed on North Atlantic swordfish between 2003 and 2024. Twenty-three were tagged off the Atlantic coast of Florida, six near the Grand Banks off Canada, three in the southern Sargasso Sea and two in the Gulf of America, also known as the Gulf of Mexico. Twenty-four were probably adults and 10 were probably juveniles.

The tags stayed on for one to six months and logged depth, temperature and light. Together, they covered 3,666 days of swordfish life.

The data came from a partnership with NOAA’s Southeast Fisheries Science Center and the Massachusetts Division of Marine Fisheries.

“It wouldn’t have been possible to analyze this from just a single tagging operation, or from a single lab,” mentioned Simon Thorrold, a fish ecologist at WHOI and an author of the study.

The team flagged 39 days on which a fish went unusually deep for its own normal pattern. On 25 of those days, recorded by 10 tags, the data were detailed enough to confirm a distinct extreme dive.

These dives averaged about 3,250 feet (991 meters) at their deepest point, and the deepest reached roughly 5,460 feet (1,664 meters), more than a mile down. On ordinary days, the fish’s deepest point averaged about 2,090 feet (637 meters).

A single extreme dive lasted about 45 to 55 minutes on average. When a fish made one such dive in a day, it usually dropped two to three times faster than it climbed back. In one fish’s full-resolution record, it spent between a few seconds and about six minutes at the bottom.

It has been revealed that the water at the bottom of these dives averaged about 47 degrees Fahrenheit (8.4 degrees Celsius). On other days, the coldest water the fish met averaged about 54 degrees Fahrenheit (12.1 degrees Celsius).

Most dives started and ended in the twilight zone, during daylight. In 12 of 16 such dives, the fish came back to within about 33 feet (10 meters) of the depth where it began.

The authors weighed seven possible reasons for deep dives, including feeding, escaping predators, saving energy and navigation.

Feeding seemed unlikely. A hunting fish would be expected to linger at depth, but these fish barely paused at the bottom before heading back up. The dives also did not cluster at dawn and dusk, when prey is easiest to reach.

Escape did not fit well either. The descents were steady, about 3.3 feet (1 meter) per second, and the fish behaved normally afterward. Only one dive began and ended near the surface at night, when the authors think predators may be more likely to be around. The authors could not rule out that the two juveniles, which made several dives in a single day, were avoiding predators.

Extreme dives were much more likely where sea surface temperature varied a lot and where the sea surface stood higher. In the team’s model, each extra degree Celsius of temperature variation made a dive about 23 times more likely. These conditions mark swirling eddies, fronts and major currents such as the Gulf Stream.

It has been revealed that the authors suggest that crossing into a new water mass may prompt a swordfish to check what lies below. Short, repeatable dives of the same shape would fit that kind of sampling.

“They could be coming into an ocean weather system, like an eddy or a frontal system, where we have a change in water masses,” said Ciara Willis, who led the study as a doctoral student in the MIT-WHOI Joint Program and now works at the Monterey Bay Aquarium Research Institute.

Deeper water could also give a clearer reading of Earth’s magnetic field, which many fish can sense, away from the busy, changing layers near the surface. Some dives happened near seamounts, ridges and magnetic anomalies, but those links were weak, though rough seafloor highlighted a smaller but significant effect. Other ocean travelers are under similar suspicion, as oceanic manta rays also dive deep, apparently not to feed.

The authors stress that their conclusions are inferences. Satellite tag positions carry an average error of about 60 to 90 miles (100 to 150 kilometers), and possibly more for deep divers like swordfish. That makes it hard to match a dive to a specific seafloor feature.

It is still unclear how common these dives are among swordfish, and whether they differ between populations or ages.

Swordfish support valuable fisheries, so knowing what steers them could help predict where they go as the ocean changes.

The information was obtained from the study published in Marine Biology and from the Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

It has been revealed that A cordless stick vacuum has the potential to be one of the most convenient cleaning tools in your home. These lightweight machines make it easy to clean up pet hair from area rugs and hidden dust along baseboards, without having to haul out an upright vacuum or wrestling with a power cord. Most models also convert into handheld vacuums, giving you more flexibility to clean furniture, stairs, and other hard-to-reach spots.

Suction power, battery life, maneuverability, and dustbin capacities vary between models, so the right cordless stick vacuum ultimately depends on your home’s flooring, how much debris you’re dealing with, and the features that will actually make your cleaning routine easier.

We’ve rounded up the best cordless stick vacuums worth considering based on our hands-on experience, with options for everything from everyday maintenance to deeper carpet cleaning.

🔎 Looking for more ways to keep your floors and furniture clean? Check out our stories on the best robot vacuums, the best vacuums for pet hair, the best vacuums for hardwood floors, and the best handheld vacuums.

Industry observers note that I’ve spent considerable time researching, testing, and vetting all types of vacuums, so I’ve developed a pretty good understanding of what separates a genuinely useful appliance from one that is just going to take up space in your storage closet. I’ve evaluated a wide range of models, including full-size uprights, canister vacuums, robot, and handheld models vacuums, paying close attention to performance, ease of use, and features that can really make a difference in a your regular cleaning routine.

Sources indicate that when testing cordless stick vacuums, we assessed how well each model could handle common household debris, its ability to transition between carpet and hardwood floors, and how easy it was to move around furniture and into tighter spaces. We also looked at the practical considerations like battery life, suction power, dustbin capacity, weight, filtration, and included attachments.

Industry observers note that beyond just how the vacuum cleans, we also considered the overall experience for an owner. Removable batteries, self-cleaning docking stations, washable filters, and easy-to-empty dustbins can also make daily vacuuming less of a drag. The below recommendations are both powerful and dependable for a wide range of cleaning needs and surface types.

The Dyson V15 Detect is the most expensive stick vacuum in our lineup, but if you can stomach the price tag, you’ll get a cordless stick vacuum that (quite literally) leaves the competition in the dust across the board. It delivers top-notch performance on floors and carpets to tackle everything from fine dust and pet dander to larger debris.

According to recent reports, its motor spins up to 125,000 rpm and it comes with two cleaning heads, including an upgraded version of the brand’s “fluffy” head that features a green laser headlight to detect fine dust. During testing, we found that being able to switch from cordless to handheld made it easier to transition from tackling small messes to deeper cleaning sessions.

It has been revealed that the auto mode is a nice feature for conserving battery life, as this model only runs for about an hour off one charge. Another highlight is the motorized pet tool.

Full Dyson V15 Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

The PowerClean FurFinder is a more affordable alternative to the PowerClean FurGuard we recommend, but that doesn’t mean you have to give up useful features.

Industry observers note that this cordless stick vacuum is intended for use on a variety of floor types, and the flat-lay construction makes cleaning under furniture much more accessible. The vacuum also stands up on its own which leads to fewer interruptions during a cleaning session.

We love that both the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment come with headlights because it makes it a lot easier to see hidden dirt and debris. The brush roll is a tangle-free design, and the FurFinder is equipped with a HEPA filter for trapping small particles and allergens.

The motor on this vacuum is less powerful than the PowerClean, but it still provides plenty of suction for daily household cleaning.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurFinder Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

Since we’re big fans of the Shark AZ2002 Vertex upright vacuum for deep and thorough cleans, it’s no surprise that we like the cordless model in this lineup, too. The brush roll is excellent at pulling hair and large debris from carpets, as well as polishing up your hardwood floors. The cordless stick vacuum features an advertised runtime of 60 minutes.

According to recent reports, it also offers a HEPA filtration system and converts to a hand vac, and it also bends at the center of the wand to get around and under furniture. The Vertex comes with plenty of accessories for cleaning a variety of spaces. However, this may not be the best choice if you regularly clean stairs, as the cordless vacuum weighs roughly nine pounds—significantly more than other vacuums we cover.

In a recent development, I have two cats and live with my partner, which means there is plenty of mess to go around, from pet hair and dust to tracked-in dirt. I appreciate all the thoughtful features of the Tineco Station 5 because they make daily maintenance much easier.

Automatic suction adjustment has proved useful on my laminate and tile floors. I can hear when the motor gets a boost of power in a particularly dirty area, and it helps on carpets and area rugs where crumbs and debris tends to get trapped between the fibers. Add to that a green laser light for dust detection and you’ll hardly ever miss a spot.

I particularly like the base station. It has a 2.5-liter capacity, and after two months of using the Station 5, I still haven’t had to empty it. When I dock the vacuum onto the base, it automatically empties the onboard dustbin, cleans the floorhead brush roll, and charges the vacuum. Combined, these intuitive features make for a cleaning routine that is virtually hands-free.

Full Tineco Pure ONE Station 5 Pro Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

Even though the Dyson V11 Origin came out several years ago, that doesn’t mean this model has stopped being useful.

Sources indicate that the motorbar cleaner head works exceptionally well on carpet, successfully agitating fibers to pull up embedded dirt, dander, and hair. Suction is equally impressive, and there are three power modes depending on the level of cleaning you need. I ran the vacuum on medium most of the time, but I used boost occasionally whenever an area needed the extra attention.

This model doesn’t come with a soft roller brush vacuum head, and while it does work on all floor types, it can be loud on hardwood and laminate. But if your home is mostly carpet, this is a cordless stick vacuum I would reach for.

Full Dyson V11 Origin Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

Industry observers note that our tester has a busy household six pets, so there’s no question that she’s regularly cleaning up after her animals. Pulling out the upright vacuum daily isn’t convenient, so she turned to the Levoit LVAC-300 to fill the gap.

Recent findings suggest that this cordless stick vacuum has three different cleaning modes—eco, medium, and max—and she was able to cycle through each right from the handle depending on how much suction power she needed. She found that the vacuum was able to pick up litter and sand on different surfaces and between thresholds with ease.

Industry observers note that the attachments are useful for cleaning curtains, cushions, and staircases, but she was disappointed that there’s nowhere to store these tools on the vacuum itself. The LVAC-300 runs for up to 60 minutes depending on what mode you’re using, and the HEPA filter is a great feature if you have animals.

Full Levoit LVAC-300 Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

I used the Bissell PowerClean FurGuard across my apartment to clean laminate floors, area rugs, carpeting, and upholstery, and I fell in love with several features.

Recent findings suggest that the vacuum lays completely flat, making it really easy to get underneath furniture, and the swivel steering helps guide the FurGuard around tight spaces. Being a pet owner, I appreciate that the brush roll is tangle-free, so I don’t have to cut hair loose as often as I would with a standard, bristled brush roll.

Other highlights were lights on the main vacuum head and pet hair attachment. I was able to see collected dirt and debris that I would normally miss on hardwood flooring, carpet, and furniture. I also like that this model is designed to be self-standing.

Recent findings suggest that it’s hard to come by a cordless stick vacuum that you don’t have to re-mount or set on the ground during your cleaning session. With this model, I was able to stop and start with ease.

Full Bissell PowerClean FurGuard Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

In a recent development, we recently got our hands on one of the latest cordless stick vacuums from Shark, and we were impressed by the PowerDetect’s construction. The pole has a hinge in the center and when you release it, the vacuum bends to extend under furniture and hard-to-reach places. Our tester didn’t have to kneel down or adjust angles while he was cleaning thanks to the intuitive design.

In a recent development, beyond that, the PowerDetect vacuum uses sensors on the bottom of the floor head to discern between surface types, and adjusts suction power when needed. During testing, the motor could be heard transitioning speeds when used on hardwood and shag carpet.

Sources indicate that this vacuum also comes with a docking station, which automates the process of emptying out the dustbin. The vacuum itself can’t hold that much debris onboard, so it’s nice having a one-stop-shop for clearing out the bagless canister during a cleaning session. It’s a little heavy for a cordless stick vacuum, but it still gets the job done.

Full Shark PowerDetect Cordless Stick Vacuum Review.

Not every cordless stick vacuum we test ends up in this roundup. However, these other models still perform well and are reliable recommendations:.

Recent findings suggest that levoit Aero Cordless Vacuum Cleaner: The Tineco we’ve included above has more raw suction power, reaching up to 27,000Pa versus the 14,000Pa of the Levoit. However, one of the highlights of the Aero is the 3.5-liter-capacity dust bag in the docking station. Depending on your cleaning frequency, you could potentially go months without having to empty and replace it, and this design is better for keeping dust and dander from being expelled back into the air.

According to recent reports, dyson Gen5Detect Cordless Stick Vacuum: This cordless stick vacuum certainly commands a premium price, and you get a lot of the same features as the Dyson V15 Detect we recommend above, such as an LCD display screen, the Fluffy Optic cleaner head, and pet hair attachments. If you’re an allergy sufferer, you may prefer the Gen5Detect because its filtration system captures particles down to 0.1 microns, while the V15 filters down to just 0.3 microns. Plus, runtime is slightly longer on the Gen5Detect.

According to recent reports, the main advantages of owning a cordless stick vacuum are easy portability and storage. But what you trade for the convenience is battery life and runtime. Most models clean from 30 to 60 minutes, but that’s also dependent on what setting you’re using. If you’re running the vacuum on its highest speed the entire time, it might die faster. Be wary of manufacturers’ advertised total runtime because it may represent performance on the lowest setting or using two fully charged batteries, for instance. Battery charging should also be factored in, so initiative your cleaning session accordingly so you don’t lose power in the middle of a floor swipe.

Industry observers note that like we mentioned earlier, the dustbins on cordless stick vacuums are significantly smaller than those of an upright or canister unit. You should consider your cleaning habits and the spaces you usually vacuum to find a model that aligns with your needs. If you live in an apartment or are using the cordless vac to supplement your other cleaning supplies, then a dustbin with at least half a liter capacity should do. Some of the models we recommend hold up to one liter of debris, which helps limit the number of trips to the trash can.

Although not a necessity, having a good amount of attachments with your vacuum is especially helpful for cleaning hard-to-reach places or targeting specific problems. Crevice tools pick up dirt and dander from corners and couch cushions, while bristled brushes and motorized pet tools agitate and lift hair and fur that’s been embedded into upholstery.

A good filtration system helps combat allergens such as dust and pet dander that are being kicked up by a vacuum. The best option is a HEPA filter, or “high-efficiency particulate air” filter, which traps 99.97 percent of particles that are 0.3 microns or larger in size. A fully sealed or multi-step filtration system also has the potential to trap a wide variety of airborne allergens without releasing them back into your home.

Cordless vacuums are very effective at picking up pet hair, especially models designed with high suction power and specialized brush rolls. Some of the models we recommend include motorized attachments that lift embedded hair from upholstery and carpets. Anti-tangle vacuum heads are also a key feature that helps prevent hair from wrapping around the brush roll. While not all models perform equally, a high-quality cordless stick vacuum is able to handle pet hair just as well as traditional versions.

The lifespan of these vacuums typically lasts from three to five years, depending on usage, build quality, and maintenance. Battery performance plays a major role, since lithium-ion batteries start to lose capacity over time.

Avoiding overcharging and storing the vacuum properly could help extend the battery life significantly. Running regular maintenance like cleaning the vacuum filters and emptying the dustbin completely preserves suction and functionality. Higher-end models often last longer due to better materials and replaceable parts, but either price point has potential to last for years with proper care.

Recent findings suggest that modern designs are increasingly more effective at cleaning many surface types, including rugs and carpets. Advances in battery tech and general efficiency have allowed for strong suction performance that is comparable to corded models. Adjustable power modes allow for deeper cleaning on thicker carpets, and multi-roller and motorized brush heads agitate fibers to loosen dirt and debris.

It has been revealed that performance may vary depending on the type of flooring. Some vacuums are designed to work on low-to-medium pile carpets, while others are able to handle high-pile. It’s best to consult the listed features and specs of the model you’re considering to ensure it aligns with the flooring types in your home.
